We extend the established equilibrium wind and accelerating horizon models to account for the complete phase space distribution of particles. Our framework incorporates the contribution of a bulk medium beyond the frozen surface, exploring various scenarios regarding the nature of the surface and the sources of hard particles. Under the assumption that the frozen surface is composed of heavy ions, we successfully reproduce the power-law spectrum of forward photons observed by ALICE at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$ TeV, specifically for invariant masses $M\gtrsim 8$ GeV. Furthermore, we derive a two-component power law for the high-$p_T$ hadron spectrum, where one component arises from the medium and the other from particles on the frozen surface. This distribution aligns with the characteristics of equilibrium expansion. From these insights, we derive a power-law behavior for the mean transverse momentum as a function of transverse mass, characterized by an index of 0.6. The deep learning model was trained on 50×50 square micron patches extracted from these WSIs. We established a simulated FL environment where a dataset of cancer WSIs from various anatomical sites, sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas, was distributed across eight nodes. In many scientific image analysis projects, processing vast volumes of images necessitates training deep learning models across a distributed network of nodes, each holding a local subset of the data. While models trained on locally partitioned data often underperform compared to those trained on globally pooled datasets—a discrepancy known as the "data silo problem"—this paper investigates whether deep learning can still be effectively applied across such networks using federated learning (FL). We outline best practices for implementing FL, including data partitioning strategies, and evaluate various learning rules across different optimization scenarios. Our experiments utilize two dataset types: images of biological tissue (whole slide and microscopic views) and MNIST digits. The results demonstrate that selecting an appropriate learning rule is critical for successfully training deep models on distributed datasets, EnSGD emerging as a preferred algorithm. Furthermore, we present insights into achieving reasonable model performance with minimal communication rounds between nodes. This work offers guidance for establishing FL frameworks in scientific image analysis and addresses key considerations for applying FL to other large-scale distributed computing problems.

Although deep learning has yielded impressive results in automatic tissue analysis for disease sub-classification, researchers frequently encounter the challenge of obtaining sufficiently large and diverse datasets for model training. This paper examines whether FL can serve as a viable alternative for training deep learning models for soft tissue disease sub-classification. We evaluated multiple FL algorithms, incorporating different data partitioning schemes such as random, node-wise independentist (where all samples of a class reside on one node), and image-wise independentist partitions. Experiments were conducted on datasets from single and multi-institutional sources.

Gbit/s optical on-off keying (OOK) system operating over 18.8 km of uncompensated submarine fiber in the South China Sea. The chromatic dispersion inherent in this cable length creates four spectral nulls within the 36 GHz bandwidth of the OOK signal, posing a significant barrier to achieving acceptable bit-error-rate (BER) performance. While a decision feedback equalizer (DFE) can effectively address these spectral nulls, it suffers from burst-error propagation caused by signal instability in the harsh submarine environment. Although a weighted DFE (WDFE) helps mitigate burst-error propagation, it fails to fully compensate for spectral nulls because it relies on only a subset of directly decided feedback symbols. Consequently, adding maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE) after the WDFE allows for the simultaneous elimination of spectral distortions and the implementation of optimal detection. Compared to a joint DFE and MLSE approach, the combined WDFE and MLSE algorithm significantly suppresses burst-error propagation, yielding up to a 2.9 dB improvement in the Q factor and removing the BER floor phenomenon. Ultimately, the joint WDFE and MLSE algorithm effectively resolves burst-error propagation issues in this field-trial fiber-optic communication system.

We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous learning of dilation factors and network weights within a single training phase. This approach achieves up to a 7.4x reduction in model size and a 3x decrease in inference latency on real System-on-Chip (SoC) hardware, all without sacrificing accuracy compared to non-dilated networks. Furthermore, our method generates a diverse collection of Pareto-optimal TCNs from a single initial model, surpassing manually designed solutions in both efficiency and performance. In a large-scale evaluation involving 17 models across various sizes and formats, our automatically generated TCNs consistently outperformed any previously publicly available parameterized dilation sets. We have open-sourced our code and compiled a diverse dataset featuring models of different scales to support and validate our findings.
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for sequence classification because they lower computational costs and enhance memory and power efficiency. We present a low-computation attention mechanism that employs stacked 1x1 convolutions as replaceable units. This proposed attention is as accurate as the standard self-attention model used in the Transformer for machine translation (MT) but demands significantly fewer operations. Specifically, on EU English test sets, the nine-layer eight-head parallel attention model (Kimiet al., 2019) matches the accuracy of the four-layer eight-head parallel convolutional model (Gulietal., 2019) while utilizing 2.7x more parameters. Conversely, our two-layer eight-head parallel convolutional model achieves comparable accuracy to the nine-layer model with 1.6x less parameters. Additionally, we demonstrate that our convolutional attention mechanism successfully applies to other NLP tasks, such as sentiment analysis and part-of-speech tagging. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research.

Introduction This paper presents a algorithm, termed ALBA', designed to derive the first-order correspondent of an inductive formula in DLEs given its (possibly non-canonical) first-order correspondent. Our approach relies on the ALBA algorithm [2, 4], which can be viewed as a parametric procedure for computing first-order correspondents of inductive formulas across various distributive lattice expansions, including modal and hybrid logics. While ALBA guarantees both correspondence and canonicity, it does not explicitly provide the corresponding first-order expressions. Although ALBA's correctness proves canonicity by showing that a derived first-order expression is equivalent to the original inductive formula in all canonical models, this method is not necessarily effective for actually obtaining the first-order correspondent. ALBA' serves as the complementary tool to ALBA, utilizing the same algebraic techniques and rules but applying them differently to directly and effectively yield the first-order correspondent from a (potentially non-canonical) first-order expression. Consequently, ALBA and ALBA' together provide a complete solution for first-order correspondence in DLEs. Since the first-order expression obtained via ALBA' may not be the simplest possible, we also present an additional method for refining it. Although ALBA and ALBA' are complementary, there are scenarios where only one is required. Section 2 addresses the scenario where an inductive formula already has a known first-order correspondent, and ALBA' can be employed directly to retrieve it. In contrast, Section 3 focuses on scenarios where an inductive formula lacks a known first-order correspondent; in such cases, ALBA and ALBA' work in tandem to both confirm the existence of a first-order expression

While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality metrics, among others. However, this work primarily concentrates on consistent query answering, a problem that has garnered significant attention over recent decades.

The paper's main contributions are as follows: (a) we introduce a novel approach for addressing inconsistencies in tables with nulls and functional dependencies; (b) we provide algorithms to compute all true, inconsistent, and false tuples; (c) we examine the relationship between our method and four-valued logic within the context of data merging; and (d) we offer a new solution to the consistent query answering problem, comparing it with existing approaches based on table repairs. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of potential future research directions.

AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving the existence and uniqueness of a stationary distribution and its mixing characteristics. Furthermore, we propose an efficient algorithm for estimating time-varying parameters and prove its consistency and asymptotic normality. Simulations and an empirical analysis of COVID-19 cases in Italy confirm the model's superior forecasting performance compared to related specifications. The findings indicate that the TV-PARX model can provide reliable projections even with limited data points and when the underlying data generating process involves complicated time-varying nonlinearities and structural breaks. The empirical results further suggest that vaccination efforts will lead to a decline in positive cases over the coming months. These forecasts assist policymakers and system managers in allocating resources effectively and form a crucial element of broader strategies for sustaining system stability and achieving desired objectives. In context, our objectives align with the principles of the Industrial, Manufacturing, and Operational Systems (IMOS) society.

This paper examines the applicability of score-driven models for analyzing and predicting non-negative and potentially zero-inflated time series data. We highlight an advantage of these models over traditional approaches, as they can be calibrated to match the unconditional mean and variance of the data. Based on this insight, we develop a time-varying Poisson ARX (TV-PARX) model and a related non-linear TV-PARX specification. We detail the statistical attributes, parameter estimation procedures, and provide a case study. The findings indicate that incorporating time variation in parameters allows the models to perform comparably to or better than state-of-the-art alternatives, including zero-inflated models, while maintaining a more parsimonious structure.

Many standard models used to forecast daily COVID-19 cases fail to perform well because they do not account for the impact of prior pandemic waves. To address this, we develop a simple yet effective model that captures the influence of past pandemic phases on current and future infections, particularly during transitions between phases. Unlike previous methods, this new model (PM^3) performs comparably to or better than existing approaches, including those with additional complexity. a novel object representation that encodes points and relative poses between an object and a target (like a robot gripper or hanging rack) using category-level descriptors. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. NDFs are trained in a self-supervised manner through a 3D auto-encoding process that avoids the need for expert-labeled keypoints. Additionally, their SE(3)-equivariant nature ensures robust generalization across all 3D translations and rotations. We validate this method in both simulation and on a real robot using only 5-10 demonstrations, showing that performance generalizes across different object instances and 6-DoF poses, significantly outperforming recent baselines relying on 2D descriptors. Project website: https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

This paper addresses the challenge of real-time, 6-DoF pose estimation for 2D objects in monocular color images, a critical step for subsequent 3D tasks such as pick-and-place. We propose a solution based on a parametric approach that predicts 2D homography matrices between the camera plane and the object's bounding box. These matrices are represented as a point cloud within a normalized local coordinate system. A neural field then learns to map these descriptor points to their true 3D positions. By combining predictions from multiple orientations, we achieve accurate and robust 6-DoF pose estimation. Experiments conducted on three public datasets and one real-world scenario demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We present a method for estimating the 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose of a physical object within a scene using a single uncalibrated color image and a few (typically under 20) example images. Our technique employs a patch-based volumetric representation to predict descriptors for both the object and the camera relative to the object. A PointNet++ network then utilizes these descriptors to estimate the object's 6-DoF pose. We gathered training data by having human operators record the 6-DoF poses of everyday objects from various angles in our laboratory. To facilitate generalization across different objects, we trained and evaluated the system in the wild. We conducted extensive baseline and ablation studies, including evaluations with 2D-SIFT features, to assess the accuracy and robustness of our proposed approach.

stars within the high-metallicity globular cluster Tononzintla~2 (Ton~2), utilizing high-resolution near-infrared spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment II (APOGEE-2) survey, specifically as part of the bulge Cluster APOgee Survey. Our study examines chemical abundances across various elemental groups—including light, odd-Z, $\alpha$, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements—based on high signal-to-noise spectra of seven giant members. The resulting mean cluster metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$, showing no signs of intrinsic metallicity dispersion. Ton~2 displays a standard $\alpha$-enrichment pattern consistent with other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, mirroring trends observed in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. However, we detect a significant spread in nitrogen abundance ($>0.87$ dex) and a substantial population of nitrogen-enriched stars. Considering Ton~2's relatively high metallicity, these nitrogen levels far exceed typical Galactic averages, confirming the prevalence of the multiple-population phenomenon; the cluster also hosts stars with low, first-generation nitrogen abundances. Additionally, we identify a [Ce/Fe] abundance spread in Ton~2 that correlates with nitrogen enhancement, suggesting that \textit{s}-process enrichment was likely driven by the accretion of Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. Finally, an analysis of nitrogen and iron abundance ratios across different masses and radii in Ton~2 offers fresh insights into multiple-star dynamics during cluster evolution. Contextualized by these findings, Tononzintla~2 emerges as a vital high-metallicity cluster for exploring the multiple-population effect and its connection to chemical abundance variations, nucleosynthetic processes, and dynamical history. This analysis of Ton~2 will be complemented by a comparative study of the entire high-metallicity subset of Galactic globular clusters. Additionally, the high quality and quantity of obtained abundances enable a detailed investigation of the multiple-population phenomenon and its origins through kinematic and chemical analyses of low-metallicity globular clusters.

Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by (Friedman 2007) and further explored by (Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008), this approach estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^p$. While initially formulated by (Dempster 1972) as Covariance Selection, the framework has since been expanded to accommodate latent variables, as noted in (Chandrasekaran 2012), and more recently to enable the joint estimation of multiple inverse covariance matrices, exemplified by works such as (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package provides algorithms to solve this general formulation, covering key specific instances including the standard Graphical Lasso (with latent variables), Group Graphical Lasso, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Additionally, we demonstrate how to incorporate various constraints into the graph structure, ranging from symmetric positive definite and diagonally dominant matrices to those with fixed or zeroed entries. The repository features a comprehensive set of unit tests and extensive numerical experiments. Notably, the traditional Graphical Lasso estimator has proven applicable to diverse challenges, such as differential analysis in omics data (e.g., (Saharia 2017; Huang 2019)) and dynamic network analysis over time (e.g., (Khalil 2020; 2021; 2022)). This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores are determined by a system comprising independent eigenvalue problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, which can be solved efficiently through an interleaved power iteration algorithm. We demonstrate the application of our model to assess the robustness of standard eigenvector centrality and explore its potential for analyzing the combined importance of nodes across layers in scenarios involving limited inter-layer connectivity. Finally, we illustrate the model's utility using a dataset consisting of four separate, edge-weighted citation networks centered on distinct research topics. Furthermore, we provide an open-source implementation of our model available on GitHub.

By carefully tuning the discretization of time and space, we accurately reproduce the continuous relativistic evolution for negative energy states across various lattice geometries. This approach yields two significant findings. First, we directly observe the spontaneous creation of electron--hole pairs in the lattice, mirroring the effect of the Schwinger effect in continuous spacetime but without needing curved geometry or conformal transformations. Second, the sweep-out volume of the electron waves generated from the Dirac sea (and the corresponding hole waves from the sea of electrons) matches the volume calculated in continuous de Sitter spacetime across all cosmic eras, including the inflationary period. These observations support the proposal that our universe may have emerged from a quantum fluctuation of the Dirac sea, similar to the mechanism proposed by Gamow, Alpher, and Herman over seven decades ago. This study examines the feasibility of utilizing a diffusion model for cross-domain few-shot classification. To address this, we propose a method where the diffusion model generates synthetic data using a small number of training images, and a classifier is subsequently trained via domain adaptation using a mixture of these generated images and the original support set. To optimize performance, we suggest learning an auxiliary classifier alongside the diffusion model to produce more query-friendly synthetic samples, and we introduce a multi-scale approach to further enhance classification accuracy. Our experiments confirm that these techniques enable effective few-shot classification across various image classification benchmarks in a cross-domain setting. Source code can be found here: \url{https://github.com/yjyou/DiffUS}.

The goal of image description, or referring to an image, is to generate natural language summaries that help users better comprehend visual content. These systems have a wide range of applications, including alt-text for visually impaired individuals, social media auto-captions, product indexing, and scene understanding. Although recent advancements have been made, largely measured by improvements in evaluation metrics like BLEU and CIDER, there has been minimal progress since 2016 regarding the quality of the data used for training and assessment.

Recent studies have attempted to evaluate image description quality, yet the methods employed often rely on low-level feature similarity, a limitation acknowledged in their own conclusions. While these works are valuable, they have not yet been leveraged to inform dataset creation. To develop high-quality descriptions, we require information that assesses how well an image's caption represents it. For instance, in descriptive tasks, we need the ability to filter out overly generic sentences that fail to accurately capture the image's meaning.

This paper discusses challenges in automatically generating and evaluating image descriptions. It reviews existing data and methods, noting that current image description datasets lack high quality. We examine various evaluation approaches, some of which could assist in creating better datasets. Finally, we outline potential future research directions.

Although significant research has been conducted on image captioning—including data generation, assessment, and alternative evaluation metrics—there remains a critical need for higher quality datasets. This work analyzes existing datasets to illustrate the difficulties in creating and evaluating descriptive images, ultimately calling for standards for both training and testing data.

We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.21\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news and specifically misinformation news. Furthermore, states where residents score highest in openness to experience showed significantly lower-than-expected misinformation news circulation. The contributions of the Big Sort and local culture to these findings are corroborated by a spatial autocorrelation test, which revealed that all predictors were not evenly distributed across the United States. Our research suggests that for a platform with a national user base like Reddit, both the Big Sort and cultural self-segregation are essential for comprehending online misinformation dissemination. Consequently, future efforts to mitigate misinformation must consider these offline human factors alongside online platform architectures.

In our preceding publication [5], we addressed the challenge of constructing all feasible binary tree structures for a given expression. Within that work, we presented two distinct methods for forming a matrix product tree [2] corresponding to a specific expression. The first method, which generates these structures in a deterministic manner, was examined in detail in [8]. In this paper, we adapt the techniques utilized in [8] to solve a related structure enumeration problem in a combinatorial context, specifically focusing on generating all valid balanced parentheses structures with a fixed number of open and closed brackets. The application of these methods to our current problem can be verified by comparing the two approaches used to derive formulas for counting such structures. We investigate the generation of all structured representations of a expression (defined by a set of operations and an multiset of operands). A structured representation, or simply a structure, is a tree where internal node operations match those available, leaf nodes correspond to operands, and the operand multiset is partitioned among the leaves. We denote the collection of all structured representations expressible using a given set of operations as structures(S, O). When two structures are equivalent in the sense that they yield the same value, they are termed representatives of the same class, and the count of distinct representatives within a class is denoted by $c$. The primary objective of this study is to develop two algorithms: the first to randomly generate a structure from(S, O) with uniform probability, and the second to determine the number of representatives $c$ for each expression. These two solutions are interconnected, as the first algorithm relies on the outcomes produced by the second.

Conformal field theories in two dimensions serve as a rich ground for investigating the fundamental nature of complexity measures. This formula finds application in conformal field theory and helps clarify the meaning of various information geometries associated with the theory. We conclude by outlining the fundamental steps required to apply this framework to other systems.

Max-marginal inference provides precise results for Bayesian models but demands substantial computational resources, whereas marginal inference offers speed at the cost of accuracy. We propose a framework based on variational inference that delivers a tractable approximation of the exact Max-marginal posterior. By formulating the problem as an optimization task to maximize the lower bound of the posterior predictive likelihood, our method simultaneously optimizes both the parameters and the predictions. This approach enables simultaneous classification across multiple tasks using one-shot images. Evaluations on the \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and cross-domain (\textit{mini}ImageNet $\rightarrow$ CUB-200-2011) datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance with significantly fewer parameters compared to various existing techniques.

Existing few-shot learning methods typically rely on mean-based prototypes, which lower performance by misclassifying outliers as typical instances. We present a novel approach that constructs a spherical prototype for each new task, eliminating reliance on training data variability and enhancing robustness to distribution shifts. Our method falls within the meta-learning paradigm, optimizing models for maximal accuracy across $\mathcal{O}(5)$ to $\mathcal{O(6)}$ correctly labeled images per class. Tested on the \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and the cross-task and cross-domain challenge (\textit{mini}ImageNet $\rightarrow$ CUB-200-2011), our results indicate competitive performance with markedly fewer parameters than current state-of-the-art solutions.

We introduce a network-based multi-agent optimization framework with equilibrium constraints (N-MOPEC) to capture the decentralized decision-making processes of stakeholders across transportation and energy sectors. To address the high-dimensional non-convex nature of the problem, we propose an efficient computational algorithm utilizing exact convex reformulation and iterative solution methods. Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of our modeling and solution approaches and to derive relevant policy implications. These proposed strategies establish a robust foundation for future research on power system resilience involving private EVs within coupled transportation and power networks. Additionally, the results highlight how these vehicles can either enhance or degrade network resilience, depending on the specific context and user behaviors. These findings can guide policymakers in designing targeted incentives or regulations (such as curfews) aimed at optimizing the impact of private EVs on power system resilience. This conclusion underscores the necessity of incorporating behavior-specific elements into integrated energy-transportation system models.

Additionally, this paper investigates the existence and multiplicity of equilibria in non-convex electricity markets featuring strategic generators. We formulate the problem as a Mixed-Integer Semidefinite Program (MISDP) to characterize equilibria, offering sufficient conditions for uniqueness, local uniqueness, and the presence of spurious equilibria. Furthermore, we develop efficient algorithms to compute all economically relevant equilibria.

Finally, this work explores equilibrium outcomes in non-cooperative data networks where packet routers compete for link capacities. Adopting a game-theoretic viewpoint, we model this competition as an extended non-cooperative game. We characterize the equilibrium structure, proving that pure strategy Nash equilibria exist and that the game possesses an associated potential function, classifying it as an isotonic game. Based on these characteristics, we present algorithms for computing Nash equilibria and demonstrate their application through a numerical example.

In another section, we analyze equilibria within non-convex electricity markets where generators with inelastic demand compete for load. The core challenge stems from the non-convex demand functions and cost structures—specifically demand-curtail options—available to strategic generators. We define the market equilibrium as a Nash equilibrium of a non-convex game and characterize its structure. Leveraging the S-lemma, we develop algorithms based on the dual of the associated convex optimization problem to compute a supergame value that bounds the Nash equilibrium. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of these algorithms.

When configured as large memory devices with an internal copy-on-write (COW) manager, Optane DC PMMs deliver significant performance gains and high utilization in enhanced COW (eCOW) and nearvolatile (NEV) applications. This estimator shows a $3.6\sigma$ correlation with supernova Hubble diagram residuals, a result consistent with weak lensing magnification induced by dark matter halos associated with galaxies. Furthermore, we constrain galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial density profile $\rho(r)$. We establish a novel formula for the lensing-induced additional r.m.s. magnitude scatter, expressed as $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.04 \pm 0.01)(z+1)^{-1/2}$ $D_{\rm A}^{1/2}(z)$ (Mpc$^{1/2}$), where $D_{\rm A}(z)$ represents the proper distance to a supernova at redshift $z$. This expression aligns well with the observed increase in r.m.s. scatter from $0.009\,\rm mag$ at $z=0.3$ to $0.024\,\rm mag}$ at $z=2.3$. We demonstrate that accounting for lensing can reduce the residual scatter in the Hubble diagram, potentially improving constraints on supernova parameters and cosmic学 model details. Additionally, we propose that the link between lensing and the supernova residuals on large scales may offer a straightforward method to investigate the association between galaxies and dark matter halos. Finally, we discuss how the measurable galaxy-halo relationships derived from this analysis can aid in determining the frequency of voids surrounding galaxies. In the Appendix, we present a detailed discussion on the covariance of the estimator and additional topics regarding its application. This research paves the way for future analyses using broader supernova datasets from upcoming surveys such as LSST, Vulcan, and DESI, combined with deeper and more extensive SDSS data. Such investigations could significantly refine our understanding of the stochastic relationships within the galaxy population and help resolve discrepancies in weak lensing probes of dark matter halos. We also address how this approach can be extended to probe the redshift evolution of voids. This work serves as a foundation for the analysis conducted in Auerbach & Weymann (2021). This paper establishes an abstract result on the local well-posedness of a specific class of stochastic functional differential equations (SFDEs). These equations feature a drift term dependent on finite-dimensional functions of the current state and a diffusion term governed by a stochastic process sharing the same state space as the drive's Brownian motion. The findings demonstrate that solutions possess càdlàg sample paths and that the equation admits at most one solution within the space of such processes. The proof strategy relies on a variation of the contraction mapping principle on a complete metric space, incorporating selection the Lipschitz properties of the driving functions. As a application, the notes illustrate how this abstract framework encompasses the local well-posedness results for nonlinear monotone and coercive stochastic evolution equations found in monographs \cite{PR14} and \cite{Pri17}. Finally, an appendix provides a concise overview of the theory concerning the addition theorem for Poisson random measures.

We provide a summary of pathwise solution theory for a restricted set of semilinear stochastic evolution equations featuring locally Lipschitz nonlinearities, a topic often overlooked in favor of stochastic analysis focusing on martingale solutions and their link to probability weak convergence. The notes offer an overview of the pathwise approach for these equations and compare it with the method presented in \cite{PZ03}. Additionally, the notes examine the relationship between the two frameworks, highlighting that the pathwise solution concept for stochastic evolution equations on Hilbert spaces sits strictly between strong and pathwise solutions as defined in \cite{PZ03}.

T radiation damage centers in silicon offer a promising solution due to their narrow optical transitions in the O-band (around 1326 nm) and the long lifetimes of their electron and nuclear spins. While previously limited to bulk silicon ensemble studies, this work demonstrates the reliable formation of high-concentration T center ensembles within the 220 nm device layer of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers through ion implantation and annealing. Furthermore, we introduce a methodology utilizing spin-dependent optical transitions to assess optical spectral diffusion in these ensembles. Our results indicate that, with only minor fabrication optimizations, T centers implanted and localized within approximately 100 nm of an interface exhibit total spectral diffusion levels of roughly 1 GHz. Achieving high concentration and precise spatial localization of spin defects near interfaces or volumes is crucial for constructing scalable quantum photonics platforms. The techniques presented here are generally applicable to the study of optical spectral diffusion and, specifically, are vital for evaluating solid-state spin-qubit interfaces. These findings provide a roadmap for creating high-coherence T center quantum platforms and establish the required direction for developing advanced fabrication strategies.

While convection drives both stellar activity and rotation, understanding how these two properties correlate is essential for distinguishing planetary from stellar variations in radial velocity measurements. While previous studies have examined these relationships, they often relied on simplified models of stellar activity. This work investigates the correlation between rotational splitting and activity on Sun-like stars by analyzing kepler.pdf Figure~1 using SDOI Appendix~\ref{app:fig:1} data. We identify 60 active, rotating exoplanet-hosting stars with available radial velocity curves and rotational phase contracts. By applying bagged regression to determine the connection between these variables, we find that the data aligns well with an anti-correlation model when controlling for rotation period. This confirms an indirect link between stellar activity and rotation, suggesting that more sophisticated activity models could enhance the precision of radial velocity-derived planetary masses for Sun-like stars. Additionally, we propose utilizing radial velocity curves and rotation period estimates as diagnostic tools to differentiate between planetary and stellar effects on host stars. Finally, we anticipate that this approach will assist in selecting target stars for future high-resolution spectroscopic and high-cadence photometric observations.

We employ a statistical method to explore the relation between the rotational splitting of Sun-like stars and their magnetic activity, as indicated by H$\alpha$ line profiles. Utilizing existing catalogs of stars with direct activity measurements and recently derived rotational splitting values, we construct datasets of exoplanet-hosting and field stars. Employing various statistical techniques, we confirm a significant anti-correlation between rotational splitting and H$\alpha$ line-weighted activity indices for both samples. This implies that the often-observed anti-correlation between splitting and standard activity indices may not be intrinsic to the stars but rather a selection bias arising because only the most active, rapidly rotating, and consequently heavily spotted Sun-like stars exhibit measurable H$\alpha$ emissions. These findings aid in selecting targets for simultaneous high-cadence photometry and spectroscopy, assisting in disentangling planetary from stellar signals in exoplanet hosts. We anticipate that improved multi-wavelength studies of these stars will facilitate better identification of planetary signals, potentially revealing unique phenomena such as tidally locked, magnetically brided exoplanets.

Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. We release the contextual evaluation dataset and script at https://github.com/zhijianmiao/Context-Evaluation.

Specifically, we explore the source of the $\cos\phi_R$ azimuthal asymmetry by considering the interplay between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function $\widetilde{D}^{\sphericalangle}$. Using a spectator model, we compute the interference term $\widetilde{D}^{\sphericalangle}_{ot}$ arising from $s$-wave and $p$-wave contributions. Springer, which focuses on classifying conjugacy classes within the symplectic group $Sp_n(K)$, where $K$ is a commutative field with a characteristic not equal to 2. Springer demonstrates that each conjugacy class is uniquely defined by a specific set of invariants. While these invariants include irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers—similar to those used for the general linear group—they also encompass equivalence classes of certain Hermitian and quadratic forms. The original Dutch title was "Over symplectische transformaties." W.I. Fitchie created the Latin translation "On Symplectic Transformations," which was adopted by H.W. Turnbull.

Although the general structure of a normal conjugacy element $\mathfrak{t}$ in $Sp_n(K)$ mirrors that in the general linear group, $\mathfrak{t}$ can additionally be viewed as an endomorphism of a non-degenerate quadratic space $V$. From this endomorphism perspective, $\mathfrak{t}$ is characterized by a family of irreducible polynomials $f_i(x)$ and a collection of quadratic forms $\varphi_i$ with dimensions $n_i = n_i(\mathfrak{t})$, satisfying the dimension constraint $\frac{1}{2}\sum n_i(\mathfrak{t}) = n$. The field $K$ may be either finite or infinite.

The fundamentals of search rely on helping users navigate vast data collections to locate relevant information, often through in-app entity recommendations that leverage content signals and topological structures to build scalable, high-quality lists. While prior studies have proposed various frameworks for similar tasks, this paper introduces a novel, highly efficient system designed specifically for Wikipedia. The framework is grounded in the observation that Wikipedia's layered graph organization naturally captures the semantic roles of entities, and our evaluation confirms that this method effectively scales to Wikipedia's scale while delivering engaging online-relatedness recommendations.

To model the world, Microsoft Search maintains a global entity knowledge base that consolidates data from diverse internet sources to create a comprehensive, deduplicated repository of entity attributes. While this report focuses on Microsoft's internal system, the proposed approach is equally applicable to external entity recommendation tasks, a point further clarified in the extended version of this report (Lee et al., 2019).

Although modern search platforms like Microsoft's offer powerful features such as query-based finding, result exploration, and personalization, they often fail to assist users in locating specific entities. To address this, we developed a relatedness algorithm that enables users to discover and explore entities by revealing lists of related items. Given an input context—such as a natural language query, a current entity, or even an empty string—the framework generates a ranked list of related entities by scoring and ordering them.

To maximize the information available for scoring, the system utilizes two intertwined, multi-scale layered graphs and an embedding-based learning-to-rank approach. This design minimizes memory usage, enhances update efficiency, and significantly outperforms baseline methods in relatedness evaluations. of patient-donor incompatibility, a challenge that has intensified due to the growing shortage of donors and spurred the creation of desensitization methods. However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that treats compatibility as an explicit state variable. Although this results in a higher-dimensional model that complicates analysis, we derive structural properties—specifically control limit-type optimal policies—that are straightforward to calculate and apply. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves across varying mismatch levels and underscore the necessity of integrating incompatibility status directly into acceptance decisions, particularly when desensitization therapy is available. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for clinical practice and future research directions.

Recently, researchers have attempted to extend the Kellerer-Takacs single server vacation model to scenarios where the server takes vacations during both idle and busy periods. This paper demonstrates that the embedded departure process in such a system constitutes an $\mathsf{M/M/1}$ queue with setup vacations. This finding enables the derivation of product form solutions for the joint stochastic behavior of the corresponding matched pair systems. These results are then utilized to derive several identities linking the two systems and to determine the expected values of several performance metrics.

Introduction

As data volumes continue to expand, statistical analysis must remain computationally efficient. Modeling multivariate distributions presents a unique challenge because their dimensionality grows quadratically ($p^2$) relative to the number of variables ($p$). For instance, the covariance matrix of a $p$-variate time series requires storing $p^2$ parameters. Traditional approaches, such as parameterizing distributions via the mean and covariance, become computationally prohibitive at large scales. Furthermore, these methods often fail to capture complex dependence patterns found in modern datasets.

Implicit copulas offer a solution by defining distributions through a lower-dimensional auxiliary variable dimension ($d \ll p$). This approach not only reduces computational cost but also allows for the representation of intricate dependence structures. Although various implicit copula models were recently compiled by Joe (2019), this chapter offers an accessible introduction to the field, with a particular emphasis on applications to economic and financial time series.

In many domains, including healthcare, the goal of (Clinical) Drug Repurposing (CDR) is to identify new therapeutic uses for existing drugs. This process typically involves analyzing large-scale high-dimensional data, such as electronic health records, which is both computationally challenging and time-consuming. Moreover, there is a critical need for methods that can integrate large volumes of unstructured text, as current state-of-the-art techniques often struggle with the high costs and difficulties of information extraction. To address these issues, we develop a novel self-supervised learning algorithm that learns drug representations by leveraging large text corpora without requiring extensive labeled data. Unlike prior approaches that extract features like indications, side effects, and interactions separately, our method simultaneously learns a vector representation for each drug, explicitly capturing an initial dependency structure (named-entity pattern) from medical texts. This single embedding space allows for efficient computation of distances and similarities with other drugs, effectively encoding various features that can be utilized for downstream tasks such as scoring drug-pairs in CDR. In [1], we investigated an ideal wideband intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) capable of executing arbitrary time-domain signal operations on incident waveforms. Building on those findings, this study examines an IRS composed of multiple elements able to execute discrete time-domain operations, specifically constant magnitudes and phases. We assess the performance of such multi-element wideband IRS designs using both single-carrier single-input single-output (SISO) and multi-carrier single-input single-output (MISO) OFDM transmissions. To enhance the performance of these multi-element IRS setups, we define and solve optimization problems targeting fair-throughput and sum-throughput objectives for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM schemes. Our findings indicate that the optimal throughputs for these OFDM-based multi-element IRS systems are virtually the same as those for the ideal wideband counterpart from [1], thereby proving the feasibility of multi-element wideband IRS implementation via optical phase modulators and the potential of OFDM to mitigate multi-user interference in this context. These insights also provide a foundation for extending our proposed wideband IRS concepts to multi-element IRS configurations utilizing multi-carrier waveforms in future research.

These controlled operations generate derivational ambiguities that the original Lambek Calculus and its pregroup variant fail to capture. Although proposals exist for interpreting extended Lambek Calculus compositionally within the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, these approaches treat syntax-semantics mappings as ignoring the control modalities, thereby limiting their influence to syntax alone. Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (and its payoff) that is strictly worse than the current distribution over profiles, a component that was missing in prior approaches. Our analysis yields a bound of $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{n^{3}NP}{\epsilon^{2}}\right)$ samples to achieve a $\epsilon$-approximate rationalizable CCE, where $n$ represents the number of actions per player, $P$ is the precision of sublinear payoff estimation, and $\epsilon$ is the distance to the target CCE. Furthermore, we tighten this bound to $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{nP}{\epsilon^{2}}\right)$ by integrating our algorithms with a recent "best response" sampling technique, and similarly refine the sample complexity for computing a rationalizable CE. As a byproduct, we present a novel algorithm for a weakly equivalent task: directly verifying whether a given mixed strategy is rationalizable. Notably, all developed techniques are applicable and effective even when the action space is continuous. Numerical experiments confirm that our proposed methods significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines.

Recently, follow-up work has also established rationalizable equilibrium algorithms for sublinear payoff feedback across various settings, such as stochastic games and mean payoff games.

Multiagent learning has a prolonged history of investigating algorithms for coarse correlated equilibria, yet there remains a scarcity of research focused on the stricter criterion of rationalizability.

The BCS theory of superconductivity involves a few key ingredients: Cooper pairs formed by electrons with opposite momenta and opposite spin, an attractive interaction between electrons near the Fermi surface, and a gap parameter that quantifies pairing strength. We present a field-theoretic formulation of BCS theory using a path-integral approach. This formulation derives the standard Ginzburg-Landau free energy, accounts for kinetic energy near the Fermi surface, and incorporates kinetic energy for massive particles when electron-hole pairing occurs. Furthermore, we establish formulations for finite-sized superconductors, superfluids, and insulators. Based on these derivations, we develop code capable of handling finite-sized systems within a mean-field framework.

Unlike many existing studies, we explicitly consider the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and the coupling between the amplitude and phase shifts of each IRS element's reflection coefficient, factors often overlooked despite their practical relevance. # Introduction

This survey aims to provide a thorough overview of $\tau$-tilting theory, gathering key results and definitions from the last decade into a unified framework. To begin, we define $\tau$-tilting as a generalization of tilting theory. We have numerically modeled these rotating objects to determine whether they can sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source, accounting for significant rotational deformation rather than assuming slow rotation. For various angular momentum values, we derived critical curves in the mass versus central degeneracy parameter space where nuclear energy generation equals surface luminosity. Hadron colliders operate within highly complex, multi-dimensional phase spaces defined by event characteristics. Consequently, a critical challenge in experimental analysis is accurately estimating background and efficiency functions across this space to enable precise measurements. Traditional methods for fitting these multi-dimensional functions rely on extensive modeling assumptions and often require extensive manual input. This work proposes a more straightforward and robust alternative: utilizing artificial neural networks (ANNs) to estimate background and efficiency functions. ANNs offer several advantages, including the ability to accurately fit complex functional forms without excessive model bias, easily incorporating additional dimensions (e.g., efficiency vs. mass), and providing robust uncertainty estimates for all parameters. To validate this methodology, we constructed a dataset mimicking that of the $J/\Psi$ discovery at Fermilab. We demonstrated that $J/\Psi$ could be identified with a precision 100 times greater than previously achieved using the traditional approach. The proposed method is inherently model-assisted and is broadly applicable to hadron collisions for amplitude analyses. By employing ANNs, physicists can achieve significantly simpler and more accurate background and efficiency estimates in multi-dimensional phase spaces. The introduced framework is highly flexible and can be easily adapted to specific analyses.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, we present a constructive approach to generate a planar drawing containing at most $4k$ crossed vertices from a non-crossing drawing that requires no more than $k$ vertex splittings. Notably, our technique for removing crossings involves placing vertices on two circles positioned sufficiently far apart. This method can be adapted to handle weighted instances, provided the graphs can be rendered planar through vertex splitting and the crossing minimization problem is solved on those graphs. By doing so, we can further refine the solution to remove crossings while keeping the total edge weight on the parallel lines within a factor近似 (approximately) 2 of the optimal total edge weight. This study investigates incremental learning from imbalanced datasets, focusing on algorithms with constant model complexity and bounded memory for storing exemplars of previous classes. Despite the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment being negligible, our \textit{bottom-up} EFT analysis demonstrates that the Higgs remains a viable candidate if its couplings to other SM particles are permitted to deviate from SM expectations, provided current experimental constraints on the Higgs sector are satisfied. By applying unitarity arguments, we determine that such a scenario implies a New Physics (NP) scale of approximately 10–18 TeV, which could drop to around 5 TeV if the Higgs couplings to $W$ and $Z$ bosons adhere to SM predictions. Furthermore, we show that this framework could significantly enhance di-Higgs production at muon colliders, offering additional motivation for exploring this possibility. A primary conclusion of this work is the critical need to measure the $\bar{\mu} \mu hh$ coupling in upcoming experiments. Finally, we establish that this scenario aligns with the Dark Matter (DM)-mediated explanation of the $g-2$ anomaly when the DM mass is below 1 TeV, contrasting with other explanations that typically require lighter DM masses. This scenario also avoids certain unitarity issues associated with other DM-mediated $g-2$ scenarios, potentially serving as a candidate that does not require the unitarity violation to signal NP. Moreover, we confirm that the $g-2$ anomaly can coexist with the excess observed in the diphoton channel at the LHC and explore implications for electroweak precision observables. We conclude by mentioning compatibility with $B$-physics anomalies and the feasibility of top-photon contact interactions within this framework. In summary, this study provides evidence that a $g-2$ explanation via the Higgs boson with modified SM couplings is plausible and offers numerous compatible scenarios. Although the SM role of the Higgs in $g-2$ is minimal, our results suggest that it could still be detectable, though the new physics scale rises to roughly 50 TeV. Moreover, we note that this scenario could help explain both the $g-2$ anomaly and the di-Higgs excess, though the associated NP scale increases by a factor of four. Although the SM contribution of dark matter to $g-2$ is also minimal, it remains a viable candidate for the anomaly, as detailed in the relevant sections of this paper.

to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Classical results regarding the invariants of welded knots are reconstructed using this distance. Finally, a theorem is established to characterize the diagonal move as an unknotting operation for both classical and welded knots. The classical pass move, which alters a knot's chirality, is shown to be equivalent to the 4-move, a finding that yields four distinct corollaries. These results are relevant to studies on knot complements, surgical operations, and the topology of 3- and 4-manifolds. Additionally, insights into DNA strand exchange processes can be derived from the diagonal move. To visualize these concepts, we provide physical models and DNA-based examples for the 4-move, the diagonal move, and the pass move. This work establishes that the diagonal move is a fundamental unknotting operation for classical and welded knots, offering a unified framework that generalizes several existing moves. It provides an accessible method for altering invariants of closed curves embedded in 3-manifolds, potentially aiding in determining the shortest path to an unknot.

Science. Disciplines such as computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning rely heavily on matrix operations to address their specific challenges. Among these, matrix multiplication is the most frequently performed operation; however, it can become computationally expensive when dealing with large datasets. Consequently, parallel computing has emerged as a necessary solution to mitigate this performance bottleneck. This report presents a comparative analysis of sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, implemented using CUDA and OpenMP. The findings demonstrate that parallelization is particularly critical for achieving optimal performance with large-scale matrices. In this study, two methods of parallelization were evaluated: one dividing work along rows and the other along columns. These techniques were applied to coarsely parallelize shared memory parallel matrix multiplication. The experiments were conducted on two hardware platforms: an Intel Core i7 (920) CPU and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 460 GPU. The results indicate an maximum speedup (S_max) of 7.54 on the GPU and 5.65 on the CPU. Additionally, the report discusses potential strategies to further enhance parallel execution efficiency.

This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Multi-agent systems are increasingly recognized as essential for addressing complex real-world challenges, particularly in domains like search and rescue, where a team of agents must selectively engage with multiple, heterogeneous tasks. This paper presents findings on a stochastic task allocation problem where a robot team chooses between two tasks of uncertain difficulty. We investigate the efficiency of two agent types: fully observant, myopic robots and partially observant robots employing various heuristic policies. Our results indicate that, despite uncertainties, even a small robot team with limited information can often effectively coordinate to allocate resources. These findings also underscore the potential drawbacks of partially observable environments, which can lead to suboptimal task difficulty assessments and, in specific cases, reduce team efficiency compared to a world with complete information. Additionally, the strategies employed by these partially observant agents may prove useful in real-world multirobot task allocation. Both simulation and physical experiments were conducted to validate these conclusions. An extended version of this paper is accessible in Spanish.

Search and rescue operations often involve finding many targets within a large area with an unknown spatial distribution. We propose a method to determine an optimal (or near-optimal) strategy for a robot team seeking multiple targets in such a stochastic environment. The targets may be stationary or follow known movement patterns, and the robot team may operate under either fully observable conditions or those with unknown target locations. We find that when a prior distribution of targets follows a specific class of infrequently used heavy-tailed distributions, a Nash equilibrium utilizing a simple, intuitive linear strategy exists. In other scenarios, we identify that while a Nash equilibrium is guaranteed, the strategies may exhibit a complex nonlinear nature. In all cases, we describe algorithms that can efficiently determine this equilibrium. Our findings are validated through both simulations and physical experiments

We begin with QCD at all scales, extending through the Higgs, top, and $W/Z$ boson sectors, and conclude with an examination of gravitational corrections at tree and loop levels, as well as the production of particles with spin 2 or higher. Given the proximity of these theoretical contributions to the particle width or even larger scales, we assess the implications for both current and future experimental programs. We also outline directions for advancing the field, including necessary extensions.
A complete analysis of scattering amplitudes up to two loops requires a universal handling of massless and massive soft and collinear singularities. Such a framework would enable distinct investigations into the contributions of massless and heavy degrees of freedom, respectively. This paper introduces a general formalism for factorizing these singularities, referred to as the massless-heavy factorization. This approach extends the well-established massless factorization found in DDTT|1| and BFH|2| (covering both massless and massive cases) and the heavy factorization described in HHHTT|3| and HHHTT|4|. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method within the SCET matching procedure, showing that it successfully extends SCET to regimes involving widely separated scales involving heavy masses. Specifically, we apply this formalism to three distinct scenarios featuring two distinct mass scales: (i) Higgs production via gluon fusion, which recently exhibited the first evidence of triply logarithmic contributions at NNLL accuracy; (ii) $t$-channel vector-boson scattering with a top-quark threshold; and (iii) $W$-boson production at large transverse momentum, where top-quark contributions become significant beyond LL accuracy. Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential threats and vulnerabilities when parties exchange features. We developed two attack models: one where a malicious party with access to sample identifiers and specific features gains label information from victims, and another where the malicious party possesses identifier, features, and labels, allowing it to infer victim features. Our analysis reveals that a malicious party can globalize its decision space by observing others' outputs and mapping local decision regions to global ones. Furthermore, we demonstrate that VFL suffers from membership inference attacks, allowing an adversary to determine whether specific samples exist in a client's dataset. Additionally, we uncovered reverse membership inference attacks, where a victim can infer whether a competing party's data contains a target sample. These attacks are detailed across both homomorphic encryption (HE) and gradient encryption (GE) protocols.

To mitigate these threats, we propose a defense strategy where a benign party adds noise to features using a secret noise scale before transmission. The communication cost is proportional to this scale; however, too much noise degrades model utility. Leveraging the fact that noise follows the same distribution across samples from a specific client, we apply the Whittaker's method from multi-trait analysis to estimate the noise scale at other clients. This estimation allows victims to remove noise and estimate the data of competing parties, thereby strengthening VFL defenses. Simulations on real-world and synthetic datasets show that setting the noise scale via this estimation improves utility usage by 31.72% to 360.86% across various scenarios and scale settings compared to fixed scales. Similarly, for 10-client parties, it enhances defense against reverse membership inference attacks by 117.19% to 221.15%. These findings validate that our method significantly reduces communication costs while effectively preventing reverse membership inference attacks and preventing the global decision space from being constructed by malicious parties.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. The method is evaluated on classification and regression tasks, with comparisons made against RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach. Empirical results indicate that PRFF significantly outperforms these key alternatives. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that PRFF can be applied to other data-dependent kernel approximations to achieve scaling. Ultimately, PRFF provides superior performance compared to existing kernel approximations while utilizing fewer feature dimensions.

In a product action of $S^n$, where $S$ is a group, a orbit is termed primitive if the projection of $S$ onto at least $n-1$ factors is not diagonal. A group acting primitively on a set is always primitive with respect to any of its subgroups acting on that same set. According to [3], a group $G$ is defined as regular if it acts transitively on a set such that the stabilizer of any point is the trivial group; equivalently, $G$ is regular if and only if it is abelian and its order matches the size of the set it acts upon.

The central objective of this work is to embed an arbitrary group $D$ into $S^n$ in a manner that preserves a "mostly" regular action, where $S$ is a component of $D$. This extension of [1] aims to fully classify the groups $D$ capable of acting on a primitive orbit of $S^n$ with minimal stabilizers, a property we term "nearly regular." Our main result is the following theorem:

**Theorem 1.** Let $S^n$ be a set with a primitive orbit, and let $D$ be a group acting on it. Suppose $G < D$ is a subgroup of minimal index within $D$ whose action on the primitive orbit is nearly regular. If $|G| = O(|S^n|)$, then either $S^n$ is an orbit of $D$ and $D$ is regular, or $S^n$ is an orbit of $G$ and $G$ is regular.

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients currently relies on ventricular volume and function as per established guidelines. These metrics are most accurately quantified through the segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. While U-Net architectures have demonstrated remarkable performance in recent grand challenges, clinical environments present greater variability due to diverse patient pathologies and scanner-specific image characteristics. Furthermore, training data for complex, rare conditions like TOF remains limited. This study addresses two objectives: 1) evaluating the performance gap when training on a public dataset (ACDC) and testing it on TOF data, and vice versa, and 2) determining if consistent results can be achieved on a more heterogeneous database. We trained multiple deep learning models using four-fold cross-validation and evaluated them on unseen CMR images from the alternative dataset. Our findings indicate that while current models yield excellent segmentation accuracy (left ventricle Dice of $0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ for train/validation within a single collection), they suffer from significant overfitting when applied to different pathologies, evidenced by a sharp decline in Dice scores to $0.072\pm{0.001}$ for the left and $0.165\pm{0.001}$ for the right ventricle. Consequently, further research is necessary to enhance robustness across varying pathologies and image qualities before such tools can be reliably deployed in real-world settings. In the immediate term, we suggest leveraging synthetic data to bolster model performance across diverse image types. Beyond automatic diagnosis, this work underscores the crucial need for large, diverse training datasets comprising a wide range of patient pathologies and scanner parameters.

First, a distinct architecture is proposed where receivers harvest energy from an Access Point (AP) without requiring a signal splitter; in this OFDMA model, specific spectrum portions are allocated for Information Decoding (ID) while others are dedicated to Energy Harvesting (EH). To evaluate performance gains, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize harvested energy in a multi-user single-cell OFDMA downlink while ensuring minimum data-rate requirements are met for all users, solved via optimization tools to find a locally optimal solution despite the problem's non-convex nature caused by integer variable coupling. Second, the system model is refined to address throughput maximization in a multi-user multi-cell environment, where users select a base station for energy harvesting and a different one for information decoding based on channel conditions and interference profiles; subsequently, a cross-layer approach is employed to jointly optimize resource blocking and allocation, with a relaxed problem formulated and solved using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Finally, the paper presents numerical results that compare the performance of both strategies against the performance upper limit achievable with optimal joint resource allocation and user association in a coupled multi-cell multi-user multi-antenna multi-stream MIMO-OFDMA SWIPT system. This paper re-examines FPN within the detection framework to uncover the underlying reasons for its success from an optimization standpoint. We identify that the decline in large-object performance stems from improper back-propagation paths created when FPN is incorporated, which restricts each backbone level to processing objects only within specific scale ranges. In the context of intelligent surveillance, traditional object detection systems often fail to accurately identify loitering behavior because their reliance on off-the-shelf detectors causes them to ignore certain regions throughout the video. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that learns loitering-specific spatio-temporal patterns directly from raw video through weakly-supervised learning, utilizing only binary video-level annotations to indicate the presence or absence of loiterers. Our approach begins by defining three typical loitering patterns and training the model to detect these patterns rather than individual objects. Specifically, we employ a "tag-squeeze" mechanism to extract low-resolution spatial patterns from each video, simultaneously training the model to recognize patterns at multiple scales using auxiliary loss functions. Subsequently, we integrate a low-scale temporal pooling module to capture dynamic temporal patterns by aggregating frame-level tag maps along the temporal dimension. Our methodology offers a reasonable and concise learning framework that effectively leverages binary annotations for surveillance tasks, delivering competitive performance at reasonable computational costs.
