We apply General Relativity to calculate the quasi-orbital frequencies of photon motion around a Kerr black hole. By integrating these frequencies with the characteristics of a general relativistic accretion model, we derive the radial profiles of the magnetic field, which must exert a relativistic outward force on the plasma within the inner accretion zones to counteract gravity. This profile yields a dimensionless magnetization parameter, $\chi$, representing the ratio of magnetic energy density to matter rest-mass energy density. Assuming the outer accretion disk maintains a weakly magnetized state ($\chi \ll 1$), we determine the resulting dimensionless spin value, $a$, of the central Kerr black hole. Our analysis of a sample of jetted AGNs reveals that their central black holes generally exhibit spins in the moderate range, $a \sim 0.3-0.5$. Consequently, the photon sphere analysis of electromagnetic spectra serves as a reliable method for measuring the dimensionless spin of massive black holes in these systems. Furthermore, if the derived spin values are accurate, they can facilitate more precise calculations of gravitational wave signals from merging black holes. This study also offers a novel methodology for investigating AgN jets. Although this paper focuses on electromagnetic spectra from external observations, it can be extended to scenarios where an electron-positron pair plasma generates a strong magnetic field via the Schwinger effect. In such cases, the external spacetime becomes the Kerr-Sen metric, and the subsequently derived spin values of merging black holes could provide crucial data for studying gravitational wave emissions. In these contexts, physically viable code patterns are inherently non-negative, systematically structured, and often lack the incoherence properties found in other patterns like Gaussian codes, which can hinder reconstruction quality. This paper addresses this by designing code patterns for video compressed sensing and demosaicing that minimize the mutual coherence of the matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi\Psi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is the sensing matrix derived from the code and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ represents the signal basis. Our primary contribution lies in explicitly incorporating the specific constraints associated with these applications: (1) non-negativity, requiring all code pattern elements to be $\geq 0$ to ensure hardware implementability; (2) structured patterning, meaning the code should admit efficient factorization; and (3) uniform pixel participation, indicating that every pixel should contribute equally to the measurements. Furthermore, our proposed patterns achieve lower peak signal-to-quantization noise ratios compared to codes with uniform entry elements. The pattern patterns, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{vid}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{dem}}$, were validated using two datasets: natural image textures and typical CMOS demosaicing algorithms. Validation revealed a superior mean angular error in reconstruction for $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{vid}}$ across various signal coherences and noise levels relative to other patterned codes, while $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{dem}}$ successfully generated accurate color images from coded sensor readings. Additionally, in confirmation of the predicted reduced mean angular error, both patterns were tested in two-and-three dimensional reconstruction tasks using Tikhonov and $\boldsymbol{\ell}_1$ minimization, again demonstrating improved color accuracy. Finally, the patterns were evaluated in video demosaicing, a task where existing methods currently fail. These validation results were generated utilizing a real-time factorization of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\text{dem}}$, a feature supported by its structured nature. The ultimately recovered video demonstrated higher PSNR than standard demosaicing techniques, exhibited reduced temporal noise, and showed more accurate color reproduction.

Active matter comprises out-of-equilibrium systems made up of individually consuming, moving, and often interacting components. In this study, we investigate the universal characteristics of active systems influenced by spatially fixed disorder, a topic that has received limited attention. By deriving a mesoscopic framework for active particles in confining potentials, we demonstrate that a phase transition can occur where particles cluster into localized groups that exhibit coherent orientation and collective motion. Specifically, we show the necessity of incorporating an additional variable representing coherent motion within the mesoscopic theory and identify the dimension-dependent scaling laws for active and localized phenomena. Consequently, the influence of disorder on active particles can be described through a latent variable, a feature that may be applicable to various experimental observations.

We introduce a method for securing OFDM-based wireless systems against subsymbol attacks by leveraging legitimate users' knowledge of the channel. Employing a multi-carrier phase shifting (MCPS) scheme, legitimate users adjust the phases of subcarriers based on their channel estimates to distort the receiver's channel frequency response (CFR). This modification spreads the multipath components, mitigating inter-symbol interference (ISI). Furthermore, these users apply adaptive beamforming to maximize signal strength at the receiver. Computer simulations demonstrate that this strategy effectively defends against subsymbol attacks. Additionally, we show that the scheme preserves most of the system's spectral efficiency and maintains strong resistance to additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). The proposed solution offers low complexity and requires no cooperation or knowledge of the network topology from the legitimate users.

This paper addresses the challenge of allocating subcarriers and power in an OFDM downlink when a potentially malicious user is present. We reformulate the allocation problem as a mixed integer linear program (MILP) that maximizes the end-to-end rate of a specific target user. Simulations compare the performance of this malicious user against several defense strategies. We then assess the performance gains and computational costs of optimal defenses, which were solved using Gurobi. Subsequently, we analyze optimal defense schemes against attacks where the malicious user can manipulate the CFR. Finally, we examine the performance of subcarriers assigned to the targeted user under these modified attacks and their resistance to stochastic noise. This research paves the way for future developments, such as implementing these solutions in practical OFDM systems and creating suboptimal defense schemes with lower computational overhead.

Although many Kepler host stars are too dim for detailed follow-up, TESS has identified planets around nearby bright stars suitable for RV analysis. This paper introduces the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV initiative utilizing approximately 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES telescope to study TESS-discovered exoplanets. The survey's main goals include exploring the relationship between stellar properties and the composition of small planets, examining how system architectures vary with dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity, pinpointing prime targets for JWST atmospheric studies, and understanding how stellar evolution influences planetary systems. We present a fully automated target selection algorithm that identified 103 planets in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. The majority of TKS hosts are inactive, solar-like main-sequence stars with effective temperatures between 4500 K and 6000 K, spanning a broad range of metallicities. The selected sample features 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re), 16 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 4 sub-day period planets, and 3 planets located in or near their host stars' habitable zones. This selection strategy will enable comparisons between measured planetary masses, densities, and eccentricities and predictions from population models. Our results reveal that the mass range of sub-Neptune planets (6 < m/mEarth < 22) detected via transit surveys is directly linked to orbital semi-major axes and stellar mass. Finally, we release our complete sample selection code online for future exoplanet surveys. TKS data will help define the precision requirements for JWST observations of small, short-period planets and establish a selection strategy for the forthcoming NASA RV instrument NExSS. Discoveries from the full TKS observation will be published before the end of 2020.
Transit surveys such as Kepler and TESS have confirmed that sub-Jovian planets are abundant. While small planets on short orbits are well-documented, those with intermediate sizes (0.4 to 1.3 RJ) and longer orbits (P > 10 d) remain largely unexplored. Using data from Kepler, TESS, and external sources, we constructed samples of small planets around both evolved and main-sequence stars to investigate how the detection limit of these surveys depends on effective temperature, radius, and surface gravity. Amidst rising fraud in the current era, verification processes utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for ID card extraction have been implemented to prevent account fraud. OCR technology converts images into text, enabling the extraction of data from Indonesian identity cards (KTP) to facilitate easier data entry for service operators. To enhance accuracy, NLP methods are employed to correct the extracted text. Testing on 50 Indonesian ID card images yielded an F-score of 0.78, with an extraction time of 4510 milliseconds, and the corrected script achieved an accuracy of 0.82. Replacing OCR with a document template form is recommended to improve extraction speed, accuracy, and overall system performance. Additionally, expanding the training data diversity is suggested to further increase system robustness.

Although NLP can correct errors in extracted text, it is limited to linguistic patterns and cannot verify the authenticity of IDs or extract data from other document types. To address these limitations, a document classification method based on template forms was implemented, allowing for the extraction of data from various ID cards in addition to Indonesian identity cards. Testing on 25 Indonesian ID cards and 25 foreign ID cards produced an accuracy of 0.96 and a time complexity of 531 milliseconds. This approach is expected to significantly reduce processing time and enhance the system's ability to extract data from diverse document types, thereby increasing overall accuracy. Future improvements could involve training a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) for language correction and integrating feature extraction to detect data from additional document categories.

To simplify data entry for call center operators, a form was developed to extract information from Indonesian identity cards (KTP). However, certain features like the National ID (NUPTK) and address required manual input because the extraction algorithm performed poorly on them, resulting in low accuracy and an F-score of 0.78. The NUPTK, located on the chip, was extracted with an accuracy of 0.54, while the address, derived from the card's reverse side, had an accuracy of 0.94. Improving address extraction involved adding capital letters, removing unnecessary characters, and applying NLP techniques, yielding a corrected accuracy of 0.89. Substituting the OCR method with a template-based solution is advised to boost both accuracy and extraction speed, and expanding training data will help the system handle Indonesian address variations more effectively.

Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We gathered archived light curves and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1620) Geographos, and (1685) Toro. Using light curve inversion, we fitted the data to convex shape models, modeling the YORP effect as a linear variation in rotation frequency ($\upsilon \equiv \mathrm{d}\omega / \mathrm{d}t$) and optimizing it alongside other spin and shape parameters. For asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, we detected a rotational acceleration of $\upsilon = (8.3 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, which aligns well with theoretical predictions for its specific shape and spin model. Regarding (1685) Toro, we measured $\upsilon = (3.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, which is consistent with a prolate shape, although the signal is significantly weaker than expected. Conversely, the result for (1620) Geographos, $\upsilon = (3.1 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, rules out a prolate shape and suggests that its shape model may be triaxial or bumpy. We further discuss how photometric parameters, such as those derived from inversion, can serve as proxies for the acceleration caused by the YORP effect. These findings suggest that optimizing photometric data across a broad range of phase angles is an effective method for rapidly identifying asteroids with extreme rotational accelerations. Our results underscore the value of light curve inversion, particularly when combined with astrometric data, in selecting targets for radar observation to ultimately determine the complete dynamics, shape, and model of small asteroids. This study examines online political discussions on Instagram through a network lens, specifically focusing on the formation of "co-commenter communities"—groups of users who frequently interact by commenting on the same posts and potentially steer ongoing conversations. astrophysics and exoplanet research. Within the M-dwarf sector, significant research has focused on developing empirical relations that utilize easily obtained observables to determine physical properties. While these relations often express the target quantity as a non-linear function of data, Bayesian modeling requires the inverse approach. This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework designed to simultaneously and self-consistently apply multiple empirical calibrations to fully characterize the mass, luminosity, radius, and effective temperature of field-age M-dwarfs. The framework introduces a new M-dwarf mass-radius relation exhibiting a 3.1% scatter at fixed mass. Additionally, we present the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS) and apply our methodology to derive consistent stellar parameters for these nearby low-mass stars, which were selected for their availability of ultraviolet spectroscopic data. These targets are primarily valuable as exoplanet hosts or benchmarks for multi-wavelength stellar activity studies. We utilize the field MUSS stars to define a low-mass main sequence in the solar neighborhood via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. These findings allow us to empirically identify a feature in the GP derivative at $\mathcal{M}_{b} = 0.337 \pm ^{0.013}_{0.026}$ $M_{\odot}$, marking the transition point where M-dwarfs shift from fully to partly convective interiors. Finally, we establish simple boundaries in the derived stellar parameter space that effectively separate mostly and partly convective M-dwarfs. This study delivers consistently characterized parameters for 762 MUSS members and defines B-V color boundaries that empirically separate these two subgroups. We suggest that these newly determined boundaries and their associated uncertainties may prove useful for both astrophysical investigations and the planning of observations with the upcoming Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs). The newly formulated Bayesian framework can be applied to extend these results to other contexts, such as defining main sequence features across the entire stellar population or characterizing the sample of K2-70 (Bennett et al. 2016). The derived boundaries may also aid in resolving discrepancies in the interpretation of exoplanet host-star observations, as seen in K2-70 where current data cannot definitively explain whether the planet is still accreting or if observed variations stem from stellar activity. The code employed in this work is publicly accessible at github.com/awdavidson/MUSS.

Prior theoretical and experimental investigations have identified these waves in microwave and terahertz frequency ranges, demonstrating their emergence through a symmetric resistance transition from negative to positive values combined with uniform surface reactance. Finally, near- and far-field distributions are analyzed at their optimal operating frequency, confirming the existence of these line waves in the proposed optical structure. This work suggests that graphene-based mirror-symmetric metasurfaces can effectively realize nonradiating line waves in the optical domain, a feature potentially valuable for sensing applications. This is, to our knowledge, the first report of nonradiating line waves in optical frequencies. Furthermore, the findings may be extended to other metallic metasurfaces exhibiting mirror symmetry in both directions.

existing fine-grained complexity classifications for conjunctive queries currently exclude those containing self-joins. This paper investigates the impact of self-joins on enumeration complexity to extend current results into a general classification. We achieve this by analyzing the extension of two established dichotomies: one concerning linear delay and another regarding constant delay following linear preprocessing. Given the complexity of this inquiry, the paper adopts an example-driven approach to initiate the analysis. We demonstrate enumeration algorithms that utilize self-joins to efficiently evaluate queries that lack equivalent guarantees otherwise. Consequently, hardness proofs for these cases are more intricate than those for self-join-free queries. We illustrate how a known tagging technique can be adapted to establish hardness for queries involving self-joins. Our findings provide both necessary and sufficient conditions for tractability, resolving the complexity for low-arity queries and those with cyclic cores. However, several cases remain unresolved. We present detailed hardness constructions for queries with linear delay and provide upper bounds for additional queries, aiming to bridge the gaps in our classification. We anticipate that this work will encourage future research to fully resolve the complexity of the remaining open cases. In addition, we expect our hardness constructions to serve as a resource for proving hardness for other self-join-containing queries. Finally, we contribute to the tractability analysis of specific queries by adapting techniques previously used for self-join-free queries. This paper represents an extended version of the findings presented in [10].**Abstract:** While previous fine-grained complexity classifications for conjunctive queries exclude those with self-joins, this paper addresses that limitation. We demonstrate that certain queries with self-joins are tractable for both their linearity and core predicates, thereby extending classification dichotomies for constant and linear delay. Our findings resolve the complexity for low-arity and cyclic-core queries, while also addressing several other cases. To achieve this, we employ generic enumeration algorithms, prove novel hardness results, and, most significantly, introduce new tagging-based hardness constructions. These constructions can be adapted to establish hardness for conjunctive queries with self-joins, differing from those for self-join-free queries. Our results help extend existing classifications or provide insights for completing them.**Key words:** Database theory, Query evaluation, Fine-grained complexity, Enumeration queries, Self-joins.

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this decision can be made in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ (previously established as $\mathsf{PTime}$ by Prieur). Similarly, we effectively characterize the uniform continuity of regular functions and connect it to the concept of uniform computability, which provides stronger efficiency assurances. Furthermore, we define the complexity of regular functions via the growth rate of the composition with regular sequences and demonstrate its effectiveness in assessing the efficiency of Turing machine computation of these functions. As a practical application, we employ the uniform computability of regular functions to transform an approximate algorithm into one with explicit efficiency bounds. This yields a streaming algorithm with linear time complexity for computing the Parikh vector of a word, and linear space complexity for the same when the mapping is viewed as a regular function. Additionally, we examine the relational version of our problem, proving its undecidability. Since the computability of regular functions is equivalent to their continuity, this result implies that, in general, it is undecidable whether a regular function is approximated (with possibly different complexities) by regular functions. We also briefly discuss the non-decidability of comparing the complexities (such as time complexity) of two regular functions. Notably, our approach to characterizing continuity is independent of the specific definition of regular functions, meaning it applies equally to other regular function variants, such as those defined by regular expression transducers.

A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating many algorithmic hyperparameters to automatically identify high-performing traditional reservoir computers. This study examines a difficult scenario involving a dynamical system with multiple co-existing attractors and disparate time scales. By comparing NGRC and traditional reservoir computing using metrics that assess the geometry of both the true and predicted attractors, we analyzed a four-dimensional system. Results show that NGRC requires approximately 1.7 times less training data, needs $10^3$ times less warm-up time, involves fewer hyperparameters, and achieves roughly 100 times greater accuracy in predicting co-existing attractor characteristics than traditional reservoir computing. Additionally, the method successfully predicts the basin of attraction with high precision. These findings reinforce the superior learning capabilities of this new algorithm for modeling dynamical systems. The code is available at https://github.com/aharmandel/NGRC.

We introduce a streamlined version of next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), which can automatically select the best-performing traditional reservoir computer algorithm from a vast array of hyperparameters with minimal tuning. Comparing NGRC against traditional reservoir computing on the task of simulating co-existing attractors and their characteristics in a dynamical system, we find that NGRC requires approximately 1.7 times less training data. Furthermore, NGRC achieves the necessary warm-up time for traditional methods (roughly $10^3$ times less) and reduces hyperparameters by a factor of about 100. The code is accessible at https://github.com/aharmandel/NGRC.

For a regression model defined by $Y_i = X_i^{\top}\beta_0 + \epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_i$ follows a symmetric median distribution, we propose a bias reduction scheme for the corresponding LAD estimator. The paper commences with a review of the standard bias expression. Leveraging the representation from van der Vaart and Wellner (1996), the representation from H\"auser and Scharstein (2011), and a recent finding by Yuan and Liu (2023), we derive a bias correction term applicable even when $np \to \infty$. We further provide a rigorous proof of the convergence rate for this bias term. The core strategy involves representing the cumulative distribution function of the normalized sum
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\psi(X_i^\top \beta_0)}{\sigma f_0(0)} - \nu n,
$$
as
$$
P \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{np}} Z + R_n \right),
$$
where $\psi$, $f_0$, and $\nu$ denote the influence function, the standardizing function, and the asymptotic bias, respectively. Establishing the rate of $R_n$ constitutes the primary challenge. While recent advancements have enhanced their capacity to capture high-frequency details through periodic activations or positional encodings, these methods often sacrifice generalization, typically being optimized for only a single signal. We introduce a novel representation that generalizes across multiple instances while achieving state-of-the-art fidelity. Our approach employs a dual-MLP framework: a synthesis network maps a low-dimensional input (e.g., pixel coordinates) to an output domain (e.g., RGB values), while a modulation network translates a latent code specific to the target signal into parameters that adjust the synthesis network's periodic activations. Furthermore, we propose a local-functional representation that facilitates generalization by partitioning the signal's domain into a regular grid, where each tile is associated with a latent code. During testing, the signal is reconstructed with high fidelity by inferring or directly optimizing the latent codebook. Consequently, our method produces generalizable functional representations for images, videos, and shapes, surpassing the reconstruction quality of previous works tailored to individual signals. In benchmarks for optical video (MS-video), our representation achieves the highest reported generalization performance, supports high sparsity (0.003), and delivers superior generalization at even lower latencies (0.0003). Additionally, we demonstrate applications in motion estimation and super-resolution. The implementation is available at https://tongzhoufu.github.io/GenRe/.

We present a latent diffusion model designed to invert natural images to generalizable point spreads functions (PSFs). This function enables the deconvolution of various blur effects, including circular, rectangular, radial, and depth-of-field blurs, even when caused by unknown optical systems. Our model generates a compact signal representation and learns a PSF from a single image. Unlike prior single-image super-resolution techniques, our representation generalizes to other signals of the same type. It also accommodates arbitrary distortions within a predefined class, tolerating moderate variations in size, style, and orientation. To achieve this, we learn a signal representation using a dual-MLP scheme similar to Generalizing Function Approximation, enhanced with a diffusion model for greater capacity. A PSF is represented as a periodic image encoded by a latent vector. We optimize this latent code either independently for prediction and inversion or jointly for both tasks. Because the periodic activation map can be predicted without video-specific knowledge, our method handles unknown blur kernels. We validated our representation on the LAFS

While the visual categorization hypothesis attributes this continuum to the presence of animal-diagnostic features, the agency hypothesis suggests it reflects the perception of animals as social agents. In this study, we tested both theories using a stimulus set where visual categorizability and agency were dissociated, based on convolutional neural network representations and behavioral data. fMRI results revealed that visual categorizability and agency account for independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC; when modeled together, they fully explain the continuum. Furthermore, regions driven by visual categorizability were located posterior to those driven by agency. These findings indicate that multiple organizing principles, including agency, underpin the animacy continuum in VTC. Consequently, future functional imaging research into animal representation should consider these alternative hypotheses. Additionally, the observed dissociation between principle-based organization supports interface designs for people with print disabilities that group animals by visual categorizability.

Although neural networks are widely employed to model the visual system, their ability to model animacy organization remains unexamined. This research investigates whether CNN representations of animals are structured by an agency hypothesis, a nonvisual principle positing that the brain prioritizes distinguishing living social agents from inanimate objects. We analyzed GoogleNet and ResNet-50 representations across 2,500 common animal and object words, calculating the first principal component and its loadings. While network activations did not mirror a continuum of agency, they closely mirrored a visual category continuum, with nearly all animals loading highly positively and almost all objects loading highly negatively. These findings suggest that at least for common animals and objects, CNN organization aligns with visual category rather than agency.

Prior to this work, the functional organization of ventral temporal cortex (VTC) regarding whether stimuli are animals or objects remained unclear. We assessed if an agency hypothesis, which attributes animal preference to the social adaptation needed to interact with them, offers a better organizational principle than a visual hypothesis, which relies on discriminative feature sensitivity. Using a novel behavioral task, we found that both principles are supported, though they account for independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC. Consequently, visual features and agency likely serve as dissociable components in how the mind represents animals. These findings support building richer, ecologically valid models of animacy that integrate multiple organizing principles. Specifically, when reasoning about pairs of programs, this logic enables quantitative analysis of the degree to which pre- and postconditions regarding the relationship between program inputs and outputs are satisfied. This logic aligns with existing frameworks for probabilistic and quantum relational Hoare logic, extending them by allowing reasoning about probabilities or Born-rule probabilities that arise from infinitesimal interference effects. Furthermore, it supports "norm-bounded" errors, enabling sublinear bounds on the magnitude of discrepancies between actual and desired behaviors—capabilities absent in the original unvariant logic. We demonstrate the utility of this enhanced logic by applying it to prove approximate symmetry under unitary conjugation and to establish bounds on the distinguishability of two ensembles of quantum states. Additionally, we provide a sketch of a complete soundness proof, which remains a subject for future research.

The core of this work lies in a library of rules for quantum relational Hoare logic with expectations, available on GitHub. These concepts find direct applications in analyzing quantum algorithm symmetry and distinguishability. We also illustrate how the library can be used to derive novel bounds on the distinguishability of quantum field theory vacuums following perturbation, based on the Enlarged Swampland Conjecture for correlators.

Exchange boson scattering has been identified as a potential mechanism for generating an anomalous Hall effect without a magnetic field in systems with a filled Landau level. We report the first observation of a large transverse voltage in graphene under a strong magnetic field, despite the absence of a anomalous Hall effect at the completely filled Landau level ($\nu=0$). By employing a conical contact geometry, we isolated the anomalous component of the Hall voltage. At $\nu = 0$, the longitudinal resistance reaches its maximum while the Hall resistance vanishes. Following contact deformation to modify the electronic density of states, we induced a significant transverse voltage. Comparing the resistance changes before and after deformation allows us to confirm an anomalous Hall contribution. We propose a model wherein exchange boson scattering from localized magnetic impurities opens a large energy gap at the Dirac point, shifting the chemical potential to the $\nu = -1$ Landau level and thereby producing an anomalous Hall effect.

\section{Introduction}

Rain removal, or derainning, is a critical task with significant implications for both safety and daily life. Although numerous deep learning methods have been recently introduced to restore clear images from rainy inputs, a performance gap persists between results on synthetic rainy images and those from real-world rain. This discrepancy is mostly attributed to the training of most state-of-the-art methods on paired data (clean and synthetic rainy images), which causes the network to concentrate heavily on generating and removing synthetic rain. A primary obstacle to effective real rain removal is the significant difference in characteristics between real and synthetic rain. Consequently, this work concentrates on bridging the gap between synthetic and real rain removal.

Although many studies attempt to enhance real rain removal, they often treat it as a two-step process: first learning a mapping from real rain images to synthetic rain images, followed by applying a synthetic rain removal network. However, this sequential approach is suboptimal because any errors introduced in the initial translation step are compounded during the subsequent removal stage.

Experimental results on the Librispeech corpus (100 hours) for few-shot ASR tasks demonstrate that BiAM enhances an ASR model's performance by 2.31 character error rates (CEMs) when exposed to unpaired text data, or improves performance by leveraging 2.2x to 4.4x more text data than the primary ASR dataset. Additionally, when trained on an end-to-end ASR model, BiAM reduces the model's parameter count by approximately 27%. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/qiushaobing/BiAM. To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate improving few-shot ASR performance using unpaired text data within an unsupervised multi-modal learning framework.

Superconducting quantum phase slip (QPS) devices are predicted to function as one-dimensional superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). We propose and experimentally verify a scheme to manipulate the wavefunction phase of a QPS device using a voltage pulse. This manipulation is confirmed through a spin-echo like experiment, where the initial contrast loss—attributed to dephasing—was not observed after applying the phase shift. Furusaki's model of alternating coherent and incoherent QPS events best explains the experimental observations. Based on these results, a single coherent QPS event is inferred. We also present constraints on theoretical models involving multiple coherent QPS events, such as those arising from intrinsic Josephson junctions in nanowires or noise from surface adsorbates.

Nanowires composed of narrow, dirty superconductors are theorized to exhibit one-dimensional superconductivity governed by a quantum phase slip (QPS) operator, $\hat{W} = \exp(i\phi)$. While thermal QPS events generate a resistive state at finite temperatures, competing quantum QPS events can completely localize charge and prevent supercurrents at very low temperatures. This setup forms a SQUID, allowing the superconducting state's susceptibility to competing QPS events to be probed by measuring the period of oscillations in the critical current as a function of magnetic flux. first T-dwarf, GJ 229B has been the subject of more extensive observations than most other brown dwarfs, yet it lacks a complete atmospheric analysis using modern methods. Its spectrum displays unique characteristics, and recent dynamical calculations regarding its mass and age have yielded conflicting results, both necessitating further study. Situated tens of AU from its host star, GJ 229B resides near the boundary between planetary and stellar formation zones, meaning its atmosphere may hold keys to understanding whether such bodies originate from gas accretion or giant impacts. This paper updates the solution from exo-tomography studies, adapting it for the HITRAN 2020 database, and employs spectral modeling with the open-source package open-source Molecular Atmospheric Retrieval Tool (OMART) and the custom script hs2fits. We derived a temperature distribution along the day-night meridian, yielding mean daytime and nighttime temperatures of approximately 780 K and 650 K, respectively. We also determined the companion's mass to be $0.049_{-0.009}^{+0.012}$ Solar masses, or $49\pm9.5$ Jupiter masses, and estimated its age at $>8.5$ Gy, assuming a surface metallicity three times that of its host star. Finally, we generated predicted spectra based on these parameters, validating our findings against observations from the Hubble Space Telescope, the Near-Infrared Spectrograph, the Very Large Telescope, the Keck Observatory, and the Subaru Telescope. These updated mass and age estimates suggest that GJ 229B will retain its status as the longest-orbiting brown dwarf companion to a main-sequence star for the foreseeable future. Documentary video retrieval enables users to locate scenes or objects of interest within a library of indexable documentaries. While prior methods primarily focused on textual descriptions, we observe that documentary videos often contain rich, implicit semantic information derived from visual and audio modalities. Although manual labeling is time-consuming and costly, these implicit patterns can be efficiently mined using self-supervised learning. Consequently, we introduce a novel textual-free retrieval framework that leverages these hidden semantic features to enhance user experience. Extensive experiments on two public datasets, TREC-DC and TREC-DS, along results from an internal competition, prove the method's effectiveness. This paper also introduces a new benchmark, TREC-DS, and a corresponding evaluation protocol. The code is available at https://github.com/heli-pan/S3DC.

In this study, we experimentally demonstrate using femtosecond laser writing that fundamental and excited orbital states can couple when situated at distinct spatial locations. We provide a comprehensive characterization of an asymmetric double-well-like potential and employ a scanning method to effectively map dynamics along the propagation axis. This key observation directly addresses the need for a spatial mode converter device, which can be integrated anywhere within a photonic glass chip. Leveraging the phase structure of higher-order photonic modes and the effective negative coupling generated, we propose a trimer configuration functioning as a phase beam splitter ($\pi$-BS), offering significant potential for multiplexing and interference-based photonic concatenated operations. Consequently, this technology is a vital component in realizing photonic quantum chips and accelerators designed for variational optimization. The overarching interaction framework presented here may also facilitate other significant applications, such as orbital angular momentum (OAM) multiplexing, accelerating elements for Fournier lenses, and creating photonic coupled oscillators that emulate a Harper-like lattice. Achieving inter-orbital coupling among resonators opens pathways for manipulating photonic higher-dimensional orbital states and could enable computational models of electron orbital interactions, thereby fostering research into strongly correlated photon systems. Ultimately, we envision the construction of devices capable of generating and controlling photonic frustrated ferromagnetism and photonic quantum Hall effects.

This study investigates airborne infection risks on an urban bus by employing unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes equations alongside a passive-scalar model for virus-laden aerosol concentrations. To aid the experimental observation of quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence, our analysis prioritizes cases where the initial and final x-ray photons exhibit differences not only in polarization but also in propagation direction—corresponding to scattering angles within the milliradian range—and potentially in energy. We determine that optimal conditions are met when the two optical lasers are aligned nearly parallel to the x-ray beam, though not collinear, and when their polarization vectors are perpendicular to the plane defined by the two optical fields. Under these configurations, the initial x-ray photon remains unaffected by the lasers, while the final x-ray photon undergoes birefringent scattering, resulting in alterations to its polarization, momentum, and energy. To assist experimental implementation, we establish a comprehensive framework encompassing relevant parameter spaces, optimal setups, and possible variations. bent and Lord (TQC'20), is an encryption scheme characterized by the property that an adversary, given a ciphertext, cannot generate two distinct ciphertexts that both decrypt to the same original message. This work revisits that concept and establishes the following results:

*   **Reusability:** The original constructions by Broadbent and Lord suffer from limitations: they either ensure one-time security (where the key is usable only once) in the plain model or rely on the random oracle model for security. We propose unclonable encryption schemes that achieve semantic security. Specifically, we offer two constructions—one for public-key and one for private-key settings—based on minimal cryptographic assumptions.
*   **Lower Bound and Generalized Construction:** We re-examine the information-theoretic one-time secure scheme by Broadbent and Lord. In their construction, the adversary's success probability was bounded at $0.85^n$, where $n$ denotes the message length. We investigated whether the theoretical ideal success probability of approximately $0.5^n$ was unattainable. By generalizing their approach to a wider range of monogamy of entanglement games, we demonstrate a cloning attack with a success probability of $0.71^n$ against a class of schemes that includes theirs. Furthermore, we present a specific cloning attack with a $0.75^n$ success rate targeting their scheme exclusively. Finally, we establish a lower bound of $0.5^n$ on the unclonability success probability for any game encompassing the schemes we defined.
*   **Extensions:** We extend unclonable encryption to the scenarios of private-key and public-key cryptography. Additionally, we define and construct versions of the scheme utilizing other quantum resources, such as entanglement. The successful cloning attacks demonstrated in this paper imply that these extended schemes are strictly weaker than those proposed by Broadbent and Lord. We also establish upper bounds on the success probabilities for such cloning attacks.
*   **Other Extensions:** We further explore the feasibility of unclonable encryption under fully homomorphic, adaptively secure, and leakage-resilient frameworks. In each case, we present constructive approaches or prove impossibility results.

In summary, this paper emphasizes the significance of monogamy of entanglement games. Beyond its applications in quantum cryptography, we suggest that this principle may be essential for constructing certain quantum cryptographic protocols.

The framework involves an encoder, a decoder, and an adversary who possesses the message, a non-causal noisy view of the transmission, and unlimited transmission power; conversely, the decoder receives a noisy observation of the sum of the encoder's and adversary's outputs. The authors propose a technique to adapt generic existing channel codes for authentication purposes. They prove that this adaptation incurs an asymptotically negligible reduction in coding rate and ensures authentication as long as the adversary's observation is not noiseless. Notably, this modification does not depend asymptotically on the statistical properties of the adversary's channel and requires no knowledge of the channel state at the encoder. Although these findings are theoretical, simulation results indicate that the proposed scheme remains effective and efficient in finite-length regimes, thereby offering practical value. To achieve these outcomes, the paper contributes original insights to information-theoretic authentication, channel coding, and stochastic dominance theory. The overall approach is grounded in polar coding, yet it remains agnostic regarding the specific construction and analysis methods used for these codes. As a consequence, the proposed framework can be readily adapted to other channel code constructions, such as those based on LDPC codes. In terms of performance, simulations reveal that the proposed construction achieves strong authentication strength and reliability. Regarding implementation, the approach exhibits very low computational complexity for both the encoder and decoder, features low memory requirements, and benefits from highly optimized open-source software libraries. This ensures that the solution meets real-time latency constraints and is economically viable. Finally, the framework is robust against hardware imperfections, including those caused by the adversary, as these issues arise primarily from finite-length effects. Although constructed using polar codes, the research holds significant implications for practical code constructions. Future improvements could involve addressing finite-length considerations, optimizing for specific channel models, and enhancing security against more potent adversaries.

Then, an algorithm is developed to resolve these conflicts when designing time-varying time-frequency (TF) codes for optical OFDM systems. This method minimizes inter-symbol and inter-frequency interference to enhance signal robustness against noise and channel fading, subject to constraints dictated by the time-frequency patterns of LA. This study examines flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ (tb-MoS$_2$) using a comprehensive tight-binding model combined with the random phase approximation. When lattice relaxations are accounted for in tb-MoS$_2$, the flat band remains distinct from remote valence bands, leading to a significantly different contribution from interband transitions to plasmon dispersion and energy. Specifically, considering only intraband transitions within the doped flat band yields low-damped, quasi-flat plasmons, while including interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands results in a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion. Additionally, plasmon energies can be tuned via twist angles and doping concentrations. Conversely, in rigid samples without lattice relaxations, lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons may coexist; however, in highly doped rigid tb-MoS$_2$, strongly enhanced interband transitions suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Based on the influences of lattice relaxation and doping, we conclude that observing the low-damped, quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides requires two key conditions: an isolated flat band and an appropriate level of hole doping. We anticipate that our findings on flat-band plasmons will provide valuable insights into the potential for current-carbon exchange interaction suppression in these materials. Furthermore, our results on plasmon dispersion in tb-MoS$_2$ may aid in selecting appropriate parameters for investigating superconductivity and other flat-band phenomena through plasmon-exciton exchange. Lastly, our study may contribute to understanding the manipulation of plasmons in layered materials using few-layer graphene.

Recently, significant progress has been made in creating stacked van der Waals materials with tunable degrees of freedom and exceptional stability. Among these, twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) has become a highly promising platform for exploring flat-band physics. This paper investigates how doping and twist angles affect the properties of plasmons in TBG. In undoped TBG, low-damped, quasi-flat surface plasmons emerge from an unusual flat band, whereas doped TBG exhibits both $\omega(q)$ and $\omega(\sqrt q)$ plasmon behaviors depending on the specific flat band and charge carrier concentration. We anticipate that our findings will assist in selecting optimal samples and parameters for future studies on flat-band physics in TBG, including superconductivity.

The powerful outflows from massive stars are believed to be powered by the line-scattering of radiative momentum, whereas the Sun and lower-mass stars experience significantly weaker mass loss driven by the thermal expansion of a mechanically heated corona. For exoplanets orbiting these low-mass stars, the interaction between radiative heating and stellar winds can cause their atmospheres to expand thermally or undergo mechanical ablation. While stellar magnetospheres arise from the internal trapping of wind outflow, planetary magnetospheres are generally shaped by the external pressure of the stellar wind. In both scenarios, this stress can trigger magnetic reconnection, producing observable phenomena such as X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review provides an overview of the underlying physics of these mechanisms, focusing on both their commonalities and differences between stars and planets. Additionally, we discuss recent observational findings regarding magnetic reconnection on low-mass stars and propose new constraints for exoplanet atmospheric interactions based on recent stellar data. Finally, we examine how these processes influence wind mass loss and angular momentum evolution for both exStars and ex- planets. As these systems age, magnetic reconnection on low-mass star exoplanets may make them detectable through all-sky surveys targeting atmospheric ablation signatures. These observations could offer novel tests for the fundamental physics of stellar winds and provide exoplanet researchers with direct methods to measure magnetic field strengths and verify models of planetary atmospheric loss.

We employ direct numerical simulations of magnetohydrodynamics coupled with radiation transport to investigate magnetic ablation in the context of close-orbiting hot Jupiter exoplanets. These simulations explicitly model magnetic reconnection within the resulting magnetotail, alongside the subsequent ablation of the planet's upper atmosphere by the stellar wind. Our results indicate that for magnetic field strengths exceeding approximately 5–7 $\times$ 10$^2$ G (as found in GJ 504 b and possibly in 51 Peg b), magnetic ablation becomes a dominant mechanism for atmospheric mass loss, surpassing both hydrodynamic escape and frictional drag. This process significantly enhances the mass loss rate by at least an order of magnitude compared to models considering only hydrodynamic escape and wind drag. Furthermore, we demonstrate that magnetic ablation efficiently converts gravitational potential energy into thermal energy at the ablation front. We introduce a straightforward method for calculating an upper bound of the Lipschitz constant across various $p$-norms for feedforward neural networks comprising standard layer types. This approach allows us to frame the training of a neural network with a bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimization problem, solvable via projected stochastic gradient methods. title: "Models With Bounded Lipschitz Constants"
author: "William R. Anderson and Michael J. Ioffla"
abstract: "We investigate the consequences of explicitly requiring a neural network to be Lipschitz continuous concerning its input. We propose a simple technique to determine a bound on the Lipschitz constant for a feedforward neural network with typical standard layers. By treating the network's bounded Lipschitz constant as a constraint within a constrained optimization framework, we can train such networks. Our findings suggest that these models outperform those regularized using other common lipshitz-like constraints. Additionally, we illustrate the implications of different norm choices and address scenarios involving limited training data."

# Introduction
Deeper and wider neural networks generally achieve superior performance but often suffer from overfitting, raising concerns about their reliability and susceptibility to adversarial attacks. Although defense mechanisms can mitigate these issues, understanding the inherent properties of the networks is crucial for developing effective defenses and designing more robust architectures. Although often implicit, many high-performance networks lack essential mathematical properties like boundedness or monotonicity. Specifically, there is a significant potential benefit to training networks that explicitly preserve these attributes. This paper focuses on one such property: Lipschitz continuity.
# Lipshitz Constant Computation
A function $f$ is Lipschitz continuous if there exists a constant $K$ such that for all $x$ and $y$ in the domain, the inequality $\|f(x) - f(y)\| \leq K \|x - y\|$ holds. The smallest such $K$ is referred to as the Lipschitz constant of

Processing (NLP) domains. However, their linear architecture prompts inquiry into how well they can implicitly grasp the hierarchical structures characteristic of human language and which grammatical phenomena they can master. This study examines agreement prediction in Basque as a case study, a task demanding an implicit grasp of sentence structure and the ability to handle a complex yet consistent morphological system. By analyzing experimental outcomes from two syntactic prediction tasks—verb number prediction and suffix recovery—we observe that sequential models underperform on Basque agreement prediction relative to expectations derived from prior work on English. Preliminary findings from diagnostic classifiers indicate that these networks rely on local heuristics as a substitute for representing the sentence's hierarchical structure. Consequently, we propose the Basque agreement prediction task as a rigorous benchmark for models aiming to learn the regularities inherent in human language. Our code is available online.

Morphological complexity in low-resource languages often hinders automatic translation, particularly when words are represented as sequences of characters or sub-words. We introduce a new benchmark, ICLONL19, consisting of morphologically complex words from 15 low-resource languages within the CloNLP corpus. This collection includes 179,800 words and 299,700 annotations detailing various linguistic features, serving as a test set for morphological prediction tasks. We conduct experiments across eleven models, including character-based neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and four statistical methods, evaluating them on four prediction tasks using four evaluation metrics. Our results demonstrate that character-based and CNN models underperform on Georgian, while RNNs struggle with Estonian; furthermore, statistical models surprisingly outperform neural networks on Romanian. Ultimately, we contend that any language model seeking to generalize across contexts must implicitly learn to represent complex vocabulary effectively.

We present a study on morphological prediction in Low-Resource languages, establishing a baseline for future research. Our focus is on the prediction task utilized in the recent MorphoDecode challenge. We assemble a corpus comprising two parts: a training set derived from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in ten languages, and a test set consisting of manually selected, morphologically rich words from ten additional languages. We evaluate four types of approaches: simple character-level mappings, sequential neural networks, non-sequential models, and morphosyntactic classifiers. The best approaches achieved an overall accuracy of approximately 80%. As a contribution to diagnostic analysis, we investigate the predictive power of featurization strategies and

transiting planet with a highly eccentric orbit (e=0.93), experiences a 1000-fold surge in insolation over its 111-day cycle. Its effective temperature rapidly spikes from 500K to more than 1400K within hours as it swiftly approaches its host star. This study employs a 3D hydrodynamic model coupled with a multiple-nuclei lattice Monte Carlo method to simulate the evolution of its atmospheric chemical composition throughout orbital phases. To validate these simulations, we calculated the secondary eclipse spectrum and full emission spectrum during the peak illumination phase, comparing the results against actual observational data. Our findings indicate that during the eclipse, the atmosphere is characterized by high temperature, low pressure, and high metallicity, marked by significant thermal dissociation of H2O and CO2. Consequently, the air becomes relatively humid, and species such as O-1, O-2, and OH dominate the high temperature regions. These outcomes offer fresh insights into how highly eccentric planets interact with their stellar environments. During the maximum illumination phase, sodium and potassium abundance ratios (M/H) rise dramatically with increasing equilibrium temperature, eventually plateauing at approximately 10^5 and 10^6, respectively, once the temperature surpasses 1500K. Notably, the H2O/CO ratio increases substantially with rising equilibrium temperature due to the preferential dissociation of CO2. Furthermore, we determined that the disk-averaged bond albedo is 0.136, and the deep trough in the light curve yields a phase albedo of 0.229 at the peak illumination phase. Chemical dissociation explains the narrow depth of this trough. Additionally, the observed spectrum at the peak phase can be accounted for by a combination of deep absorption at short wavelengths (caused by clouds or condensates) and emission at long wavelengths. Finally, the deep, narrow absorption feature observed at 1.11 um in the JWST observation can only be explained by high metallicity, elevated temperature, and the chemical dissociation of H2O. We contend that similar planets could serve as ideal testbeds for investigating cloud physics and atmospheric circulation using future space-based instruments.

This paper introduces a method utilizing a statistical model of baseline gameplay to determine design configurations that mimic behaviors consistent with standard, unmodified play. We demonstrate this approach through a case study of upper limb rehabilitation using a custom controller for a Pac-Man game. In a participatory design workshop, occupational therapists established two interaction parameters to balance gameplay and rehabilitation needs. These parameters' impacts were then evaluated experimentally with twelve participants. Our findings show that a low-latency model, incorporating both user input behavior and internal game state, can identify interaction parameter values that replicate baseline gameplay even under degraded control conditions. Finally, we discuss how this methodology can be applied to systematically resolve gamification challenges by balancing physical constraints with subjectively engaging experiences.

These approximations address limitations in prior Gamma-stable approximations by offering lower bounds that demonstrate strong convergence. Consequently, they enable the analysis of Gamma-convergence trajectories concerning geometric nonlinearity and material toughness, as well as the convergence of approximation schemes for fixed material toughness. This approach facilitates the identification of Gamma-convergence fixed points regarding geometric nonlinearity at specific material toughness levels. Furthermore, the proposed approximations support the study of Gamma-convergence across varying material toughness, strong discontinuities, and threshold stretches, as well as Gamma-convergence for displacement maps spanning continuous to discontinuous displacements. The resulting Gamma-limits accurately represent fracture energies for both nonlinear elasticity and linearized theory, encompassing materials with sharp fractures, fuzzy fractures, and mixed failure modes where fracture and separation occur simultaneously. Additionally, the findings include the separation of phases, an effect previously unexplained within Gamma-convergence frameworks. The established Gamma-convergence results align with and extend other relevant limits found in the existing literature. Our contributions provide theoretical foundations for numerical methods modeling fracture in piecewise-rigid solids, encompassing strong convergence, finite element approximation, time evolution, and dynamic fracture. While this work focuses on theoretical aspects, it supports the research detailed in two accompanying papers, which examine Gamma-convergence over moving domains and kinetic energies for both nonlinear and linearized elasticity. These extensions yield threshold stretches and fracture toughness values consistent with experimental data, alongside dynamic effects such as crack kinking and branching. The current study also addresses parameter spaces where the approaches in those preceding works are inapplicable. Finally, the methodologies employed here are anticipated to be valuable for analyzing other material discontinuities, including delamination and cracks in multilayered materials.

In this review, we summarize recent advancements in defining and utilizing derivatives for set-valued functions. Specifically, we introduce a novel definition of the derivative for set-valued functions that aligns with the Painlevé-Kuratowski convergence of the graph. We demonstrate that the Lipschitz continuity of this set-valued derivative is equivalent to the existence of a selection satisfying a global slope condition, thereby generalizing the McShane extension to the setting of metric spaces. As a application, we prove selection theorems for the Derivative of the Set of Minimizers and the Derivative of the Solution Map to Optimization Problems. Within the framework of models featuring third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks (LQs), we compute the full ${\cal O} (\alpha_s)$ corrections for the $pp \to \tau^+ \tau^-$ process, attaining next-to-leading order (NLO) accuracy augmented by parton showering (NLO$+$PS) through the POWHEG technique. We have developed a specialized Monte Carlo tool that calculates NLO QCD corrections dynamically during event generation, employing it to assess the quantitative effects of NLO$+$PS corrections on kinematic variables relevant to current experimental searches. Utilizing these phenomenological findings, we establish NLO QCD-corrected limits on the masses and coupling strengths of these leptoquarks based on the most recent ATLAS and CMS data, which are made accessible via our newly introduced public Monte Carlo tool. Additionally, we derive search limits for specific BSM scenarios based on the existing ditau data from the CMS experiment. Since these vector leptoquarks could account for the muon $g-2$ anomaly, we also examine constraints arising from the Higgs boson boson fusion channel at current colliders, noting that these limits vary significantly depending on the specific model construction. Finally, we also determine limits on these vector leptoquarks arising from ditau production at the future 100 TeV proton-proton collider. This work provides an open-source NLO QCD-corrected Monte Carlo simulator, which will be essential for probing third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks and addressing the $g-2$ muon anomaly at the upcoming LHC upgrades and the 100 TeV collider. If these particles exist, the signatures of third-generation gauge vector LQs will be most prominently revealed by ditau final states at the future high-energy hadron colliders.

Lowering the radiotracer dose or scan duration to mitigate this risk reduces photon counts, thereby compromising image quality. While recent deep neural network (DNN) techniques can translate low-quality PET images—acquired with significantly reduced doses—into high-quality results by leveraging corresponding MRI data, these methods often struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differs statistically from their training sets. We introduce a novel DNN approach that incorporates (i) the fundamental sinogram physics of PET imaging and (ii) uncertainty quantification via per-voxel heteroscedasticity in the residuals between predicted and reference images. This proposed framework, termed suDNN, generates standard-dose PET images from multimodal inputs consisting of low-dose/low-count PET and multi-contrast MRI data, enhancing its robustness against OOD acquisitions. Empirical results on in vivo PET-MRI data and various OOD scenarios demonstrate that suDNN outperforms current state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively. Furthermore, we present sPET, a simplified version of suDNN that utilizes single-contrast MRI data, which also surpasses existing states-of-the-art techniques. The code for suDNN and sPET is available at https://github.com/hahdnghia/suDNN. Quantitative improvements over the current state-of-the-art are highlighted in red within the paper.

Although recent deep neural network (DNN) methods can transform low-dose or low-count PET images into high-quality scans using multi-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MR) data, they encounter challenges when processing out-of-distribution (OOD) images that differ statistically from the training set. We develop a direct reconstruction method using regularized parallel projection that effectively handles PET images with very low radiotracer doses or acquisition times, effectively suppressing high-frequency noise in the residual between the predicted and reference images. Leveraging the multi-contrast nature of MR data, our proposed super-resolution deep direct reconstruction (sDDR) approach translates this low-quality PET data into high-quality images. Similarly, the enhanced low-dose PET (eLP) method effectively utilizes single-contrast MR data for transformation. Both methods outperform current state-of-the-art techniques on real in vivo datasets, including various OOD cases. The proposed methods are tested on NIfTI data and validated against realistic PET-MRI acquisitions, with code accessible at https://

as increasing concern grows over excessive data collection under the guise of personalization and its use for questionable purposes. Our experience developing privacy-safe personalization tools for publishers prompted an investigation into how users perceive the intersection of privacy and personalization. Through a survey examining individual experiences and perspectives across various age groups, this paper presents key findings for the publishing community and developers. These insights aim to guide the design and implementation of next-generation news recommender systems that prioritize human-centric approaches, striking a necessary balance between personalized experiences and privacy to maximize the benefits of both. Additionally, we propose a research agenda on privacy-aware news personalization, which must incorporate the principles and practices of Explainable AI (XAI) and fairness. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of enhancing technical skills in privacy and ethics among developers to ensure ethical system creation. Ultimately, we advocate for shifting the industry focus from "personalization" alone to "personalization and privacy," rebranding it to better reflect consumer interests and align with existing privacy frameworks like GDPR and CCPA. Finally, we advocate making data minimization a core component of system design, limiting data collection to only what is essential for specific, transparent tasks while avoiding unnecessary information gathering. This results in a more secure "lockdown effect," where smaller data scopes reduce vulnerabilities and lower the risk of breaches impacting users. We conclude by urging the adoption of a holistic, people-first approach to reimagining news personalization.

We introduce a structured methodology for developing news recommendation systems that adhere to ethical principles. This framework outlines four primary phases: understanding, designing, testing, and deploying. The underlying premise is that ethical consideration should inform every stage of creation, ensuring that algorithms are transparent, their outcomes comprehensible, and potential harms mitigated.

We investigate the perceptions of privacy and personalization within the news industry. It is crucial for algorithm creators to comprehend how consumers view these concepts to build systems that are both ethically sound and effective.

We highlight the significance of incorporating explainability (XAI) into ethical news personalization and define four stages of its implementation, ranging from post-hoc explanations of specific recommendations to proactive, front-end integration.

We call for the establishment of an evaluation framework to assess the ethical standards of news recommendation systems. Such a framework should involve stakeholders, including users, publishers, and technologists, to examine issues like transparency, fairness, and privacy.

This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and contemporary coreference resolution systems. We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. Our information-theoretic analysis indicates a positive correlation between coreference and centering, yet demonstrates that high-performing neural resolvers gain little advantage from explicitly modeling centering concepts. Furthermore, we find that contextualized embeddings encapsulate much of the necessary coherence information, explaining why CT yields minimal improvements for modern neural systems utilizing pretrained representations. Finally, we address coreference factors unmodeled by standard CT, such as world knowledge and recency bias. By formulating an enhanced version of CT that incorporates recency, we show it captures coreference information more effectively than the original formulation. Overall, our work provides the first empirical assessment of CT's utility in coreference resolution and establishes a recommended framework for future research.

We examine whether contextualized representations learned by transformers encode semantic and syntactic knowledge typically associated with linguistic theories. To do this, we measure the distances between vector embeddings of words, phrases, sentences, and tuples under various operations, comparing these against definitions derived from Skurtin's (2019) generalized linguistic knowledge framework. Our results indicate that contextualized representations primarily capture syntactic structure rather than semantic structure. This finding has significant implications for tasks relying on semantic knowledge, such as textual entailment, and suggests that techniques for augmenting representations with semantic information may be more effective than simply utilizing contextualized embeddings directly.

We investigate whether contextualized representations learned by transformers contain semantic and syntactic knowledge usually attributed to linguistic frameworks. We assess distances between embeddings of words, phrases, sentences, tuples, and functional types, contrasting these metrics with those from the generalized linguistic knowledge definition proposed by Skurtin (2019). Our findings suggest that while these representations mainly encode syntactic structure, they lack semantic structure. This conclusion carries important implications for tasks requiring semantic knowledge, like textual entailment, and implies that methods for enriching representations with semantic information could be more beneficial than relying solely on contextualized embeddings.

a significant enhancement in automation during the configuration process. This automation not only boosts development cycle agility but also facilitates the rapid, automated integration of decoupled workflows. This paper introduces a novel framework designed for the automated configuration of systems modeled as state machines. By utilizing model checking and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), the framework is applicable to any domain that can be expressed via SMT formulas. Our method supports modular application, thereby enhancing scalability. Additionally, we demonstrate how optimization techniques can generate configurations that are optimal according to specific metrics and more amenable to human comprehension. We illustrate the framework's versatility and capabilities by employing it to configure a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks. The resulting optimizations exceed human settings by multiple orders of magnitude. Ultimately, we propose extensions that enable the identification of configurations optimized for multiple simultaneous criteria.

Configurable hardware can be modeled using parameterized hardware description languages (HDLs) like Verilog, allowing for efficient exploration of the design space. However, two primary challenges hinder the configuration of systems with numerous parameters: the exponential increase in synthesis time and the difficulty of navigating the resulting configuration landscape. To address the first challenge, we developed a parser for vectorized SMT formulas, which predicts and caches the result of parameter combinations belonging to identical clusters. This approach reduces synthesis time for large-scale configurations by up to $7.5 \times 10^5$ while ensuring the discovery of all valid configurations. Regarding the second challenge, we analyzed the search landscape of an 11-dimensional Reconfigurable Computing Array (RCA) system. Although the map reveals promising configurations, most are unsuitable for practical use due to excessive power, area, or latency. To our knowledge, this study represents the most comprehensive examination of its kind for configurable hardware. Based on these findings, we proposed several strategies to identify high-quality solutions within such search spaces.

Modern applications demand performance, reliability, and real-time behavior, characteristics that are increasingly difficult to achieve on standard processors. Consequently, hardware acceleration has gained substantial traction. Configurable hardware, particularly Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), offers an attractive path to automatically synthesize hardware tailored to specific application needs. We developed a system capable of automatically configuring RCA devices to process images. This system successfully discovered configurations that outperform human-designed setups by five orders of magnitude in both speed and power efficiency. To achieve open-ended optimization, we employed parameterized HDLs, automated image loading and result reading circuits, and explored optimizations across multiple objective functions.

Specifically, we examine Krylov complexity, entanglement negativity, von Neumann entropy, and entanglement capacity for systems with SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetries. Our primary methodology relies on two-mode coherent states, which enable the analysis of operator growth and its entanglement structure across any system within the discrete series representations of these groups. Our findings confirm that the investigated quantities display specific universal characteristics consistent with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of leveraging symmetry, as it substantially streamlines the computation of metrics related to operator growth. Notably, we contend that the reliance on the Lanczos algorithm—the predominant tool previously used in this field—is unnecessary, since essential insights can be derived directly through symmetry arguments. Ultimately, our work aims to advance the comprehension of universal laws governing quantum scarring and quantum chaos. Based on our results, we propose investigating other information-theoretic measures, such as quantum relative entropy and Kullback-Leibler divergence, in the context of operator growth. Our strategy utilizes the parameters defining the unitary evolution, which evolve continuously from the Hamiltonian (at $t=0$) to the generic time-dependent operators under consideration (at $t>0$). Our approach relies on the concept of relative entropy applied to symmetric states, as defined in reference [arXiv:2109.02085]. We anticipate that our methodology is applicable more broadly to any system with compact or non-compact Lie symmetry. In the conclusion, we discuss potential future directions for research. We investigate the entanglement structure of operators under a many-body duality transformation in lattice systems with short-range interactions. We demonstrate that lattice systems exhibiting area law ground states for bipartite entanglement, when evolved for times $t>0$ under dynamics generated by their critical Hamiltonians, equivalently correspond to critical Hamiltonians under time evolution for $0\leq t\leq t_{*}$ where $t_{*}\sim N$ and $N$ denotes the system size. Consequently, the linear increase observed in mutual information and other non-extensive quantities across the intermediate regime $1\ll t\ll t_{*}$ reflects two features: (i) the linearity of entanglement entropy for critical quantum systems, and (ii) the spatial localization of operators in the Heisenberg picture.
