WiFi fingerprinting, which involves gathering Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements at known locations, is a prevalent technique in various positioning algorithms found in existing literature. However, accurately calculating the spatial distance between fingerprints is highly dependent on the choice of signal distance function used to map signal space to geospatial distance. This study proposes leveraging machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between fingerprints. To develop a generalizable model applicable to any indoor setting, the research analyzed data from 13 diverse open datasets. The novel approach identified key features by evaluating common signal distance metrics through a feature selection process that combined feature analysis with a genetic algorithm. To ensure venue independence, all models were evaluated on datasets that were not used during training or validation. Finally, multiple machine learning algorithms were compared using a comprehensive range of evaluation metrics, including their capacity to scale from controlled test beds to real-world, unsolicited datasets. The results indicate that estimating geospatial distances via machine learning is feasible, achieving an average error of under one meter across one to four meters on unsolicited datasets. Furthermore, the optimal model demonstrated an error of just 6.3 cm on a real-world campus building, outperforming any previously reported methods in similar experiments. These findings suggest that the proposed method is robust, efficient, and capable of delivering sub-meter location accuracy. Additionally, the paper discusses strategies for dynamically updating models when new datasets are collected. A repository of open data and code supporting this research is available at https://github.com/haroldo22/ML_loc. The authors also highlight that these results were recently recognized with an Outstanding Paper Award at the IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC 2022).

Recently, researchers have demonstrated that specific machine learning models can effectively estimate geospatial distances between WiFi fingerprints to enable grid-based positioning. This paper advances those methods by introducing a model capable of accurately estimating geospatial distances in real-world environments, even when trained exclusively on data from a single indoor venue. The study compares models trained on datasets from one, two, four, and eight different venues. To validate the venue independence of these models, their performance was tested on two unsolicited datasets from locations not included in the training or validation phases. The research further examines how model performance varies based on the quantity and diversity of training data, as well as the features extracted using different distance metrics. The findings reveal that an ensemble of machine learning models can accurately and efficiently estimate geospatial distances between WiFi

) has been active for almost six decades, with the Dyson Sphere—a hypothetical shell surrounding a star to harness its energy—remaining a primary focus. This study investigates the feasibility of constructing such a structure around a black hole. We examine six potential energy sources: the cosmic microwave background, Hawking radiation, an accretion disk, Bondi accretion, a corona, and relativistic jets. To support a Type II civilization, an output of $4\times10^{26}\,{\rm W}$ ($1\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$) is required. Among the sources listed from (iii) to (vi), an accretion disk offers the highest luminosity, reaching $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$, which is sufficient to sustain a Type II civilization. Furthermore, if the Dyson Sphere captures additional energy forms, such as kinetic energy from jets alongside electromagnetic radiation, the total harvested energy could be roughly five times greater. Based on the resulting emission from such a sphere, we find that a Dyson Sphere around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way (located 10 kpc away) should be detectable via waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet (10–400 nm), optical (400–760 nm), near-infrared (760 nm–5 μm), and mid-infrared (5–50 μm) bands. Additionally, an orbital velocity of $0.2c$ would generate a significant Doppler shift. Consequently, if these conditions are met, the sphere might also emit gravitational waves, although this is not guaranteed. Therefore, future astronomical missions should prioritize searching for Dyson Spheres around black holes within a few kiloparsecs. If these structures are as common as the habitable zones around main-sequence stars, they would be observable within the galaxy. Nevertheless, current data on supernova remnants suggest that the average star formation rate is so low that a Dyson Sphere around a black hole is likely rare on galactic scales. Consequently, we conclude that there is a low probability of existence for such spheres around stellar-mass or supermassive black holes. However, they may be more common around intermediate-mass black holes. These structures could potentially be detected through waste heat, orbital velocity effects, gravitational waves, or relativistic jets. Since their signatures are expected to appear in electromagnetic spectra and possibly in gravitational waves, multi-messenger astronomy is essential

are governed by Service Level Agreements (SLAs), necessitating rigorous monitoring to ensure compliance. A common approach utilizes active measurement mechanisms that deploy probes throughout the network to inject synthetic traffic and assess performance; however, this method is resource-intensive. Consequently, it typically covers only a subset of the network, risking missed SLA violations. Furthermore, the selection of this subset relies on human expertise, which may be both time-consuming and subjective. This paper introduces an automated system designed to select the most effective measurement subset for detecting SLA violations. Our proposed algorithm determines this optimal selection solely based on historical traffic patterns and past performance data, requiring no manual input. By leveraging machine learning techniques, the system identifies the subset of network links that maximizes the information gained from active measurements. Experimental results indicate that, despite using a reduced number of probes, our method outperforms manually selected subsets by at least 25% in terms of the number of detected violations. Additionally, the system successfully minimizes the volume of active traffic, thereby lowering both financial and environmental expenditures. In summary, our findings demonstrate that active measurement subsets can be selected automatically to maximize performance information, enabling more efficient SLA violation detection. This work also highlights that such selection can be optimized by considering the specific performance metrics being evaluated. Finally, the paper confirms that active measurement can be effectively utilized to detect network faults and failures. This research was funded by the Swedish Research Council (grant no. 2019-03932).
In this work, we address the challenge of selecting an optimal set of links for active performance measurements within a wireless local area network (WLAN). The primary objective is to maximize the informational value of these measurements for inferring unobserved link qualities, thereby minimizing the risk of overlooking performance violations in an energy-efficient manner. To achieve this, we formulate the problem as a combinatorial optimization task that minimizes an submodular objective function. We then present a greedy algorithm to compute the near-optimal subset of links that yields the richest data for energy-constrained active measurement schemes. Experimental validation confirms that our approach outperforms previously reported methods.
Wireless Shaping Codes (WSCs) were originally developed to mitigate co-channel interference in multi-user wireless local area networks (WLANs). Although effective, existing protocols lack mechanisms to adjust WSC transmission rates dynamically based on network conditions or to notify users when SLAs are breached. This paper investigates strategies for adaptively modifying WSC rates to maximize performance information for active end-to-end

accelerators, frequently serving as the primary constraint on the maximum achievable beam current. This concern is especially pertinent to multi-pass Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs), where even modest charge quantities can generate substantial beam currents. Recent investigations indicate that the selection of filling patterns and recirculation schemes in multi-pass ERLs significantly influences beam-RF interactions. This study further examines these dynamics to analyze how filling patterns impact beam breakup instability and to determine optimal design strategies that mitigate this effect. By presenting both a theoretical framework of beam-RF interaction and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the threshold current can fluctuate by factors of 2 to 4, or potentially more, contingent upon specific machine design parameters. Three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers, integral to the near detectors of next-generation long-baseline facilities, offer a solution. Before the discovery of neutrino oscillations, it was established that neutrons contain charged quarks and quark-antiquark pairs, with their properties inferred from deep inelastic scattering (DIS) of leptons off nucleons. Quark parton distribution functions (PDFs), which describe the momentum of quarks within nucleons, were subsequently extracted from DIS data. Although neutrino oscillations were discovered in the 1960s, precise oscillation parameters were not determined until neutrinos scattered off nucleons in the 1980s, revealing that neutrons consist of two "valence" quarks. This paper reviews the history of neutrons, beginning with Chadwick's discovery of the neutron in 1932, and examines how neutrino DIS data enabled the extraction of quark PDFs. It also discusses the connection between these findings and the discovery of neutrino oscillations, as both phenomena emerged from experiments at the same neutron scattering facilities. Finally, the paper speculates on the implications of these historical developments for reducing systematic uncertainties in future neutrino oscillation experiments.

This paper proposes the use of Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) to address these difficulties, allowing for the integration of arbitrary linear and nonlinear constraints. EKMP modifies the objective function and penalty terms of previous methods to accommodate these constraints, effectively avoiding collisions with dynamic and static obstacles, satisfying joint limits and other task-specific limitations (both linear and nonlinear), and achieving competitive performance in robotic arm planning tasks compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. We derive tight bounds on the social welfare achievable with a polynomial number of queries. While these general bounds indicate only a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal welfare, significantly better approximations emerge when valuations originate from specific combinatorial structures. For instance, when valuations correspond to bipartite matchings, directed graph arborescences, or Boolean satisfiability, simple query-efficient algorithms achieve a $2$-approximation. We also address truthfulness concerns, demonstrating how certain algorithms can be made truthful via VCG-like payments. Furthermore, we define and analyze the "price of serial dictatorship," a metric offering an optimistic assessment of the solution quality produced by action sequences in combinatorial optimization. We provide general upper and lower bounds for this metric and establish tight bounds for specific valuation types. Notably, although the price of serial dictatorship is at most $2$ for all valuations, we construct counterintuitive counterexamples showing that randomly selected action sequences yield significantly worse outcomes. To mitigate this variability, we define a "variance of serial dictatorship" and prove that medians of randomly ordered serial dictatorship processes yield at most a $\sqrt{2}$-approximation. We also examine other combinatorial settings where the price of serial dictatorship remains at most e factor of $2$. Beyond theoretical analysis, we present a computational study on scheduling tasks on machines to highlight the substantial performance gains of serial dictatorship over randomly chosen action sequences. Additionally, we explore "warm starts," where agents refine actions to improve outcomes for subsequent agents rather than acting solely in self-interest. Even without true altruism, this setup yields approximations of optimal welfare exceeding $1.5$ with high probability. Finally, we define an "inverse serial dictatorship" mechanism where a central planner predicts valuations for all subsets of agents, uses this information to determine the optimal action for each agent, and subsequently predicts the resulting social welfare. In this work, we introduce a cohort-based susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) epidemic model featuring an asymptomatic class. Unlike prior models, infection rates for symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals differ, and the proportion of asymptomatic infectives is treated as an endogenous state variable. This creates a feedback loop where reduced isolation and contact avoidance by the asymptomatic group elevate infection risks, thereby increasing the overall asymptomatic infection rate. We provide formulas for the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) and the steady-state proportion of asymptomatic infectives. Notably, $R_0$ functions as a threshold parameter that separates scenarios where epidemics fade versus those where they persist. Furthermore, we prove that the SIS model may exhibit multiple bifurcations, leading to up to four positive equilibria. Consequently, the system's dynamics can be extremely complex, potentially involving backward bifurcations and a destabilizing Hopf bifurcation. A simulation on a population divided into four geographic cohorts illustrates these dynamics. The findings indicate that non-pharmaceutical interventions must be carefully coordinated across cohorts and over time to avoid destabilizing an initially fading epidemic. These insights offer crucial guidance for applying such measures to mitigate the risks of a rebounding epidemic, particularly in scenarios involving travel between regions with varying infection rates and asymptomatic proportions.

By quantitatively analyzing crustal deformation within the Central and West African rift zones, we have reconstructed the kinematic history of the pre-breakup evolution of the conjugate West African and Brazilian margins. Recent paleomagnetic analyses of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) suggest a protracted opening of the central Atlantic, spanning from the Valanginian to the Hauterivian. However, these findings conflict with established biostratigraphic and structural data regarding the final separation of Ghana and Brazil, which indicates an earlier breakup no later than the Hauterivian-Barremian boundary. By integrating recent magnetic field models with recent paleomagnetic reconstructions of CAMP, we outline a revised sequence for the initial stages of the central Atlantic opening. Specifically, we postulate that a localized weakening of the lithosphere along the present-day equatorial African margin during the Valanginian led to a minor widening of the Galway fracture zone between West Africa and the equatorial American plate. This process pulled the African margin away from the equatorial American plate and contributed to the infilling of the minor Valanginian step-over. While contrastive learning is a popular method that generates discriminative representations by creating positive and negative pairs, constructing meaningful pairs for segmentation tasks remains challenging in an unsupervised setting. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised pre-training framework that circumvents the limitations of contrastive learning. This approach is grounded in two core principles: employing unsupervised over-segmentation as a pre-training objective via mutual information maximization, and implementing boundary-aware preserving learning. Experiments conducted on two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate that our method effectively improves segmentation performance even with limited annotated images. Additionally, results from extended experiments on natural image segmentation further validate the model's generalization capabilities. Consequently, our code and experiments are accessible via the following link: https://github.com/Medicalzhang/UMPS.

To facilitate this study, we utilize Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) as our experimental platform; this role-playing game involves multiple player characters and a Dungeon Master (DM) who work together to reach shared objectives beneficial to the players. In this context, each player character represents a student with unique personas and capabilities, while the DM acts as the teacher, serving as the rule arbiter and guide responsible for helping students reach a global objective. We develop a theory-of-mind-inspired approach to train such a DM using reinforcement learning (RL). This methodology involves two key steps: first, the DM learns to anticipate player reactions to its statements by analyzing a dataset of D&D dialogue transcripts, and second, it employs these predictions as a reward function to evaluate how effectively its utterances guide players toward their goals. Both human and automated evaluations demonstrate that training a DM with RL to incorporate a theory-of-mind perspective significantly enhances the players' capacity to achieve goals grounded in their shared world. Additionally, we envision that this approach could be adapted to train helpful assistants capable of guiding users toward specific objectives, such as helping students grasp difficult concepts. We release our datasets and models as the D&D Corpus (dcorpus.org) to support future research. We further discuss the potential dangers and benefits of applying DM's theory-of-mind learning within the contexts of communicated AI and role-playing, noting that the source code for our experiments is available on GitHub.

We present TugOfWarDialogues (WOD), a dataset consisting of over 25,000 multi-turn conversation snippets featuring two opposing agents debating contradictory claims about a shared world state. These counter-arguments are essential for tasks including fact verification, rumor detection, and argumentation. To encourage world-state-aware counter-argument generation, we employ an asymmetric reinforcement learning framework to train an agent capable of producing compelling refutations of statements that contradict its prior commitments. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses baseline techniques in generating accurate counter-arguments that align with the intended semantics of the given world state.

This paper advocates shifting the focus from mere detection to discovery, specifically identifying novel word senses emerging over time across the entire vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both token-based and type-based approaches on recently published German data, we demonstrate that these models can effectively uncover words undergoing meaning shifts. Additionally, we present an almost fully automated framework for both discovery and evaluation. Our extensive experimental results confirm that both model types are capable of finding these changes, with the type-based approach proving more effective, particularly in identifying recently acquired meaning changes. Both methods significantly outperform a simple statistical baseline in an evaluation involving professional annotators. However, our findings also reveal that a notable portion of newly discovered instances represents truly novel terminology rather than evolving context. Furthermore, we estimate that a substantial number of our findings are either very recent additions to language usage or result from polarisation, where a word's usage splits into distinct, opposing contexts. Finally, we note that a significant fraction of these discoveries may be erroneously classified as context-specific terminology. Our code and data are available online.

In a related study, we addressed the challenge of detecting words experiencing a drift in meaning over time. Unlike previous work centered on recognizing a limited set of pre-selected target items, our approach aims to identify instances of meaning drift and newly emerging context across the full vocabulary. We introduced two indicators for this phenomenon: a contextual one based on contextualized embeddings and a compositional one relying on distributed word representations and n-grams. Tested on two large German corpora, our methods were evaluated against a gold standard consisting of manually selected positive examples and typical baselines. We found that both approaches can successfully discover meaningful meaning shifts and consistently outperform simple baselines. Our code and data remain accessible at https://flo-hahn.github.io/WordDrift/.

Our third contribution explores the potential of contextualized word representations for discovering locally changing language knowledge, such as newly emerging context. We introduced the term 'context exploration' to describe this process and proposed an adaptive algorithm termed 'contextialized word smoothing' to facilitate it. In experiments conducted on English and German, we demonstrated that this technique can uncover a substantial amount of previously unknown context, which we estimate constitutes approximately 20% to 40% of all usage. These findings indicate that contextualized embeddings can identify recently acquired context that standard methodologies either miss or mistake for newly coined terminology. Our code is available at https://flo-hahn.github.io/ContextExploration/.

Recent research categorizes the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by examining the distribution of their planar projections through topological entities known as knotoids. We adopt a similar analytical framework by developing a topologically grounded statistical metric to compare knotoid distributions among proteins sharing the same topology. Our method identifies geometric variations between trefoil proteins by quantifying their entanglement and successfully recovers clusters based on sequence similarity. By directly investigating the geometry and topology of native states, we can explore distinct folding pathways in proteins that form open-ended trefoil knots. Notably, our pipeline indicates that the folding process of shallowly knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the formation of a double-looped structure, a finding that contrasts with previous observations regarding deeply knotted trefoil proteins. We corroborate these results using Molecular Dynamics simulations. We anticipate that this approach will be applicable to a broad range of systems, including those with ambiguous topology, and will aid in defining the structural landscape of intermediate states in protein folding. This study benefits from the open-source python-gearbox library (https://github.com/maoripa/python-gearbox).

Knots are inherent in many man-made and natural systems, yet their presence in proteins has long been a subject of debate. While some studies suggest that certain biological functions drive the formation of specific knot types, others propose that these topologies arise as accidental byproducts of evolution. We investigate the geometry of native states and folding pathways in sharply bent, symmetric, open-ended trefoil proteins. Our analysis reveals that the geometry is defined by two primary parameters: the size of the central hole and the symmetry of the configuration. We anticipate that this method can be widely applied to analyze diverse groups of knotted proteins, potentially uncovering new categories of topologically equivalent proteins that differ in their geometric characteristics.

dark energy component in the early universe proposed to resolve the Hubble tension. However, the scientific community has not yet reached a consensus on whether EDE can simultaneously alleviate this tension while adequately fitting Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and large-scale structure data. This study deconstructs existing constraints from Planck CMB observations and full-shape clustering data from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) to clarify the sources of conflicting conclusions found in previous literature. By employing two distinct analytical methods—grid sampling and profile likelihood—we investigate whether current constraints are skewed by volume effects during marginalization or biased toward specific values of the EDE fraction, $f_\mathrm{EDE}$. Our results indicate that the data-allowed range for $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ is highly sensitive to the choice of other model parameters, with certain parameter configurations favoring larger $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ values than those derived from standard Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analyses. This sensitivity suggests that volume effects are the primary cause of the discrepancies in the field. Consequently, we apply a simple profile likelihood approach to the EDE model to calculate a robust upper limit for $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ that is resilient to these effects. Using this approach, we derive $f_\mathrm{EDE} \lesssim 0.15$ at 95% confidence for the full EDE model, and $f_\mathrm{EDE} \lesssim 0.06$ at 95% confidence when the EDE equation of state is fixed to match the ΛCDM value ($w_\mathrm{EDE} = -1$). These limits are comparable to, or weaker than, those from models varying two components but are superior to limits from models with a single component being varied. Finally, we demonstrate how the profile likelihood method can be integrated into MCMC analyses and use it to establish robust lower limits for $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ within both the complete EDE framework and the more restricted $w_{-1}cdm$ model. Our analysis confirms that the EDE model can relieve the Hubble tension up to $\Delta \chi^2 \sim 9$, equivalent to $3\sigma$, without violating constraints from combined Planck full CMB and BOSS full-shape clustering data. We hope this work serves as a robust framework for future investigations into the EDE hypothesis. Comments are available at http://www.home.zhaokai.org/hubble

We consider a compact, exact, symplectic 3-manifold $X$ that contains at least two non-boundable exact Lagrangian curves. We prove that the fundamental group $\pi_1(X)$ must be trivial. This extends a previous finding by the second and third authors, which established that the presence of two heteroclinic orbits in a constant magnetic flow on a closed, genus-2 Riemann surface forces the underlying Riemann surface to be with bounds. Furthermore, if $X$ contains a closed exact Lagrangian curve whose linking number with every other such curve is rationally trivial, then $\pi_1(X) = \mathbb{Z}$. The investigation focuses on mathematical foundations spanning Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The basis of the NG boson counting law in the anomalous context is explored through both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. A quasi-Heisenberg algebra is identified as a generic feature across various symmetry-breaking schemes of the anomalous NG theorem; this algebra suggests a violation or modification of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation within the NG sector, a phenomenon that is potentially verifiable experimentally. The formalism of the effective potential is introduced to elucidate the mechanism of the anomalous NG theorem using the derived Lie algebra results. Following an examination of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential as an explicit Lorentz-symmetry-breaking parameter, a general model Lagrangian approach to the anomalous NG theorem is proposed. This analysis not only determines the conditions for the counting law of true NG bosons but also reveals the mechanism for generating the mass of massive NG bosons. Furthermore, the emergence of a massive mode in the NG sector is interpreted through the quantum uncertainty relation of the Heisenberg algebra, which arises from Lie algebra symmetry breaking and is realized within the effective potential of the kaon condensation model. Based on this perspective, the general implications of the anomalous NG theorem are summarized. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the general significance of NG bosons in the early Universe and cosmology, along with suggestions for future research directions. This analysis offers a comprehensive and model-independent understanding of the anomalous NG theorem, filling critical gaps in the theoretical formulation of general NG boson counting laws and massive NG modes. Additionally, it clarifies the underlying mechanisms of the counting law and massive mode generation in specific models, such as the charged boson sigma model and the Ginzburg-Landau-Loggartlandau (GLLL) superconductivity model. These findings also offer new insights into the massive Higgs boson within the Standard Model. The research further proposes a novel and insightful method for constructing effective models on the critical surface near a second-order phase transition. Ultimately, this work provides valuable insights into the theoretical framework of the massive Higgs boson in the post-Higgs boson discovery era at CERN. To overcome these challenges, we present DISCO, a novel framework designed to automatically produce high-quality counterfactual data at scale. Nevertheless, definitive experimental proof of this remote mechanism has remained absent. Frequently, contaminants at the graphene/substrate interface allow alternative processes, such as pinhole-seeded lateral or van der Waals epitaxy, to account for the formation of exfoliable single-crystalline films. In this study, we demonstrate that growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene atop sapphire substrates yields a 30-degree rotated epitaxial superstructure that neither pinhole nor van der Waals epitaxy can explain. As growth temperature decreases, the proportion of this 30-degree domain rises relative to the direct 0-degree epitaxial domain; we attribute this to reduced surface diffusion at lower temperatures, which promotes remote epitaxy, whereas higher temperatures facilitate longer diffusion lengths that favor pinhole epitaxy. Furthermore, we establish that achieving epitaxy on clean graphene without pinhole-seeded mechanisms is possible even with substantial mismatches exceeding 10°. Heusler films can be remotely epitaxied on clean graphene with mismatches as large as those observed, and the stability of the resulting 30-degree rotated superstructure suggests that this approach is universally applicable to any epitaxial scenario not accounted for by van der Waals or pinhole epitaxy. This work provides the first robust evidence of remote epitaxy, offering new insights into how contaminants at the graphene/substrate interface can obstruct these growth pathways. Ultimately, our findings indicate that remote epitaxy on clean graphene can produce exfoliable, magnetically ordered Heusler films at temperatures accessible near or below current heating capabilities. This strategy holds promise for expanding the range of achievable epitaxy, potentially encompassing alloys and compounds currently deemed impossible due to significant mismatches, substrate reconstruction, multilayer formation, or toxic/reactive constituents, thereby eliminating the need for clean substrates as the sole prerequisite for epitaxy.

To address this, this study investigates the "single positive" scenario, where each data instance is labeled with only one positive tag and lacks explicit negative labels. Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed the maximum overlap between two metric balls of radius $r$, provided their centers are separated by at least distance $d$. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations using Hamming distance. Within this framework, we define a Cayley graph and calculate the precise value of the largest intersection of two metric balls under Hamming distance for the cases where $r=4$ and $d\geqslant 5$, as well as when $d=2r$. These calculations are fundamental to addressing the sequence reconstruction problem. Consequently, we establish that for $r=4$ and $d\geqslant 5$, at least 19 channels are required to guarantee the unique recovery of a permutation of length $n$ from a specific set of permutations, given that the sequence is at distance $d$ from any other sequence within the set. This finding slightly improves upon the previous best threshold of 18 channels. Furthermore, for the scenario where $r=d-1$, we demonstrate that at least $r+1$ channels are needed to ensure unique recovery. This result represents a significant advancement over the prior threshold of $4r$, which was previously known only for specific values of $r$. The primary contribution of this work is the release of MADDOG, a novel framework for disambiguating acronyms by integrating context and coreference information during inference. Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-rigid pendulum model that enables a clear discussion of the emergence of antiferromagnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum," alongside phenomena such as large-amplitude pair oscillations and atom-molecule entanglement. Finally, based on entangled atom-molecule states, we propose a viable scheme for generating entangled spin states of "spin-1" by utilizing an effective Hamiltonian equivalent to Ising interaction. This proposal offers a potential new method for producing entangled spin-1 bosons, which is essential for implementing quantum error correction in spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates. The theoretical framework presented here may provide an alternative pathway for creating entangled spin-1 bosons through two-body interactions.

Entropy can be defined for quantum states that are not in equilibrium, particularly when described by the more general positive semi-definite operators known as $\mathcal{L}$-divergences. This paper introduces a specific measure called quantum $L$-entropy, formulated as the time derivative of an appropriate $L$-divergence for an initial state not in equilibrium. This measure captures the rate of entropy change as the system evolves toward its final equilibrium state. We establish several of its fundamental properties, including non-negativity, monotonicity, and strong subadditivity. Notably, the effective temperature associated with this entropy can be negative, even when the initial state lacks a thermal distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated entropy flux, representing the heat exchange rate with the heat bath, can also be negative. The formulation of quantum $L$-entropy offers a potential new perspective on the entropies of non-equilibrium states.

Instead of encoding each fragment individually, we group them into "pages," where every page carries a unique EB. This approach leverages the vast capacity of modern high-throughput sequencing, which can process up to one terabase of data in a single run, to pack entire pages of EBs onto single DNA molecules. Consequently, digital information is stored across a field of EBs rather than in isolated bits within each molecule, allowing a single hard drive to hold $10^{16}$ times more information than typical DNA-storage systems. A key innovation is the use of editable EBs, which can be rewritten in situ using CRISPR technology without the overhead of molecular assembly. We have implemented both binary and LC-based (Logic-10) EB encoding schemes and evaluated them through comprehensive sequence-simulation tests, which identified and corrected errors and weaknesses in the page design. Finally, we propose using high-throughput sequencing to read these EBs via efficient matrix factorization algorithms. Building on these findings, we are constructing a hardware prototype to validate the end-to-end endogeneity of this page-based DNA-storage framework. The source code for the error correction algorithms presented here is available at https://github.com/shlomo-ben-shachar/EB-HR.

Although numerous studies attempt to enhance model robustness against adversarial attacks by utilizing data from untrusted sources, there remains a lack of understanding regarding the attacks themselves, their defenses, and, most critically, the underlying nature of the corruption. Even researchers with extensive expertise in specific sub-areas of robust machine learning have previously noted the field's fragmentation. Furthermore, existing surveys often fail to address the fundamental categories of noise and attacks adequately. To remedy this, we present an overview of adversarial machine learning that offers a unified perspective on various attacks and corruption types, suitable for applications ranging from machine learning to virology. By employing a framework of Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Recovered (SEIR), we view data as susceptible, which becomes exposed and subsequently infected due to corruption. Additionally, we propose several extensions to this classical model.

ytic fixed bed reactors hinge on managing internal temperature distribution; however, achieving in situ temperature measurements with both spatial and temporal resolution remains difficult. This study addresses this challenge by utilizing real-time magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) alongside the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF) shift of water to measure temperatures within a cylindrical fixed bed. This MR thermometry approach offers new avenues for investigating mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds and holds potential for future application to reactive gas-solid systems. More importantly, this work paves the way for developing an in situ thermometry method capable of monitoring temperature fields in industrial gas-solid fixed bed reactors. Resolving temperature fields in these systems is critical not only for determining reaction kinetics and optimizing operations but also for managing safety when dealing with highly exothermic processes. Additionally, the methods demonstrated here may be adapted for use in batch crystallizers. The techniques presented in this work are transferable to magnetic tomographs commonly found in chemical engineering research facilities or even medical centers. In our specific case, we employed a clinical 1.5~T MRI scanner. Our results further indicate that PRF-based MR thermometry can effectively capture temperature distributions during adiabatic, non-isothermal gas-solid fixed bed reactions, even when significant gradients are present. This approach represents a first step toward future applications in mass and heat transfer studies and potentially reactive gas-solid fixed bed reactions. Finally, the methods and equipment described here are affordable, making them accessible for extensive use in magnetic tomographs at chemical engineering research centers or within medical settings.

Myocardial mechanical behavior is modeled using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, which are discretized via finite elements to generate large-scale nonlinear algebraic systems. These systems are solved using a Newton-Krylov method, with BDDC/AMG preconditioners accelerating the resolution of the Jacobian linear systems. To ensure a fair comparison, we comprehensively investigate key BDDC parameters, specifically examining the performance of various direct solvers for local and coarse problems, the effects of different choices for BDDC primal degrees of freedom, and the impact of finite element shape functions. Scalability assessments are conducted across diverse mesh types, including structured 2D and 3D grids, as well as unstructured 3D tetrahedral and hexahedral biological meshes. Additionally, the numerical experiments adhere to the minimum requirements of a realistic cardiac simulation, incorporating anatomically accurate boundary conditions and a cyclic gait. Our scalability results demonstrate that the proposed method can solve systems with over one million unknowns in under three minutes on a single CPU core, a capability essential for coupling with other processes in a simulation workflow. Ultimately, this research provides insights into the performance of computational mechanics simulations in cardiac modeling. The code employed in this work is open-source and available at https://github.com/marcelo-casquilleros/Cardiac-Mechanics.

While traditionally created by professionals—a process that demands significant time, labor, and resources—the rise of AI-empowered persuasive video generation (AIPVG) has made large-scale content production more feasible. As an interdisciplinary field, AIPVG can be difficult for newcomers to navigate, and to date, no comprehensive survey has addressed it. This paper fills that void by examining essential AI techniques for automatically crafting persuasive videos. We present an original taxonomy categorizing AIPVG into three core stages: 1) visual material understanding, which identifies relevant information from visual assets; 2) visual storyline generation, which selects and sequences high-quality assets to construct a compelling narrative; and 3) post-production, which includes generating background music and animating stills to improve the viewer experience. Furthermore, we outline standard evaluation metrics and datasets used in this area, critique the strengths and limitations of current approaches within these stages, and explore promising avenues for future research. Finally, we provide references to help readers locate relevant publications and studies on AIPVG. In summary, this survey offers foundational insights into AI-driven persuasive video generation to facilitate future advancements in the field.

Recently, researchers have attempted to establish evaluation protocols for evaluating large language models (LLMs). However, these efforts often lack empirical data, remain confined to specific model families or task categories, and, most critically, offer limited practical utility for assessing professional-grade evaluations. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework comprising three components: an automated method to extract claims from videos, a dataset of 10,000 videos spanning diverse categories, and a technique to measure semantic alignment between LLM-generated summaries and the extracted claims. Our findings reveal a significant gap in the current state-of-the-art, highlighting the need for further work in video understanding. Specifically, we demonstrate that recent methods and even prominent LLMs fail to accurately evaluate high-quality summaries produced by professional systems. To support this observation, we have released our code and resources at https://github.com/zhiyihuang/VideoEval.

Although defenses relying on this trait are deemed ineffective and vulnerable to bypass, there remains a significant gap in methods for quantifying gradient masking and comparing its magnitude across various networks. This work shifts the perspective from viewing gradient masking as a binary condition to analyzing it through the lens of measurability. We introduce and justify multiple metrics for this phenomenon, supported by extensive empirical evaluations on defenses suspected of varying degrees of masking. These metrics are computationally efficient compared to robust attacks, facilitate inter-model comparisons, and eliminate the need for resource-intensive, custom attacks tailored to specific architectures. Our findings demonstrate that these proposed metrics effectively capture the extent of gradient masking across different neural networks. By standardizing the measurement of this attack surface, our methods enable researchers to assess how strong or weak the gradient masking effect is in a given defense network. This insight is crucial for advancing the development of truly robust adversarial defenses. Empirical results are accessible at: https://github.com/Noah-DeVries/Measuring-Gradient-Masking.

### 1 Introduction

Recent advancements have clearly demonstrated that many proposed adversarial defenses suffer from gradient masking (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Metaxas et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). While this behavior causes models to appear resistant to current attacks, it does not guarantee protection against future, potentially stronger, methods. The community urgently requires a reliable method to measure this attribute across a spectrum of defenses, a challenge that remains largely unaddressed. Effectively quantifying gradient masking would allow us to evaluate its presence not just as a binary state, but with greater nuance. Furthermore, such measurement could guide the development of attacks specifically designed to overcome different magnitudes of this effect.

### 2 Background

Adversarial examples are images tweaked so subtly that humans can't detect them, yet they trigger wrong predictions in machine learning models. Creating these examples involves an optimization process that adjusts the image to maximize the model's confidence in the wrong answer. Many proposed defenses against this threat are criticized for masking gradients—the information guiding the optimization. This means the model *appears* resistant because the gradients are hidden, but it's not actually secure. We need a way to measure this gradient masking, especially since some models might mask it more than others.

In this paper, we examine the well-posedness of the magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations within an ideal torus domain, where the torus geometry is defined by the magnitude and the direction of the magnetic field. Based on recent findings indicating global well-posedness for initially small data in $\mathbb {R}^3$ \cite{LP2019}, we establish a similar result for ideally conducting MHD in an ideal torus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the norm of the magnetic field in $L^\infty (\mathbb {T^2},L^2 ([0,1]))$, a quantity closely linked to blood pressure in biological applications, is conserved over time. These results extend to other periodic domains as well.

We explore the concept of optimality for solutions to variational problems involving nonconvex functionals, specifically focusing on the lack of lower semicontinuity in $BV$ space. To address this, we introduce and characterize the notion of rescalable functionals, which encompasses most standard examples. For such functionals, we prove the existence of $\Gamma$-reducible measures and demonstrate that optimality can be fully characterized by this property, thereby generalizing a result previously established for Sobolev functionals. Additionally, we illustrate the practical application of this concept through examples.

We contend that this failure to represent uncertainty stems primarily from the closed-world assumption inherent in the softmax function, which compels models trained via cross-entropy loss to assign high probability to one of $K$ predefined categories. To resolve this, we introduce a novel $K$+1 softmax formulation that integrates open-world uncertainty as an additional dimension. This approach facilitates the simultaneous learning of accurate closed-world discrimination and robust open-world uncertainty. To implement this dual objective, we propose a straightforward energy-based objective that encourages approximate maximum likelihood matching between the true data distribution and the model's output distribution. Our experimental findings across multiple benchmarks and tasks demonstrate significant improvements in open-world uncertainty modeling compared to existing methods, with minimal impact on closed-world accuracy. Consequently, our method equips deep learning systems with the capability to signal when they encounter unfamiliar inputs. This paper introduces a discovery algorithm that generates Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs representing declarative processes from event streams. Dynamic processes are increasingly common, yet current process discovery techniques mainly apply to static scenarios. To address this gap, we introduced a method for constructing process models in a declarative format from event streams. The core innovation lies in treating process changes as typical event stream data, followed by a technique for identifying and representing these variations. We developed a quantitative approach to measure discrepancies between declarative process representations and qualified them against changes in a process database. Additionally, we demonstrated how process variations can be understood qualitatively. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed technique effectively captures process changes. The core methodology is available at: https://processchanges.delftuniversity.nl/.

Process mining typically assumes that processes remain unchanged over time, a limitation that hinders its effectiveness when changes do occur. Existing change detection methods often rely on costly additional information, such as BPMN diagrams or operational logs. Furthermore, when processes are defined declaratively, no specialized change detection technique is currently available. This paper presents a novel approach for identifying process changes directly from event data. We propose three distinct techniques for this task and validate them using processes from the BEPS dataset. Our results show that these methods can accurately capture three types of changes: the introduction of new activities, the emergence of new activity relationships, and the addition of new activity attributes. These techniques function exclusively on event data, requiring no prior knowledge of the processes under analysis. The core technology is demonstrated via a website at: https://processchanges.delftuniversity.nl/.

Although processes are inherently dynamic and change over time, process mining often treats them as static, focusing on reconciling process definitions with event logs to reveal discrepancies. When definitions and logs align well, the process is deemed "mineable." This study examines three strategies for incorporating process dynamics into mining activities.

**Reentrant Localization in One-Dimensional Quasiperiodic Photonic Crystals**

We examine the propagation of light in one-dimensional quasiperiodic optical lattices, specifically focusing on the Fibonacci sequence. Numerical simulations indicate that for certain eigenstates, the localization transition becomes sharp and can exhibit a remarkable pattern: states initially localized by weak quasiperiodic potentials become delocalized as the modulation strength increases, and vice versa. This "reentrant localization" is caused by the fractal structure of the eigenvalue spectrum in quasiperiodic systems. We also demonstrate that the phenomenon can be qualitatively understood through a long-range dimerized tight-binding model. Our study provides a methodology for investigating localization and the Hofstadter butterfly in photonic quasicrystals.

Previous proof-of-concept studies and certain two-dimensional experiments have demonstrated that spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) maximizes collected field information, thereby achieving resolution that surpasses the Rayleigh criterion. To date, SPADE methods have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction. In this work, we examine a scenario involving a bi-photon source generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, where a horizontal separation is applied to one of the photons. We demonstrate that a separation introduced in the signal photon arm can be super-resolved through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes. Notably, the Fisher information linked to this measurement is enhanced by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$ compared to standard SPADE techniques, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number of the two-photon state, a metric quantifying the spatial entanglement between the photons. Consequently, this approach yields a significant gain in quantum efficiency, rendering it especially advantageous for experiments involving low-light conditions. To illustrate the practical viability of this technique, we use a simulated scenario showing that it can yield a measurable factor of 1.5 improvement in resolution.

This study examines a two-trophic ecosystem involving two predator species that compete for a shared prey resource, incorporating explicit interference competition. Through appropriate rescaling, the system is modeled as a singularly perturbed setup characterized by rapid prey dynamics and slower predator dynamics. Near a singular Hopf bifurcation, the model exhibits chaotic mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs), which consist of concatenated small and large amplitude oscillations and act as prolonged transients before the system settles into its asymptotic state. To identify the dynamical trigger for a large amplitude oscillation within an MMO orbit, the model is simplified to a normal form near the singular-Hopf point. This normal form includes a separatrix surface that distinguishes between the two oscillation types; a large amplitude oscillation begins when a trajectory crosses from the "inner" to the "outer" side of this surface. Furthermore, specific conditions on the normal form variables are derived to predict whether a trajectory will undergo additional MMO cycles before a regime shift occurs. These derived conditions offer potential early warning signs for sudden population shifts in ecosystems. In the presented model, regime shifts result from large amplitude MMOs that drive one predator species to local extinction. Alternatively, if this predator can regenerate through a Allee effect, the system may return to the coexistence state via a smaller MMO. The proposed prediction method for regime shifts is not limited to ecological systems capable of exhibiting MMOs; it can also be adapted for other systems by determining the conditions under which their trajectories intersect a "dangerous" region of the phase space. Additional criteria for predicting regime shifts in those contexts may include approaching a critical threshold, specific pattern formation events, or the onset of a chaotic attractor.

To achieve a sustainable increase in crop yields, understanding the complex interactions within plant roots and their surrounding soil is essential. These root systems naturally organize into a repeating structural pattern known as the "root palm." To explore how root ensembles react to changes in the solid-to-fluid ratio, we developed numerical simulations based on the immersed boundary method. These simulations model the dynamics of multiple flexible fibers interacting with a viscous fluid. Our results demonstrate that as the fluid-to-solid ratio decreases, the overall drag force on the fluid rises significantly, while the power required to sustain a given Reynolds number drops. By analyzing the flow fields and stress distributions generated by these multi-fiber assemblies under varying viscous conditions, our model provides insights into the coupled dynamics of individual organisms and their environment. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n$>2.0 exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n$<2.0, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. This implies that bulge star formation depends more strongly on $n$ (or central mass density) than on the B/T ratio. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 rises sharply with mass for $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. Since the likelihood of having an $n$>2.0 body increases with a larger disc, this suggests that in massive galaxies, the more evolved (redder) bulges result from bulge formation or processing driven by the surrounding disc. Consequently, bulge processing by the disc contributes to the observed flattening of the MS at high masses. This finding aligns with the scenario where gas in the bulge is replenished from the surrounding disc, and the degree of replenishment varies with the system's shape. These data also support models where the transition from small to large $n$ occurs at a fixed galaxy mass within the body, but at different radii. Finally, we note that the results for $n$ are robust against a $\sim10\%$ uncertainty in size measurements. These conclusions are derived in models where gas surface density is constant (or rises only slightly) across the whole disc but is significantly higher in the bulge, and where the timescale for processing bulge gas is longer than a Hubble time. Nevertheless, these mechanisms induce memory instruction reordering, leading to unintended program behaviors. We introduce a new formal model that encapsulates the semantics of programs executing under such protocols, incorporating a set of fences that interface with the coherence layer. Leveraging this model, we developed an algorithm to analyze reachability and verify if a program adheres to a specified safety property given the current fences. Furthermore, we present a technique for inserting optimal fence sets to guarantee program correctness. This approach employs a counter-example guided insertion strategy and supports diverse fence types with varying costs, requiring the optimization of total cost rather than merely the count of fences. To validate our methodology, we implemented a prototype and tested it across numerous examples and benchmarks, subsequently evaluating the performance of the resulting fenced versions in a simulated hardware environment. Our findings indicate that while reaching data hazards necessitates fence types offering extensive visibility into the coherence protocol, ensuring correct program behavior can be achieved without any fences in many instances. Furthermore, we observe that the time required for our verified programs to complete on simulated hardware differs significantly from that of unverified executions, as the latter encounter incorrect behaviors such as infinite loops and crashes. The implementation of this work is available at https://github.com/zhanmaobing/coherence-fencing.

In multi-core systems employing fine-grained caches, developers often face challenges in writing programs that are simultaneously correct and performant. We propose a technique for automatically introducing cache-friendly synchronization, termed as downgrading-synchronized last-level caching (DSLLC). This approach supports various forms of synchronization, from coarse to extremely fine-grained, utilizes private caches for each core, incorporates a sophisticated priority-based schedule for main memory accesses, and ensures that program correctness can be guaranteed in the absence of hazards. Regarding performance, our solutions demonstrate superior speed compared to counterparts using equivalent fine-grained caching, as evidenced by both experimental analysis and a theoretical consideration of execution time. Additionally, we present methods for optimizing main memory access schedules to enhance performance further.

For programs utilizing fine-grained cache sharing, ensuring correctness may necessitate frequent updates or migrations of cached data, potentially sacrificing performance. To mitigate this, we suggest restricting data movement within the cache or to main memory based on specific properties, such as safety, which minimizes moves for correct execution, and liveness, which prioritizes performance by limiting movements to what is required for correctness. Our experimental results indicate that this restriction can lead to significant performance improvements.

Chaos, often defined as deterministic randomness, represents a complex phenomenon where non-linear deterministic systems exhibit behavior indistinguishable from stochastic stochastic systems under specific conditions. While extensive research has been conducted on this topic, a unified theoretical framework remains elusive. In this paper, we utilize the JK method to explore the chaos characteristics of the Henon-Heiles system within both classical and quantum regimes. Our results indicate a quantitative correspondence in the phase space structures of classical and quantum non-linear chaos, specifically showing that classical chaos can emerge in classically integrable (non-chaotic) quantum states and vice versa. Additionally, we find that the Lyapunov exponent in the classical limit converges to its classical value as $\hbar$ approaches zero. These discoveries provide a quantitative description of the interaction between classical and quantum chaos and offer potential avenues for observing quantum chaos in actual experiments. Our work suggests that the coexistence of classical and quantum chaos can be achieved in systems governed by separable one-body Hamiltonians through appropriate selection of initial conditions.

Recent efforts have focused on detecting lesions in ICU patients via deep learning. Furthermore, to tackle low-frequency, challenging false positives characterized by high spatial ambiguity, we enhance SABRA's spatial modeling capabilities through two mechanisms: a lightweight multi-head heterogeneous graph attention network (MH-GAT) for capturing global spatial object interactions, and a spatial mask decoder for learning local spatial configurations. We introduce a novel approach to detect road defects using a multi-sensor system that captures both visual data and the relative motion between the vehicle and the road. To enhance training data availability, we employ a synthetic dataset generated from images of a specific location, augmented with various defect types. Furthermore, we develop a neural network method tailored for poor lighting conditions. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed system significantly outperforms baseline models by a margin of over 15%. In comparisons against datasets from diverse geographical areas, our model achieves an F1 score of 78%. We also examine several transfer learning strategies, determining that a simple method yields the best results even when trained on a limited number of categories. Finally, we analyze performance across lighting conditions, reporting an mAP of 71% on data containing road defects.

We address the challenge of automatic sign language translation, which involves translating continuous sign language videos into textual language. While extensive research exists on this topic, it largely depends on datasets with high quality and ample lighting, leaving under-exposed low-light conditions under-explored. Although previous studies have explored single-image super-resolution, this strategy is ineffective for video translation due to temporal correlations and can even degrade performance. To mitigate low-light issues, we propose a simple yet effective approach where the model learns to translate from well-lit to low-light conditions while ignoring super-resolution. This method yields better results than incorporating super-resolution in the training pipeline. Additionally, we introduce the Larimar dataset, a collection of low-light sign language videos, and establish new benchmarks for sign language translation under these challenging conditions.

We present a method for detecting road defects under low-light conditions. Our approach utilizes a canonical network framework adapted with image enhancement networks at the input stage to convert low-light images into pseudocolorized pseudowell-lit images before processing. Foster's parallel processing vision, specifically addressing features like parallel writes and output value combination that are typically absent in standard CAM designs used for network routing. The resulting CAPP communicates with a host computer via a USB/UART interface through a simple serial protocol, which is demonstrated using a Python-based driver. A performance evaluation compares the proposed CAPP against both a sequential CPU implementation and a CAM realized on an Analog Devices SHADED FPGA, highlighting significant speedup factors achieved by the CAPP. These elements collectively illustrate how Content Addressable Memory can be transformed into a parallel processor that is accessible, cost-effective, and capable of outperforming both CPU and FPGA alternatives for specific tasks.

While many researchers and developers have created various versions of Content Addressable Memories (CAM) and Contents Addressable Memories (CAMe), which can function as simple associative memories or more complex parallel processors, this paper focuses on the latter. Following a review of existing work, we outline a comprehensive set of features for an enhanced Contents Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP). Although a full parallel implementation was beyond the scope of this project, we successfully implemented a simplified two-channel parallel variant with support for an external function interface. This specific implementation was then evaluated against its expected performance benchmarks.

Although FPGAs are a natural choice for prototyping CAM designs, which is the central topic of this article, there has been a notable lack of attention to providing these devices with appropriate I/O interfaces. Typically, only a few addresses are accessible via on-chip JTAG, while the majority require lengthy off-chip methods, such as reading from an SRAM through a serial peripheral interface (SPI). To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a minimal protocol designed to easily access the vast majority of the CAM memory space from the host system.

The core objective of this work is to develop a simple interface suitable for controlling and accessing a large number of addresses within an FPGA-based CAM. To illustrate the utility and necessity of this interface, the article uses the example of a search engine, where efficiently accessing stored data is crucial for the system's functionality.

Each galaxy features compact, kiloparsec-scale starburst cores with characteristics indicative of forming bulges, situated within extended, massive stellar disks. Notably, these disks are both distinctly quiescent and severely asymmetric. This configuration suggests that "outside-in" quenching is actively occurring in these group members. We propose that the significant asymmetry in the old stellar components (traceable in both the optical and sub-millimeter bands) provides robust evidence of recent major mergers, which trigger the inside-out quenching of gas disk stars. As these group galaxies continue to evolve, they will likely develop the quiescent, asymmetric stellar halos and central starbursts observed, consistent with the merging formation of massive galaxies. This process paves the way for the evolution of group galaxies into the symmetric, bulge-forming quenched systems seen in lower redshift clusters. These findings offer a novel perspective on the influence of major mergers during rapid assembly and emphasize the value of high-resolution multi-wavelength studies in analyzing the physical structure of high-redshift galaxies. This approach is crucial for formulating robust scenarios for the assembly of massive galaxies, particularly those with kinematically decoupled stellar components.

Specifically, we implemented a custom Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to thoroughly scan the model's viable parameter space, incorporating both leading and next-to-leading terms from its effective operator product expansion. For the first time, we derive robust UTZ predictions for the poorly constrained leptonic CP-violating phases and ratio observables associated with neutrino masses, as determined by oscillation, $\beta$-decay, and cosmological data. Furthermore, our findings underscore the effectiveness of using MCMC routines for rigorously investigating multi-parameter flavour models. ### I. Introduction

Predicting physical observables is a central objective in physics, serving as the ultimate test for models of fundamental flavours. Recently, significant efforts have been made to derive predictions for mass eigenstate mixing angles, phase differences, and absolute mass scales within such models. While these predictions are especially critical for emerging sub-GeV flavour models where long-baseline experiments may soon measure leptonic CP violation, they remain valuable even when direct determination of mixing phases is not yet feasible. Although the three-generation UTZ model was introduced over four years ago in arXiv:1710.01741, it has remained free of experimental exclusions. However, as the body of flavour data has expanded, it is crucial to re-evaluate the UTZ model's predictions for mass eigenstate mixing, absolute masses, and CP-violating phases in light of this increased data volume.

Although we previously employed analytical techniques to derive estimates for these quantities in arXiv:1710.01741, those approaches relied on simplified assumptions regarding the hierarchy and structure of flavour coupling matrices and their associated coupling constants. In the current work, we enhance these analytical methods by utilizing an established algorithm to execute comprehensive scans across the model's parameter space. These scans account for the enriched experimental dataset available today. Although significant progress has been made recently in connecting kinetic theory to various hydrodynamic formalisms, one critical aspect remains underexplored: the behavior of fluid perturbations with wave vectors perpendicular to the direction of bulk flow. This issue is particularly pertinent to recent advancements in heavy-ion collisions, which suggest the emergence of helical fluid dynamics. When kinetic theory is modeled via the relaxation time approximation, transverse waves are purely diffusive. However, in gravitational systems described by holographic fluid dynamics, transverse waves exhibit finite wave velocities. These findings have attracted considerable attention because they potentially explain recent observations of spin polarization in quark-gluon plasma produced at RHIC and LHC. Unfortunately, standard causal first-order hydrodynamics incorrectly predicts spinning particles in expanding quark-gluon matter. Since the perpendicular component of the heat flux (or superfluid velocity in Bose-Einstein condensates) generates spin, the presence of spinning particles implies a non-vanishing transverse flow component. Our study demonstrates that this component emerges in both kinetic theory and the specific divergence-type causal relativistic hydrodynamics formalism considered. This confirms the existence of waves with finite velocity in a model connected to kinetic theory and validates the emergence of such waves in holographic fluid dynamics, providing a bridge between the two approaches. These results indicate that the tensor stress-energy component present in kinetic theory and holographic dynamics can be reconstructed from general principles, specifically by enforcing consistency with kinetic theory. The ultimate goal of this research area is to develop a framework for determining when testimony implicitly contained within an action is already known to the government. While this paper adopts a narrower scope, it introduces a framework for defining actions where all implicit testimony is, by construction, a foregone conclusion. Our methodology places the burden of proof on the government to show that it is not relying on the respondent's "truthtelling."

Leveraging original legal analysis alongside precise computer science formalisms, we introduce "demonstrability" as a core concept for characterizing compelled acts. Furthermore, we provide a language to assess whether a compelled action meaningfully achieves the government's objectives as effectively as desired. We then apply these definitions to evaluate the compellability of various cryptographic primitives, including decryption, multifactor authentication, commitment schemes, and hash functions. Notably, our framework yields a new conclusion regarding compelled decryption in scenarios involving deniable encryption: while the government may compel the act, the respondent remains free to choose any password. Consequently, the resulting message is not a confession but rather noise indistinguishable from encryptions produced by the respondent's voluntary use of a deniable encryption scheme.

In this study, we trained GNNs to learn time series data from a specific nonlinear dynamical system known as the belief propagation algorithm. Our analysis revealed that the learned representations and model components have straightforward interpretations that align with the fundamental properties of probabilistic inference. We successfully developed a "graph translator" that maps statistical interactions in belief propagation to the parameters of the trained network. Ultimately, our graph translator establishes a surprising equivalence between the hidden states of a trained GNN and magnetization in the physical approach to probabilistic inference. We demonstrate strong nonlocality for two specific sets of multipartite orthogonal product states of qubits and qudits, which had previously been shown to lack remote distinguishability even with prior classical communication. This finding reveals strong quantum nonlocality in a scenario where only weak quantum nonlocality was known, thereby advancing the study of quantum correlations across multiple parties.

In the standard Bell scenario, parties perform measurements on shared quantum states to reveal nonlocality. Since its inception, research has focused on how strongly nonlocal a quantum state can be. A maximally entangled bipartite state exhibits strong nonlocality, allowing its parties to distinguish among four local orthogonal measurements without classical communication. However, certain sets of four-bipartite orthogonal product states can be distinguished only with minimal classical communication, a phenomenon termed "steerable nonlocality." We investigate the strong and steerable nonlocal characteristics of two sets of four-partite orthogonal product states of qubits and qudits, which were recently found to be remotely distinguishable without classical communication. Our results confirm that these product states exhibit both strong and steerable nonlocality, indicating that the strong quantum correlations inherent in these states enable the remote identification of their shared quantum state type. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the distinct nature of quantum and classical correlations in multipartite systems.

Targets fall into two categories: "new sources," which have not been observed before, and "monitoring sources," which are already in the database. Existing target acceptance strategies are often simple, such as allocating new source quotas uniformly across all known sources and monitoring source quotas based on the total number of sources. This uniform, risk-averaged allocation does not necessarily optimize data utility for scientific purposes. We propose a more advanced acceptance algorithm that treats these source types distinctly. Our method calculates new source quotas using a top-K approach within several magnitude bins, while monitoring source quotas are derived from the application's magnitude limit. Although this approach is not optimal globally, it is sufficient to allow astronomers to allocate resources for applications with varying priorities and explore diverse data acquisition strategies to meet specific information needs. The resulting acceptance curves for KMSC demonstrate higher data utility, offering valuable insights for the mission. This work

Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL), applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework initially establishes two distinct CL graphs to precisely define positive and negative pairs, followed by the determination of a projection matrix through the minimization of a contrastive loss function. Furthermore, the approach integrates both similar and dissimilar samples to harmonize unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, the study proposes three methodologies: an unsupervised contrastive learning approach, along with two distinct supervised contrastive learning methods. Extensive numerical experiments conducted across five real-world datasets confirm the validity and efficacy of the proposed framework and its constituent methods. Finally, the research discusses potential future extensions involving multi-view data and transfer learning. This work aims to clarify the commonalities and distinctions among various existing contrastive learning methods from a theoretical standpoint.

This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs.
