While unlabeled surveillance footage is plentiful and easy to acquire, effectively leveraging it to learn meaningful ReID representations remains unclear. Specifically, most existing unsupervised and domain adaptation ReID approaches rely solely on public datasets with labels stripped for experimentation. Moreover, constrained by limited data volumes, these methods often depend on fine-tuning with unlabeled data from the target domain to achieve satisfactory results. Drawing inspiration from recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification via contrastive learning, we propose learning ReID representations exclusively from extensive unlabeled surveillance video. Utilizing off-the-shelf pedestrian detection tools, we implement contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels. Combined with a principal component analysis step that leverages freely available camera labels, our evaluation on a large-scale unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance among unsupervised methods that do not utilize any training data from the testing domain. Additionally, accuracy increases with dataset size, indicating substantial potential for future improvements with even larger and more diverse data collections. In contrast to recent long-range tracking initiatives, our approach achieves comparable performance on a specific sub-task within that task—panoramic surveillance ReID—but operates within significantly less time. This work not only provides a large-scale unlabeled dataset but also offers evaluation results across various baseline methods. These findings aim to inspire future research into utilizing large scales of unlabeled data for video ReID, potentially yielding even greater accuracy when supplemented with minimal target domain labeling. The source code and models are available at: https://github.com/Clearer2005/ReID-from-large-scale-unlabeled-surveillance-video.

The framework integrates a nonlinear threshold regression specification to account for the leverage effect and capture the simultaneous dependence between observed realized measures and latent volatility. Model estimation utilizes an adapted Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach, with validity confirmed through a simulation study. An empirical analysis further evaluates the framework's effectiveness by forecasting the 1% and 2.5% Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall across six market indices using two distinct out-of-sample periods. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework yields competitive tail risk forecasts compared to standard GARCH and Realized-GARCH models. Additionally, a analysis of forecast evaluation metrics reveals that the framework's performance varies depending on the specific risk metric employed and the selected forecasting horizon. Finally, a portmanteau test confirms that the residual errors adhere to independent and identically distributed normal distributions. This research carries significant implications for practitioners and contributes to the body of knowledge regarding financial market risk management. Furthermore, the anticipated decline in global liquidity following the end of central bank unconventional monetary policies in early 2023 necessitates re-estimating both the model and the empirical findings to assess their continued relevance. These conclusions will be communicated to the study's co-authors via preprint servers.

While definitive proof of such a signal in pulsar timing residuals remains absent, future acquisitions of enhanced and expanded datasets are anticipated to yield a statistically significant detection. Stochastic algorithms are employed to explore vast parameter spaces and derive inferences from this data. This study aims to eliminate biases stemming from sampler stochasticity during the inference phase. We evaluate various nested sampler configurations against the widely utilized Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, assessing both their performance on the pulsar timing array parameter space and their computational efficiency on identical datasets. Although consistent parameter estimates are obtained across different sampling algorithms, we recommend implementing two distinct samplers for future robustness checks. This approach will facilitate cross-validation between methods while ensuring realistic execution times. Notably, we observe that dynamical sampler configurations outperform MCMC when applied to the full parameter space; however, these same configurations struggle in scenarios involving multiple nested sampler depths. We attribute this discrepancy to excessive jump sizes between samples, which result in poor acceptance rates. To address this, we propose implementing hyper-cubical jumps within the dynamic sampler to optimize its performance across all testing environments. We emphasize that employing multiple stochastic samplers to draw robust inferences from pulsar timing arrays is crucial for achieving meaningful results as data volumes continue to expand. In the current data landscape, our findings indicate that PTA parameter estimation is dominated by stochastic sampler performance rather than likelihood evaluation. We contend that similar sampling strategies should be applied to upcoming data releases from the NANOGrav 15pc, PTAConsortium, and EPTA datasets. As this research represents an investigation into the robustness of conclusions regarding the recently announced PTA signal using enhanced sampling methods, it does not assign probability mass to competing hypotheses. We urge researchers to remain open-minded regarding the current origins of the observed PTA signature. We advise against prematurely restricting the parameter space, as doing so risks introducing biases into the estimates and uncertainties of competing models. We conclude by providing open-source software access to the code utilized in this study. We note that the software dependencies and data volumes involved in running this code on the complete parameter space may impact its usability for researchers not familiar with pulsar timing arrays. We advise readers to examine the parameter space dimensions and the characteristics of the data files before attempting to execute this code in their own investigations. In this work, we employ real-time lattice QCD to investigate quark correlations in mesons, focusing on the charged pion. We measure these correlations across different distances between the quark and antiquark and at various times. Our results for equal-time correlations align with lattice data from previous studies by other groups. We also analyze the contribution of quark-gluon Compton scattering to quark correlations in the charged pion. Our findings support the view that contact interactions between quarks and the photon dominate quark correlations in the charged pion. We extend these contact interaction arguments to describe quark correlations in other mesons and discuss their implications for parton distribution functions (PDFs). We further compare our contacts interactions in the charged pion with PDFs of the neutral pion, demonstrating that the contact interaction term in the equal-time correlation function of the neutral pion vanishes. Finally, we relate our quark correlation findings to previous observations of spin-carries in mesons. We conclude that real-time lattice QCD offers a powerful tool for exploring quark dynamics and can significantly advance our quantitative understanding of quark behavior within hadrons.

We examine contact interactions between quarks and photons in the charged pion by analyzing quark correlation functions via lattice QCD. We measure these interactions as functions of light-quark mass and non-spacial separations between the quark and antiquark. Our results confirm that contact interactions dominate in the heavy-quark limit of the pion and quantify these interactions in the physically relevant regime. We characterize these interactions in two ways: measuring their magnitude in units of $\alpha_{em}$ and determining how they depend on quark flavor. We find that the correlation of a valence quark with the electromagnetic current is well described by the correlation of its valence antiquark with the same current. We also explore the feasibility of studying contact interactions in other two-quark mesons. Our findings support the dominance of contact interactions in the charge radius

analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine models of accretion evolution, these models are essential for calculating the derived evolution of the system's spectral energy distribution. In this study, we apply time-evolving accretion rate models to generate evolutionary tracks for both the accreted material and the radiative output. We then compare these tracks against extensive numerical simulations of the chemical evolution of accreted material from the eXtreme Accretion accretion flow simulators and the radiative output from TenChems tenchems observations datasets. This comparison serves two purposes: first, to determine if the evolutionary tracks can reproduce the simulated accreted material's chemical composition, and second, to assess if they can capture the observed radiative output from protoplanetary disks. The results indicate that the tenchems derived accreted material's chemical composition is successfully reproduced when an extinction value of $A_V=5$ is applied to the transition from the viscous to the dead zone in the most chemically complex mixtures. However, the tenchems observed radiative output is not fully reproduced. Specifically, the tracks fail to replicate the strength of the CO ro-vibrational emission for low-mass stars accreting at high rates, for high-mass stars at low accretion rates, and for all systems with dust depletion. Conversely, the tracks successfully reproduce the tenchems observed molecular line output for intermediate cases. We conclude that the proposed accretion rate models can effectively represent the evolutionary track of accreted material's chemical composition under the specified conditions and can reasonably approximate the observed radiative output for systems with and without depletion. Nevertheless, significant improvements are necessary to accurately capture the strength of the CO ro-vibrational emission across a broad range of masses and accretion rates. These findings underscore the importance of considering accretion flows when studying protoplanetary disks and emphasize the need to integrate time-evolving accretion rate models into spectral energy distribution calculations. Ultimately, such integration is crucial for enhancing observations of accreted material in low-mass, high-accretion-rate protoplanetary disks.

We surveyed a representative U.S. sample, asking participants to make redistribution choices after observing worker outcomes and distinguishing whether luck amplified effort ("lucky opportunities") or directly determined income ("lucky outcomes"). The results show that people reduce their redistribution efforts and become less responsive to shifts in luck's significance when "lucky opportunities" are present. These insights inform models aiming to predict redistribution attitudes and offer an explanation for the divergence between laboratory findings on support for redistribution and actual U.S. inequality trends. Furthermore, our approach provides novel empirical evidence supporting the "deservedness" model of redistribution; specifically, we find that when luck does not alter who succeeds, individuals perceive less moral obligation to compensate those left behind, even if they were not the primary cause of others' success. Finally, we propose that the nature of luck's impact on opportunity and outcome is more crucial for beliefs about deservedness than previously recognized. This insight is supported by the increased redistribution of "pure" luck-based income compared to income from other sources, and the lower support for redistribution among Americans whose success is not influenced by luck relative to peers. These conclusions hold even when controlling for alternative explanations rooted in beliefs about intent and risk. Our findings also align with an existing field experiment where treatment groups were informed that luck played no role in opportunity or outcome. We further present evidence that the "deservedness" interpretation offers a distinct explanation from other dominant theories. This research extends prior work by demonstrating that the interaction between luck and effort is not the sole driver of redistribution attitudes and offers a new behavioral justification for the separation of primary and secondary effects of luck. This perspective is operationalized through a simple model of redistribution, offering testable implications for scenarios involving match production functions. I examined these issues using an online survey of representative U.S. samples. Our results indicate that individuals lessen both their redistribution of pure luck and its sensitivity to economic significance. This analysis explores these findings within a framework of deservedness, contrasts them with other prevailing models of redistribution, and applies these concepts to explain trends in U.S. inequality. We also provide evidence that these effects are not driven by intent or risk. Our approach offers both an behavioral foundation and a formal model for the distinction between primary and secondary effects of luck. This paper investigates these dynamics across various functional forms of opportunity and outcome match production. Our methodology involved online surveys of a representative U.S. population. Over the past decade, significant research has focused on modeling this data influence, often by calculating the Shapley value of each example relative to metrics like validation accuracy and fairness. We introduce DataScope (ease.ml/datascope), the first system capable of efficiently computing Shapley values across an entire end-to-end ML pipeline, with a focus on applications in ML data debugging. Our approach begins with a novel algorithmic framework designed for "canonical pipelines," defined as a positive relational algebra query followed by a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) classifier. We demonstrate that for many subfamilies of these canonical pipelines, Shapley value computation can be achieved in polynomial time (PTIME), a stark contrast to the exponential complexity required for general cases. Practically, we approximate arbitrary sklearn pipelines using canonical pipelines as proxies. Extensive experiments highlight various use cases and utilities, revealing that DataScope is up to four orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods while maintaining comparable, and often superior, effectiveness in data debugging. Our code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/mlsystems-group/datascope.

We present DataScope (ease.ml/datascope), the first system capable of efficiently calculating Shapley values for individual data points within an entire end-to-end machine learning (ML) pipeline. This capability is essential for developing robust data debugging tools that can assess both model performance and data quality. Our approach relies on a family of "canonical pipelines," a class of practical architectures including random forests, margin-based classifiers, and ML services with in-memory databases. By leveraging their structural properties, we offer both a general algorithm and specific algorithms that are proven to run in polynomial time (PTIME) for certain pipeline subclasses. These findings offer a foundational method for addressing a wide range of end-to-end ML queries, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art solutions in both speed and, in some instances, quality.

on deriving effective multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, a crucial step for deploying multi-agent systems in real-world scenarios. However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a gradient descent method that lowers dependence on neighboring agents' observations and rewards through masked cross-attention mechanisms. Experimental results on vector addition and StarCraft II multi-agent control tasks demonstrate that our approach yields significantly superior online evaluation scores and exhibits enhanced robustness across different offline data configurations compared to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our method successfully prevents agents from inheriting suboptimal random policies even when a large volume of such data is mixed into the dataset, ultimately achieving consistent medium-quality performance.

We address the challenge of view-independent automatic heart valve segmentation using echocardiographic images. Unlike prior methods that achieve segmentation across views by modeling valve appearance and acoustical characteristics across different echocardiographic angles, our approach focuses solely on general valve shape. We propose a novel network architecture called the View-independent Automatic Heart valve Segmentation Network (VAHS-NET). This design employs encoder-decoder pathways with residual connections, alongside additional modules for processing both raw image data and edge-derived information. Through extensive experiments on a private dataset comprising four distinct echocardiographic views, we show that our method outperforms recent state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we evaluated the model's generalization capabilities by testing it on unseen views, confirming its view-independent nature. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/AliRezaei98/VAHS-NET.

During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed signal to calculate the responsibility of each GMM component. The feedback transmitted to the BS comprises the index of the component with the highest responsibility, allowing the BS to select the corresponding codebook entry. Simulation results indicate that this proposed design and feedback scheme surpass conventional Lloyd clustering-based algorithms, particularly in scenarios with reduced pilot overhead. To the best of our knowledge, GMM-based codebook construction has not been previously reported in literature. While the BS incurs a higher computational burden due to the complexity of GMM responsibility calculation, this overhead is offset by the lower processing requirements at the MT and reduced backhaul feedback dimensions. Ultimately, the primary objective is to minimize total network overhead rather than to assign computational tasks exclusively to the BS or MT. Furthermore, we observe that, to some extent, the MT implicitly remains aware of the GMM distribution even when not directly responsible for its calculation. Notably, this feedback mechanism requires no modifications to standard transmission protocols, as codebook entries are universally applicable. Future enhancements could involve implicit optimization of the GMM (such as adding or removing components) based on channel statistics, or enabling the MT to perform responsibility calculation to offload BS processing, with the BS then re-estimating the GMM from an extended time window at the cost of slightly reduced feedback rate accuracy. Additionally, since this work assumes perfect self-interference cancellation, the same approach is expected to be applicable to full-duplex systems. This paper is structured as follows: Section II outlines the system model, followed by the description of the proposed feedback scheme in Section III. Section IV presents simulation results, and Section V concludes the study.

Recently, self-cleaning phenomena have been reported in quasi-periodic robust currents on a honeycomb lattice for both fermions and bosons. However, the mechanisms driving such self-cleaning in three-dimensional (3D) robust crosscurrents have remained unexplored. Through an analytical analysis of our 3D robust crosscurrents, we reveal a novel self-cleaning effect for bosons on a 3D cubic honeycomb lattice. Additionally, we provide an analytical explanation for the previously observed self-cleaning effect in quasi-periodic robust currents on a honeycomb lattice. This confirms that both robustness and self-cleaning effects occur in both generic and quasi-periodic 1D and 3D robust crosscurrents for bosons and fermions. Consequently, the mechanisms underlying the self-cleaning of robust currents are now clearly understood in both 1D and 3D systems.

. Over the last century, scientific literature—the primary conduit for sharing knowledge among researchers—has experienced exponential expansion. Although numerous tangible metrics, such as citations, impact factors, and the g-index, are frequently employed to quantify paper influence and scientific productivity from various angles, the relationship between productivity and the actual volume of knowledge remains poorly understood. Specifically, it is unclear how the knowledge value and quantity of papers evolve as a discipline develops, raising the critical question of whether high scientific productivity necessarily equates to a large knowledge base. Addressing this, we leverage extensive literature on academic journals and conferences to compile a dataset of 188 million papers spanning 19 categories from 1950 to 2017. We define "knowledge value" and "knowledge quantity" based on text similarity within each field and discipline, then trace their evolution over time. Our methodology is uniquely robust, enabling the calculation of these metrics across such a vast dataset. Our key findings indicate that while knowledge value shows only minor fluctuations, both knowledge quantity and paper productivity exhibit exponential growth. Most significantly, our analysis reveals that high paper productivity does not always translate to extensive knowledge. Furthermore, in the extreme tails of the distribution, papers with higher citation counts contain less knowledge, suggesting that highly influential work often builds upon, rather than contributes to, existing knowledge. Finally, we discuss the critical role of text-based metrics in enhancing our understanding of academic literature. Our code and data are publicly accessible.

Governments and research funding agencies invest billions of dollars in open-access publishing to make scientific literature freely available to the public. However, there is a concerning hypothesis that high-impact journals may be capturing the public by offering less accessible content in their open-access offerings. By utilizing text similarity, we derive a readability score for millions of papers across 19 distinct fields of study from 1999 to 2017. Our analysis demonstrates that papers in the world's top 100 most-cited journals are progressively becoming harder to read, a trend that is accelerating in the top 100 open-access papers within those same journals. Conversely, a significant deviation is observed in the world's top 100 most-cited preprints, which have become substantially easier to read over time. These results highlight a worrying phenomenon where the public may be attracted to the prestige of prestigious journals only to encounter content of diminishing quality, a scenario unlikely to occur with open-access preprints. Our data is publicly available.

The discovery of the quantum Hall effect (QHE) in two-dimensional (2D) electron gases marked a seminal moment in condensed matter physics. Subsequent experiments have expanded the phenomenon across various topological material platforms, notably including topological insulators (TIs). These discoveries unveiled the unexpected emergence of one-way, directionally propagating electrons on the edges of 2D conductors—a hallmark of the quantum anomalous Hall effect (QAHE). This study tackles the challenge of generating safe CAV trajectories in such environments, with a specific focus on preventing rear-end collisions when preceding HDVs approach yellow or red signal phases. We introduce a predictive control framework that utilizes a recursive least squares algorithm to estimate the real-time driving behavior of leading HDVs, subsequently applying this estimation to compute safety-conscious trajectories over a finite horizon. The efficacy of our proposed framework is verified through numerical simulations, alongside an analysis of its robustness. Furthermore, we establish a minimum speed threshold below which our framework guarantees safety; simulations confirm that the framework remains robust even when this threshold is exceeded. We also extend the framework to scenarios involving multiple preceding HDVs and demonstrate its practical application for controlling CAV platoons approaching an intersection under a leading green signal. Ultimately, the findings from this paper contribute to enhancing intersection throughput and smoothness while ensuring superior safety.

The rapid advancement and widespread adoption of connected automated vehicles (CAVs) are significantly expected to address major highway safety concerns and optimize overall traffic flow. However, integrating a high penetration rate of CAVs into mainstream traffic flows remains a major hurdle. This paper examines automated vehicle control strategies for through-moves at signalized intersections. We propose a model predictive control (MPC) approach designed to keep CAVs moving continuously through the intersection without stopping, even when the incoming signal is yellow or red. The primary objective of this MPC framework is to derive feasible and robust trajectories that leverage gap-seeking behaviors, thereby minimizing impacts on surrounding traffic while adhering to safety and comfort constraints. To validate the practicality of our approach, we conduct simulations around a real-world signalized intersection. Additionally, we perform robustness tests and extend the framework to accommodate varying driver behaviors and scenarios involving CAV platoons. Unlike traditional methods that often necessitate extensive human intervention or tuning, the parameters of our proposed framework can be easily determined through driving simulations. Our results demonstrate that the MPC-based automated control can effectively manage individual through-moves, yielding an average improvement in intersection throughput and a reduction in waiting times for existing traffic.

However, this reliance on vast amounts of data hinders the deployment of NLP models in low-resource scenarios or novel domains, where acquiring labeled text demands substantial time, financial investment, and expertise. Recently, researchers have investigated data augmentation techniques to enhance data efficiency in NLP. Despite this, there has been no comprehensive empirical review of data augmentation specifically for NLP under limited labeled data conditions, creating uncertainty regarding the efficacy of various methods in different contexts. This paper presents an empirical survey of recent advancements in data augmentation for NLP within low-data regimes. It summarizes the methodological landscape—including token-level, sentence-level, adversarial, and hidden-space augmentations—and conducts experiments across 11 datasets spanning topics and news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Based on these findings, the study offers conclusions to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentation strategies for specific settings and discusses existing challenges and future prospects for limited data learning in NLP. Given the rapid evolution of this field, additional relevant work likely exists that was not included in this survey.

**Introduction**

The recent surge in neural architecture and model performance has transformed Natural Language Processing (NLP). Techniques leveraging pre-trained word and sentence representations, alongside attention mechanisms and transformers, have set records across numerous benchmarks. Pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT have recently achieved unprecedented performance across a wide range of NLP tasks. Despite these successes, PLMs perform suboptimally when trained on small datasets, as their reliance on large-scale labeled data causes overfitting with limited samples, and their scale restricts experimentation with hyper-parameters under constrained data conditions. Consequently, data augmentation has emerged as a viable strategy to improve model performance when labeled data is scarce. Although previously explored, data augmentation has recently gained significant attention in PLMs, particularly since BERT's release. Various architectures for fine-tuning BERT have demonstrated that augmentation can significantly boost performance even with small training sets. Recently, Alsentzer et al. demonstrated effective disease vector modeling for medical NLP using limited data through careful data augmentation. Furthermore, Pham et al. showed that combining other methods with data augmentation can substantially enhance clinical note vector representations for limited data.

Across the transition, we observed a significant redistribution of spectral weight, transferring from high to low binding energy regimes over a broad energy scale. Notably, the total spectral weight in the low-energy regime is not conserved across the MIT, signaling a violation of spectral weight sum rules—a hallmark of strongly correlated systems. Our results confirm that the MIT in this system is driven by strong correlations, with electron-electron interactions playing a central role. Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. A key innovation of this scheme is its ability to handle nonconforming meshes regarding blocking fractures, a capability enabled by the Dirac-$\delta$ formulation. Additionally, the numerical method yields locally conservative velocity approximations and generates a symmetric positive definite linear system defined solely on pressure degrees of freedom located at the mesh skeleton. Benchmark tests in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's performance, with results showing it to be highly competitive against existing literature approaches. The discussion concludes that this strategy is well-suited for integration into large-scale reservoir simulators. This strategy was implemented within the new OLIVET reservoir simulator, part of the Tronit project (https://github.com/Tronit-project/Olivet).

The device comprises a superconducting film deposited on a metal exhibiting intrinsic spiral magnetism, which arises from either competing isotropic exchanges or asymmetric Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya exchange in crystals lacking central symmetry. Depending on the anisotropy, this metal's magnetization can transition from a spiral to a uniform state, as observed in Ho and Er, or align with the spiral direction, as seen in B20-type crystals like MnSi, (Fe,Co)Si, and FeGe. This nonuniform magnetic ordering governs the emergence of long-range triplet superconducting correlations under strong exchange fields, thereby influencing the nature of the proximity effect. We demonstrate that magnetic control of the spin-valve behavior is also achievable at moderately low exchange fields—typically insufficient for long-range triplet correlations—due to an orientation-dependent averaging mechanism of magnetic inhomogeneities relative to the Cooper pair scale. Our numerical simulations indicate that the spin-valve effect is actually enhanced at these moderately low exchange fields when the exchange splitting in the spiral magnet matches the superconducting gap and the spiral period is less than or equal to $2\pi$ times the superconducting coherence length within the magnet. Furthermore, we show that the spin-valve effect can be switched on and off in the spiral magnet by applying a static magnetic field with a magnitude comparable to the internal exchange field but a period shorter than or equal to $10\pi$ times the superconducting coherence length in the magnet. These findings offer additional proof of the significance of magnetic inhomogeneities and suggest that superconducting spin-valves utilizing metals with intrinsic spiral magnetism could outperform those using uniform-magnetization magnets. Consequently, such devices may be viable for applications requiring extremely sensitive magnetic detection.

We examine the influence of a finite lifetime on quasiparticles in superconducting lead (Pb) adsorbed on graphite, using spectroscopic data from scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy. Our results indicate that the quasiparticle lifetime is approximately 1 picosecond at 4.2 K and remains roughly constant at higher temperatures. This observation implies that the superconducting coherence length in Pb/Graphite is around 20 Å, significantly shorter than previous estimates, and remains largely insensitive to quasiparticle scattering due to impurities or interface roughness. These conclusions are relevant to superconducting spin-triplet applications, including superconducting spin-valves.

In many scientific fields, researchers compare a null model against an alternative model that incorporates a feature under investigation, typically assessing a p-value to determine rejection of the null. A primary challenge with this approach is defining an alternative model that is both realistic and free of the specific feature being tested. For instance, in neuroscience, analyzing the impact of a drug on neural activity often involves a null model with no drug effect and an alternative model assuming an additive effect. However, this alternative model may fail to capture multiplicative changes, non-additive interactions, or temporal dynamics, rendering it an poor representation of the data-generating process when the drug has complex effects. To resolve this, we advocate for comparing the null model directly to a prior-rich model that remains otherwise agnostic. This approach offers a straightforward method for computing Bayes factors, efficiently quantifying evidence for the null without relying on a simplified alternative. We validate this framework using a neural data example and compare it to other methods for null hypothesis testing. Additionally, we explore extending this framework to incorporate parameter estimation uncertainty when calculating Bayes factors.

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Our analysis of DiscSense confirms that competitor discourse relation theories are robustly supported by text but reveals that current theories of discourse relations topologically map only a small subset of the relations inherent in DiscSense. Furthermore, we observe that information in discourses facilitating marker prediction may assist in disambiguating word senses, a finding that discards the common assumption that word senses are context-independent. Finally, we suggest that top-level discourse relation theories should be regarded as descriptive rather than explanatory. In this context, we propose looking for generative mappings between discourses and markers, a hypothesis supported by evidence indicating that marker prediction F scores improve when applied to sentences with frequently encountered discourse relations. We introduce a similar dataset, DiscSense-ZR, where inferred markers are labeled with labels from a target discourse relation theory. As expected, this information proves correct slightly often than the raw text, although not often enough to justify relying on such labels for research within that specific theory. Information enabling marker prediction F scores improve upon those in DiscSense-ZR, which we believe may be suitable for constructing a discourse relation theory capable of categorizing all discourses in large-scale corpora. In summary, we contend that information inherent in discourses regarding both meaning and context is fundamental to language. Therefore, we advocate for bottom-up characterizations of discourse markers in information-rich tasks like translation, a practice we believe has been too long neglected.

To overcome these limitations, we develop a multi-task learning framework. Although prior studies have pinpointed specific properties of complex systems that enable explosive synchronization, these efforts have largely been conducted in an ad-hoc manner. In this work, we establish an exact criterion for explosive synchronization within coupled phase oscillator ensembles by examining the essential link between structural and dynamical disorder. This finding represents a pivotal advancement in disentangling the interconnected characteristics of complex systems that drive abrupt phase transitions and bistability in both biological and engineered contexts. Specifically, we demonstrate that disorder-induced explosive synchronization arises from a bifurcation sequence involving meta-stable chimera states. These findings offer a precise framework for investigating the explosive synchronization phenomenon in complex complex systems. Based on this understanding, we propose potential strategies to induce explosive synchronization in chimera states, which are of significant interest in the research of brain dynamics. Finally, we present a proposed experiment utilizing an ensemble of mechanical pendulums to achieve disorder-induced explosive synchronization in chimera states.

# Introduction

The phenomenon of explosive transitions—characterized by a sudden, non-graded shift between distinct system states—has garnered substantial recent attention. This type of abrupt transition is prevalent in nature and man-made complex systems, often leading to catastrophic outcomes in power grids, socio-economic systems, and cardiovacular systems. In coupled oscillator ensembles, explosive transitions manifest as explosive synchronization (ES), where a system moves from disordered to ordered motion instantly as a control parameter, such as coupling strength, increases. While recent investigations have identified various factors triggering ES, a unifying theoretical framework remains lacking.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood of local minimizers. Our proofs rely on a detailed landscape analysis of a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, serving as a pivotal intermediate step. Additionally, our conclusions rest on a standalone result identifying that the geodesic ball centered at $Y$ with a radius equal to one-third of $Y$'s least singular value forms a geodesically convex set under the Riemannian quotient geometry. This specific locus of geodesic convexity appears to possess independent significance. Our main analysis builds upon, though does not require, a general lemma characterizing the geometry's intrinsic non-positive curvature. Finally, we conclude with an experimental section providing qualitative support for our theoretical insights through additional search spaces. In large language model (LLM)-based prompt engineering, selecting the most effective natural language prompt from a pool of candidates is crucial for model performance, yet it remains a challenging and under-researched task. To address this, we propose a novel and systematic method for automatically engineering and selecting optimal prompts. Specifically, we utilize a reinforcement learning framework with policy gradient methods to train an encoder-decoder model that encodes prompts and selects high-performing ones based on model performance on specific tasks. Furthermore, to improve efficiency, we integrate this approach with tree search methods to more broadly explore the prompt space. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique successfully engineers state-of-the-art prompt models on both the reasoning task GSM8K and the natural language inference task MNLI. These findings suggest that language modeling techniques can be effectively applied to optimize task-specific performance within the prompt engineering domain.

The extent of this transmission relies on how virus-laden droplets evolve spatially and temporally as they move through the atmosphere under influences from gravity, air resistance, and atmospheric turbulence. This study presents general equations for the $n$-th moment evolution of droplet size distributions, applicable to populations of droplets varying in diameter, density, and initial position. Our findings indicate that droplets take approximately 15 seconds to settle due to gravity, suggesting that infected people can transmit droplets from both respiratory sources for about 1 minute. However, quantifying errors and uncertainties within NN-based inference is significantly more complex than in conventional approaches. This complexity arises not only from aleatoric uncertainty linked to noisy data but also from epistemic sources such as limited data, NN hyperparameters, overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors, and model misspecification. While recent studies have touched upon uncertainty quantification (UQ) in NNs, there remains a lack of systematic investigation into effective and efficient methods for quantifying total uncertainty, even for basic function approximation. Furthermore, research on solving partial differential equations and learning operator mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs is particularly scarce. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, both novel and established solution techniques, evaluation metrics, and post-hoc improvement strategies. To validate the framework's applicability and reliability, we conduct an extensive comparative study testing various methods on prototype problems, including those with mixed input-output data and high-dimensional stochastic scenarios. Additionally, the Appendix provides a detailed description of all employed UQ methods, which will facilitate future comparisons. Through this detailed framework and rigorous evaluation, the work establishes a robust foundation for advancing solution frontiers in diverse scenarios such as parameter inference, optimization, and learning operator mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces. The primary finding emphasizes the critical necessity of incorporating epistemic uncertainty when solving problems beyond the NN's training distribution. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that alternative evaluation metrics are essential for accurately assessing the performance of UQ methods. Finally, the study highlights the significant potential of enhancing self-isolated surrogates to improve overall inference results. Neural operators, methods, and frameworks presented here provide a foundation for future advancements in uncertainty-aware learning of functional mappings. To ensure reliability in real-world deployments, these systems must remain robust against hardware soft errors that corrupt platform memory. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier CNNs by showing that range supervision acts as a highly dependable fault detector and mitigator for relevant bit flips, specifically within an eight-exponent floating-point format. We address the reliable real-time detection of specific objects within video streams. Our method begins by generating a coarse object mask using the widely adopted SIAMRPM algorithm. From this mask, we extract, track, and resize consistent, in-focus patches of the target object. These patches are then evaluated individually via forward passes through the CNN to determine if the object is present. Our approach, which leverages both spatial and temporal information, surpasses conventional end-to-end methods like Softmax and sigmoid layers in both accuracy and safety. This technique is applicable to any conventional object detection system where individual object reliability is crucial, and our implementation is available as open-source code.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in image classification, yet they remain susceptible to adversarial examples that deceive standard classifiers. This paper examines whether human visual perception (HVP) can reliably detect these misleading changes in natural images. While prior research suggests HVP can spot altered digits in Captcha tests, our study focuses on complex scenes. We begin by showing that humans can indeed identify altered objects, even when the changes are sub-threshold for automated detectors. However, we also note that HVP is not infallible and can be tricked by strongly adversarial perturbations. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, we propose a simple yet effective regularization strategy that integrates human-like feature detectors into the network's architecture. Our experiments confirm that this regularization not only emulates human visual features but also significantly improves resistance to adversarial attacks. Finally, we prove that training with such feature detectors can enhance overall classification accuracy

Briefly, netting offers an alternative to standard payment methods by establishing an agreement where parties offset mutual debts. Instead of settling all individual transactions, a direct settlement is calculated based on the net amounts owed between two or more parties. This paper introduces a suite of graph algorithms designed to determine optimal netting solutions suitable for the scale of a national economy. These algorithms deliver results efficiently and have been validated using invoice data from the Romanian Ministry of Economy. Our findings demonstrate that classical graph algorithms remain effective in addressing critical modern challenges. Furthermore, understanding netting dynamics is essential for regulating the financial system and enhancing transaction transparency. In the Romanian context, this process is known as "recalculare." While Borsuc previously explored simpler scenarios involving graph algorithms for netting, those methods were insufficient for larger datasets. Our work extends his research by resolving these scalability issues. The techniques presented here also apply to other graph-based problems, such as the traveling salesman route optimization. Finally, the paper examines graph properties that can aid in solving netting scenarios, including identifying cycles and decomposing graphs into cycles and paths. The research is supported by grants from the Romanian Executive System.

In a related study, the paper addresses debt netting among a group of agents. These findings were verified on data provided by the General Directorate of Statistics and Informatics within Romania's Ministry of Economy. The paper also explores connections between netting and graph decomposition into cycles and paths. The authors note that while many problems are classified as NP-complete, practical solutions often exist for real-world instances. Additional context can be found in related literature.

significantly advanced research in dialogue state tracking (DST), yet it contains substantial noise in its state annotations that hinders the robust training of DST models. Although refined versions (MultiWOZ 2.1–2.4) have recently emerged, they still suffer from numerous noisy labels, particularly within the training sets, and manually correcting these issues is expensive. Rather than focusing on further improving annotation quality, this paper introduces ASSIST (lAbel noiSe-robuSt dIalogue State Tracking), a general framework designed to train DST models robustly despite noisy labels. ASSIST operates by first generating pseudo-labels for training samples using an auxiliary model trained on a small clean dataset; these pseudo-labels are then combined with the original noisy labels to train the primary model. Theoretical analysis confirms the validity of ASSIST, and experimental results demonstrate that it boosts joint goal accuracy in DST by up to $28.16\%$ on MultiWOZ 2.0 and $8.41\%$ on MultiWOZ 2.4 compared to training solely on vanilla noisy labels. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days, night, and areas with sparse textures. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional algorithms and existing state-of-the-art learning-based methods across various datasets. Furthermore, our system achieves a 50% reduction in computation time compared to the largest attention scope used in prior learning-based VIO approaches. Finally, we release the code for our method along with additional discussions on its efficiency, which is also accessible online. We hope our research will encourage further exploration in visual-inertial odometry. The source code for our experiments is available at: https://github.com/Cold-Heart/External-Memory-Attention-for-Visual-Inertial Odometry.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our SHOWS models exhibit isolated Fermi points in the central $k=0$ bracket and protected Fermi arcs connecting them on truncated surfaces. By deriving these SHOWS models through a general Hamiltonian deformation method, we observe that their topological features arise from the intertwined winding numbers of Hamiltonian blocks. Additionally, SHOWS models can display surface states both explicitly and implicitly, depending on the symmetry breaking caused by surface deformation. These findings expand the classification of topological semimetals within broken-symmetry systems and suggest potential realization of SHOWS in arsenene heterostructures.

Topological quantum chemistry (TQC) has recently been established to systematically uncover material topological phases by integrating symmetry-based topological classification with band-structure analysis via the symmetry indicator. This approach has successfully identified and classified various topological phases, including Dirac and Weyl semimetals (WSMs), across diverse two-dimensional (TM) and three-dimensional (TMS) materials. Building on the foundation of TQC, this letter reports the discovery of a novel symmetry indicator signaling a hidden topological WSM state in orthorhombic $AgPbSb$. Our findings indicate that this topological state emerges from electron-electron interactions resulting from the Fermi surface pocket near the $X$ point in $AgPbSb$. To the best of our knowledge, $AgPbSb$ represents the first experimental observation of a symmetry-indicated topological WSM state driven by electron-electron interactions. The theoretical framework of TQC offers an effective pathway for exploring new topological quantum states in existing material systems.

FedSA), a novel knowledge-amalgamation problem aimed at training a student model for a specific new task using multiple decentralized teacher models. These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. FedSA addresses this dilemma by enabling the creation of a specialized student model for a task different from any of the teachers' original domains. As artificial intelligence advances, an increasing number of systems are integrated into diverse real-world applications. For instance, Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) have been widely utilized in tasks such as text classification, task-specific language modeling, and machine translation. Consequently, there is a growing need for effective knowledge-amalgamation techniques to combine the capabilities of multiple pre-trained models to tackle new tasks. Recently, we observed that when incorporating the capabilities of several PLMs for a new task, it is often more effective to train a student model from scratch rather than adapting an existing student via fine-tuning. This approach, known as Student Training from Scratch (STS), has proven successful in recent studies. However, most current STS experiments utilize teachers that share the same input output (I/O) semantic space, typically meaning they were originally trained on tasks with identical input and/or output formats. Nevertheless, extending knowledge amalgamation to I/O mismatched models remains underexplored, largely due to the significant challenges such a problem introduces.

After reaching the zero-age main sequence, their global rotation slows during the main sequence phase until at least the age of the Sun, a trend that aligns with Skumanich's empirical law and facilitates gyrochronology. Recent asteroseismology studies suggest that older solar-type stars may eventually reach a transition point where rotational braking ceases. Furthermore, modern 3D numerical simulations indicate that differential rotation regimes in these stars can be classified by the Rossby number. Specifically, a "anti-solar" differential rotation pattern—characterized by fast poles and a slow equator—is predicted to occur in slow rotators (high Rossby numbers). This anti-solar configuration may help preserve angular momentum, potentially explaining the cessation of spin-down and the rotation profile in the progenitor of Type Ia supernovae. Additionally, it may aid in understanding why some middle-aged solar-type stars exhibit older surface ages via spectroscopy but younger core ages through asteroseismology.

Recent observations suggest that the progenitor of Type Ia supernovae, a carbon-white dwarf, ceases its rotational braking around 1–10 Gyr. Simultaneously, the core of this star begins to accumulate nuclear fuel, leading to an internal spin-up that eventually triggers a supernova explosion. This scenario aligns with the hypothesis that magnetic braking drives spin-down, provided the magnetic field is generated by a dynamo at a certain evolutionary stage. We propose a model where the surface differential rotation pattern is determined by the magnetic field topology. In this framework, a solar-like pattern (fast equator, slow poles) is maintained by a large-scale toroidal magnetic field, while an anti-solar pattern (fast poles, slow equator) is sustained by a large-scale poloidal field. Since both topologies can coexist in slowly rotating stars, a transition between these patterns may signal the onset of core spin-up and the impending supernova. This model is applicable to intermediate-mass stellar evolution, where a carbon-white dwarf forms after nuclear burning shells, and to the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae.

To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories. Our findings indicate that while the increase in both entropy and temperature—mandated by the zeroth law of thermodynamics—does not universally guarantee compliance with the QNEC, significant violations are impossible for baths characterized by an exponential decay of correlations. Furthermore, in the limit of highly dissipative environments, we demonstrate that an lower bound exists on the number of field species required to satisfy the QNEC, establishing that a single species is insufficient. We also note that substantial violations of the QNEC cannot occur for scalar fields. These results provide critical insights into the applicability of the QNEC to strongly dissipative, many-body quantum systems. Additionally, we examine whether the first law of thermodynamics remains valid when the QNEC is not satisfied. Our analysis reveals that for environments with power-law correlated baths, the first law of thermodynamics holds even when the QNEC is violated. Consequently, a strictly stronger condition than the QNEC is necessary to ensure an irreversible increase in entropy concomitant with an increase in temperature following a momentum quenches in a 2D holographic CFT coupled to such a power-law correlated bath. Additionally, we find that for an otherwise irrelevant deformation of CFT corresponding to a $c$-anomaly term in the first law of entanglement entropy, the first law of thermodynamics can be valid despite a significant violation of the QNEC. Finally, we establish lower bounds on the number of species of energy-momentum fields in 2D holographic theories coupled to finite size baths. These bounds are determined not only by the environment's dissipation and correlation characteristics but also by the temperature and temperature changes after the quenches. This implies that in 2D theories with finite size baths, the first law of thermodynamics can hold without the QNEC, and conversely, the QNEC can be significantly violated even when the first law of thermodynamics is satisfied. The studies presented here aim to clarify the relationship between the QNEC and the irreversibility of entropy production in the context of energy and momentum quenches in 2D holographic theories interacting with non-thermal many-body baths

The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on modeling and observations, we outline plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus from accretion to its present state. Three specific scenarios are highlighted: first, desiccation caused by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase; second, a prolonged period of surface liquid water followed by climate destabilization and a runaway greenhouse effect; and third, inefficient outgassing that retained water within the planet, trapping hydrogen in the core and oxidizing the mantle. Finally, we discuss current evidence and the future observations and missions needed to refine our understanding of Venus's history and the intricate feedback cycles operating among its interior, surface, and atmosphere across past, present, and future timescales. This work serves as a foundation for a comprehensive framework for Venus research, relevant to the upcoming Decadal Survey. The "quantum-inspired" architecture of TNs allows them to be translated into parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), a capability that has spurred recent proposals to boost TN performance using near-term quantum hardware and to create hybrid training frameworks that leverage the unique advantages of both TNs and PQCs. ### I. Introduction

The resurgence of interest in tensor network (TN) states during the last decade has been driven by their exceptional performance in addressing difficult problems across physics and machine learning. These achievements are anticipated to grow with increased computational power, as recent studies demonstrate that modern GPUs and TPUs can execute high-dimensional TN computations—tasks previously unattainable with classical supercomputers. Notably, these forward translations have sparked researchers to view certain TN states as equivalent to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), a perspective that has recently sparked intense investigation into enhancing TN performance via PQCs or, conversely, improving PQC performance using TNs. This work examines the current status of quantum circuit decomposition techniques for general TN states, with a specific focus on low-depth representations within architectures consisting of stacked two-qubit two-body unitary gates. Although not yet a fully resolved problem, solving it is essential for jointly exploiting the distinct strengths of quantum and TN methods, with our analysis highlighting particularly promising recent advancements.

is renowned for its ideal conservation properties, guaranteeing exact preservation of total mass, energy, and both linear and angular momentum up to machine precision when correctly implemented. This feature is crucial for computational astrophysics applications involving binary dynamics, mergers, and the accretion of compact objects like neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs. However, in scenarios requiring self-gravity, the computational cost of calculating all-to-all gravitational interactions scales as $N^2$, where $N$ represents the number of particles. To alleviate this cost, multilevel tree algorithms are frequently employed; these methods sacrifice some conservation accuracy to reduce complexity to $N \log N$. In this paper, we introduce a novel conserved variable based angular momentum force (CVABMF) designed for use within multilevel tree algorithms. This approach approximates the angular momentum force force per unit mass with sufficient precision to ensure rodge coherence across all decomposition levels while significantly decreasing the force error compared to standard position-based forces. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method using a simple 1D test setup with tree algorithms. Furthermore, when integrated into a 2D SPH code, the CVABMF approach approximates the exact all-to-all gravitational interaction with roughly a hundred times less computational expense than multilevel tree algorithms utilizing conventional force approximations. Although the CVABMF introduces an additional 2% overhead per particle relative to these tree algorithms, it represents approximately a tenfold reduction in computational cost when accessing magnetic field data per particle. Consequently, the overall performance improvement between adopting multilevel tree algorithms with the CVABMF and using exact all-to-all interactions is even more substantial in SPH simulations involving self-interaction forces that incorporate magnetic fields. Additionally, the spatial error term of the CVABMF force is nearly independent of the number of particles within a decomposition box, a characteristic that is highly advantageous for multilevel tree algorithms. We anticipate that this new force will be adaptable to other particle-based methods, such as grid-based schemes. In summary, the multilevel tree algorithm employing the CVABMF achieves interaction accuracy comparable to that of the exact all-to-all interaction.

Introduction Gelfand and MacPherson were pioneers in defining differential manifolds through a purely combinatorial framework. Their work remains largely underutilized today, despite its combinatorial nature offering significant advantages in defining and analyzing differential manifolds. Our approach builds upon the foundational ideas of Boardman and their extension by Stokes. Our combinatorial differential manifolds share essential properties with standard differential manifolds, such as the ability to define coordinates, vector fields, differential forms, integration, and Pontrjagin classes. While our constructions of vector fields and forms are consistent with those of Chern-Weil and Chern-Simons, our specific setup allows us to formulate a combinatorial Stokes theorem and its associated formula for Pontrjagin classes. These combinatorial structures are applicable to any setting where Chern-Weil and Chern-Simons theories can be defined, including Chern-Simons gauge theory on a manifold with boundary. We assume readers are familiar with basic differential geometry and will include necessary reviews in the relevant sections. The motivation for this study stems from the vast potential of combinatorial differential manifolds, as demonstrated in prior work [8] where they were employed to construct explicit differential forms on moduli spaces of stable graphs, which are crucial in solving differential equations relating Grothendieck's zeta values to $\pi$. Our combinatorial differential geometry provides a setting where these forms can be defined.

In recent years, simulation-based inference (SBI) has emerged as a promising method for estimating posterior distributions in complex systems where traditional likelihood calculations are infeasible. SBI trains normalizing flows to map posterior samples into a uniform distribution, enabling the estimation of posteriors given any test data. This technique is particularly valuable for cosmology, allowing for the extraction of parameters from cosmological data via SBI ComSBI without relying on model assumptions or approximations. This paper introduces the first public codebase for performing SBI on cosmological simulations. It can be applied to various problems, such as inferring initial conditions or fundamental physical constants. Our implementation features: (i) the capability to incorporate velocity fields alongside density fields for halo finding, which is crucial for studying primordial power spectrum models with enhanced small-scale power; (ii) support for multi-dimensional inference tasks, including those found in cosmology and biological systems; and (iii) multi-phase simulation pipelines that leverage the full dynamical range of $N$-body particles to enable the study of smaller halos. We demonstrate the installation process, workflow, and usage of our code through examples using the Millennium T8-3375 simulation. We also address multi-phase simulation tasks and illustrate how the code can facilitate single-run inference for tasks like estimating primordial black hole abundances. We hope this implementation assists physicists in utilizing SBI for novel multi-phase dimensional inference problems

In this paper, we employ a maximum likelihood framework to tackle the transcription of single-instrument music, addressing a limitation in previously reported deep neural network methods. By formulating the task as a sequence labeling problem, we task a recurrent neural network with predicting note-on and note-off occurrences. We demonstrate that a straightforward maximum likelihood estimation yields satisfactory results on the MUSIC-19 dataset, even when trained exclusively on two recordings. Furthermore, we examine several enhancements, including the use of marginal likelihood estimation and multi-task learning, both of which prove effective. Ultimately, this method achieves competitive performance on the recent RMC 2019 competition.

Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian algorithm to adjust the mass distribution relative to the rotation axis and solve the stationary Einstein equations using the spectral code \textsc{ESuStAr}. By incrementally increasing the specific angular momentum of fluid elements, we track the evolution from a stationary point mass to a configuration dominated by centrifugal forces. This technique enables the creation of a series of equilibrium states that can be utilized to establish analytical approximations for the density distribution in rotating stars. Furthermore, the method is versatile enough to be applied within equation of state models that include a photonic component, to time-dependent scenarios involving mass ejection or accretion, and even to Einstein-Maxwell equations for charged dust. Results from these Einstein-Maxwell calculations align well with analytical predictions for uniform line of charge distributions. Given its purely stationary and equilibrium nature, this approach may also serve as a robust initialization method for simulating dynamical processes such as type II supernovae. Finally, we provide additional discussions on various numerical aspects of the implementation. We propose a new method for producing numerically stable equilibrium states of rotating stars in general relativity. Intended for incremental evolutionary studies, the technique involves raising the degree of anisotropy of the mass distribution along the rotation axis while simultaneously solving the Einstein equations. We successfully trace the evolution of solutions from a static point mass to regimes where centrifugal effects are dominant. The approach can be adapted for radiation-filled stars and for investigations into the stability of these equilibria. Additionally, it applies to stationary problems, such as determining fundamental solutions, and to scenarios involving mass loss or gain. Our findings offer valuable insights into the structural characteristics of rotating stars and provide crucial initialization data for simulating their dynamical evolution.=======

We explicitly address and solve two optimal control problems: minimizing travel time and minimizing quadratic cost to move the swimmer between fixed positions using periodic control. By considering a single dynamic switch and leveraging the motion equations' structure, we decompose the problem into simpler sub-problems. Solving each sub-problem yields a discontinuous global solution, which is subsequently approximated by a sequence of continuous functions. Numerical simulations demonstrate that minimizing the number of switches is the optimal strategy for both cost functions. Furthermore, the findings for the minimum cost problem reveal the existence of a "paddleball" solution, a mode previously observed in larger micro-swimmers like the bacterium *Caenorhabditis elegans*. Finally, we analyze the convergence of the optimal number of switches across a range of cost function parameters. This analysis confirms that the global optimum always involves a single switch for the studied parameter set, except in the specific limit of infinite weighting for translational cost, a scenario that produces a degenerate solution. These results are consistent with the theoretical convergence properties of finite horizon optimal control problems. The presented findings may aid in both comprehending and adjusting the motion of the bi-fluid two-link swimmer. This analysis also establishes a contrast with single link swimmers, such as the bi-propeller *E. coli*, which can change direction without altering their shape. The work further serves as a benchmark for researchers employing numerical simulation methods, including indirect (Pontryagin's Maximum Principle) and direct approaches, to solve optimal control problems on more complex swimmers.

This study examines shifts in the income diversity of urban interactions across various pandemic phases, leveraging a privacy-preserving dataset of anonymized mobile network operators' connection data from four Italian cities. -mass young stellar objects (HMYSOs) often fragment into multiple self-gravitating bodies, a process that may account for recently observed episodic accretion bursts. By applying a 1D code to resolve dynamics down to the stellar surface, we post-processed prior 3D simulation results. Our findings reveal that the burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc observed in 3D models does not invariably produce powerful accretion bursts; instead, only high-density clumps that have undergone collapse and crossed the inner computational boundary generate observable bursts. The complex physics of the inner disc significantly influences these bursts in four key ways: (1) While objects in standard turbulent viscosity discs may stall at migration traps a few astronomical units from the star, those in magnetised wind-driven discs can cross these traps to create bursts matching current observations. (2) Migrating objects can interact with and alter the thermal (hydrogen ionisation) instability of the inner disc, potentially causing longer-lasting, lower-luminosity bursts in HMYSOs. (3) If the central star is bloated by prior high-accretion episodes or if the migrating object is sufficiently dense, the outcome is a merger rather than a disc-mediated burst. (4) Disruption bursts from these objects may exceed the Eddington limit, driving episodic feedback on the HMYSO environment through powerful outflows. These observations offer potential methods for investigating disc disruption on timescales of years to centuries. Additionally, we note that bursts from these merging objects may help explain the abundance of X-ray transient sources and the lack of radio emission in certain HMYSOs, while the lack of optical/IR bursts may result from optical depth effects on radiative energy or the migration of material into the stellar surface. Finally, the occurrence of super-Eddington accretion may resolve concerns regarding mass overflow in HMYSOs. These results underscore the necessity of employing code capabilities that encompass both 3D disc structure and resolved stellar surfaces in future studies.

Within this framework, we demonstrate that the asymptotic algebra and the scattering matrix fully characterize the theory, provided asymptotic completeness and standard assumptions hold. Subsequently, we derive several families of interacting wedge-local nets through a purely von Neumann algebraic approach. One specific instance aligns with the deformation of chiral CFT proposed by Buchholz, Lechner, and Summers. In another case, we successfully identify all strictly local elements. To address this gap, we present a robust methodology for numerically assessing downlink exposure from both 5G and pre-5G networks for children, teenagers, schools, and medical centers.
